div.p: GENTLEMEN, You took me into your service last December as an a.... Me. I wish to remain in that service as a journeyman. I ask no higher wages. but only a renewal of your confidence and a continuance of your kindnese. Two years ago, Irishmen living in Ireland were, for the first time, put on an equality with you in respect of the power to send men to Parliament to represent their opinions and their feelings. Last year they returned to Parliament 85 men, out of a total of IC3, pledged and determined to demand at your hands a restoration of their ancient right to a Parliament of their own in Dublin. and Greet Britain elected a large majority of men anxious to do battle for the well-being of the people against the privileges ef a class. The statement has been made that the Irish proposals wonld never have been submitted for consideration, if Id r Gladstone had been returned to power with a sufficiently large Liberal vote to supped him against the vote of the Irish party.

Let troth prevail. Mr. Gladstone In the November of last year thus warned his oountrymen : "If 5u.,11 a matter comes forward at the outset of the proceedings of the new Parliament as I have described, namely, a demand -made constitutionally by the vast majority of the representatives of Ireland, for the concession of large local powers of self-government, aocompanied with the ad- mission that the unity of the Empire is not to be impaired the magnitude of that subject will sweep into the shade for the moment, all those subjects a ordinary legislation on which or on which others, have addressed you, and the satisfactory settlement of that subject, which goes down to the very roots and foundations of our whole civil and political constitution, will become the first duty of Pardament." When Parliament met, the leaders of the Tory party, dis- appointed in their hopes of support from the new electors, de- clared once more for the old bad policy of government by force, and were ousted from offihe. Mr. Gladstone, Primo Minister for the third time, then called upon the Home of Commons to satisfy the natioual as- pirations of the Irish peop'e, and to declare for government by consent of the governed. A vote of the House of Commons rejected Mr. Gladstone's proposal; and the manhood of the three kingdoms is now called upon for a decision. I am confident that the verdict will be given in favour of a generous and a trustful Irish policy. Depend upon this, that when Ireland shall once be governed by a Legislature chosen by her own people, intent upon devel- oping the resources of the laud and fostering the prosperity of the nation. Irishmen, with their homes and the fruits of their labour secure, will make their native island a prosperous, a happy, and a progressive portion of the British Empire, and contentedly will stay in their own land. The Protestant religion, which the majority of us hold so dear, has for many a day gone by been associated in the minds of the Irish people the world over, with a long and sad story of oppression and wrong-doing. You, whose highest aspirations and holiest thoughts have been ever inspired by its teachings, know full well that it rests upon the charity which believeth all things and lispeth all things, and that every day It urges you to do auto others as you would they should do unto you. Upon you it now lies, as a solemn duty, to re- deem the character of that religion before the eyes of these people. The performance of this duty will bring its own blessing. You will steady the Irish leaders with the weight of respon- sibility. You will add another to the magnificent group of self-governing communities which form at once the strength and the ornament of the Br Empire. You will set free the Imperial Parliament to grapple with the great problems of legislation which await solution. Again I say, that while holding myself at liberty to look beyond the programme set forth by our venerated leader, Mr. Gladstone, I avow' myself, now as heretofore, a warm sup- porter and a devoted follower of him who, more than all living statesmen, is entitled to our affection and our gratitudl. I remain, Gentlemen, Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall. Northwich, June 1886.

THE ENCHANTED SHIRT The king was sick. His cheek was red, And his eye was clear and bright; He ate and drank with a kingly zest, And peacefully snored at night. But he said he was sick—and a king should know; And doctors came by the score; They did not cure him. He cut off their heads, And sent to the schools for more. At last two famous doctors came; And one was poor as a rat, He had passed his life in studious toil, And never found time to grow fat. The other had never looked in a book; His patients gave him no trouble; If they recovered, they paid him well, If they died, their heirs paid double. Together they looked at the royal tongue, As the king on his couch reclined; In succession they thumped his august chest, But no trace of disease could find. The old sage said, "You're sound as a nut." "Hang him up !" roared the king, in a gale. In a ten-knot gale, of royal rage; The other grew a shadow pale; But he pensively rubbed his sagacious nose, And thus his prescription ran— "The king will be well if he sleeps one night In the shirt of a happy man." Wide o'er the realm the couriers rode, And fast their horses ran. And many they saw, and to many they spake, But they found no happy man. They found poor men who would fain be rich, And rich who thought they were poor; And men who twisted their waists in stays, And women that short hose wore. They saw two men by the road-side sit, And both bemoan their lot; For one had buried his wife, he said, And the other one had not. At last they came to a village gate; A beggar lay whistling there; He whistled, and sang, and laughed, andl.ollli On the grass in the soft June air. The weary couriers paused and looked At the scamp so blithe and gay, And one of them said, "Heaven save you. friend, You seem to be happy to-day." "Oh, yes, fair sirs," the rascal laughed, And his voice rang free and glad ; "An idle man has so much to do That he never has time to be sad." ".This is our man," the courier said; "Our luck has led us aright, I will give you a hundred ducats, friend, For the loan of your shirt to-night." The merry blackguard lay back on the grass, And laughed till his face was black; "I would do it, God wot," and he roared with fun, "But I haven't a shirt to my back." Each day to the king the reports came in Of his unsuccessful spies, And:the sad panorama of human woes _ Passed daily under his eyes. And he grew ashamed of his useless life, And his maladies hatched in gloom; He opened the windows, and let in the air Of the free heaven into his room And out be went into the world, and toiled In his own appointed way, And the people blessed him, the land was glad, And the king was well and gay. —Leeds Mercury Weekly Supplement.

Was it an intentional joke when an Irish tarmer de- manded compensation for the death of his donkey, which, he averred, had been "ass-ass-mated by a neigh- bour's mastiff. An illiterate publican wrote over his'<loor, "Bear sold here." "He spells the word quite correctly," said Theo- dore Hook, "if he means to apprise us that the article is of his own Bruin." An agricultural acquaintance of ours is anxious to marry and settle down, and he insists upon the lady being a spinster—he won't even look at a widow. He says that it is only natural that a farmer should object to "weeds." "Little boy," said a gentleman, "why do you hold that umbrella over your head? It's not raining." "No." And the sun is not shining." "No." "Then why do you carry it?" "'Cause when it rains father wants it, and when the sun shines mother wants it, and it's only -when it's this sort of weather that I can get to use it at all." Though peace of mind does not constitute happiness, yet happiness cannot exist without it, our serenity being . the result of our own exertions, whilst our happiness is in a measure dependent upon others; hence the reason -why it is so rare, for on how few can we count! Our wisdom, therefore, is best shown in cultivating all that leads to the preservation of this negative blessing; thus if we preserve our peace of mind it will prevent us from ever becoming wholly wretched. He who neglects himself is to that extent weak. If he exhausts his energies, they diminish ; if he strains them still more by continued endeavour, they grow yet feebler. Discouragement follows, difficulties surround him, and he has no adequate strength to cope with them, still less has he any reserve of power for active enjoy- ment or to promote the happiness of others. Perhaps he began by a sense of obligation to others and a willing- ness to sacrifice much for their sakes; but he has mis- taken the road, and has involved those for whom he toiied in his own misery. There is an old lady in a certain district who makes frantic efforts to keep abreast of the times. Circum- scribed, however, in her social sphere, and with limited opportunities of development, this is difficult, and she is compelled sometimes to resort to her imagination. Vain the effort to tell her anything she does not already know, or startle her with information. A few evenings ago she went to a church sociable, and as she entered the room one of the young ladies said, "Good evening, auntie; I am very glad you came. We are going to have tableaus this evening." "Yes. I know, I know," replied the old lady; "I smelt 'em when I first came in." "PRIDE Comrs BRPORE A FALL."—A lump of clay and the end of a wax candle found themselves by some strange chance side by side one summer day on a dust- heap. "I wonder you have the assurance to lie so close to me !" said the dainty wax, sneeringly, "a great com- mon lump of clay; and I have been on a fine lady's dressing-table." " Ah," said the clay, humbly, "We are fellow sufferers in adversity; we must make the best we can of it. I ought properly to have been in yonder brickfield." "What a come down for ',me," moaned the candle. "It does not signify what becomes of you." The clay wisely held his tongue. And the strangely-assorted companions in misfortune dropped into silence. "I wish it was a little warmer," said the clay to himself. "Dear me, how hot it is getting !" grumbled the wax candle. Presently the sun grew hotter and hotter, and the piece of wax candle gradually Melted away. But the clay only became harder and firmer than ever. Thus it is the hopeful and self-reliant, when tried by the heat of adversity, come out of the fire the stronger and firmer. But the weak and worthless pass into obscurity, and are no more heard of. AN ANGLO-SAXON Housvnoto.—Let us go into this house and see how they live at home. It was a funny place—one storey high, with what they called "eye- holes" for windows. The walls were hung with tapes- try,; and as I saw some little girls at needlework with , their mother, I fancied they might have helped to make some of the wall coverings too. There was no chimney but the fire was made on a fireplace in the middle of the floor, with a hole in the roof to let out the smoke. The principal room in the house seemed to be the hall, which was furnished with benches, carpets, and cushions, and a board with two trestles standing near. "What a funny thing that is," I said. As I spoke, a Saxon slave, with an iron collar round his neck, took up the board, placed it on the trestles, and so formed a table, over which he spread a cloth for dinner. "That reminds me of an old Saxon riddle," said my companion. "I feed people with all sorts of viands. Whilst Ido that lam adorned with a handsome cover, hut afterwards I are robbed of all I possess, and when I am robbed I lose my legs.' 'Now you have seen the Saxon slave prepare the board, you know it is a table which speaks." "How many mealg a day do they have?" "Three. You see, they have nice table-cloths, but no forks; only knives and wooden spoons; so, of course, they are very careful to wash their hands before and after meals."—Little Folks for

July. A. PRIMROSE BUTTERFLY.—It is very curious that the same combination of colour found in the primrose may als ) be seen in a very common but very beautiful but- terfly that, like the primrose, hails the warm days of spring. The lover of natural beauty will scarcely have failed to notice and appreciate this insect, the Gonepteryx rhamni, or brimstone butterfly, of the entomologist, its size, the graceful curves of the outlines of the wings, and its appearance at so early a period, all rendering it a conspicuous addition to the beauties of the wakening year. The entire surface of the wings when displayed reveals the same delicate sulphur-yellow of the primrose, except that in the centre of each wing we find a spot of deeper yellow. As possibly some entomological novice may capture an insect that, while appearing to be the one in question, by no means bears out the encomiums we have pronounced on the beauty of its colouring, we may just mention that it is the male insect that has the ground colour of the wings pure sulphur in tint; in the female the wings are of a dull greenish white. The outer edge of each of the wings, bah in the male and female, has a conspicuous projecting point or angle, a feature that no other British insect possesses to anything like the same extent, a feature, therefore, that will at once identify it —a feature, too, that gives it its first or generic name. Goneptervx signifies angle-winged, white the specific name points out that the larva, or caterpillar, of this beautiful insect feeds on the rhamnus, or buckthorn.-- Cassell's Familiar If Flowers.

It i stated that the young stock of the Hereford bulls sent into Yorkshire for the purpose of crossing Short- horn dairy cows are giving much satisfaction. A writer in an exchange says :—The way to have poor calves is to give them large amounts of cold skim milk at irregular intervals, and to turn them out to pasture where they can suck each other's ears and fight flies all day long. At the Bath and West of England show at Bristol, Mr. J. Cornish, of Thornford,Sherborne, won five first prizes and one second in the Jersey classes, which must be con- sidered a remarkable success from one herd. Professo; Low. of Cornell University, examined the milk from cows that had access to water from stagnant pools, and found it full of living organisms. The cows were in a feverish condition, owing to their blood being charged with this living animalcul. i It s a remarkable fact that in testing 20,000 samples of milk, Dr. Newton, milk inspector of the State of New Jersey, found them to average a specific gravity of 1'319. ,He found the milk of no healthy cow below 1'029. The milk of 296 cows analysed in New York showed 329 as the minimum of fats, and 9.24 of solids, or a total of I 12.53 per cent. of solids. Forcing cows by extraordinary feeding to give extra- ordinary quantities of milk or butter is of very little practical utility. The proper question for the dairy I farmer to answer is—" How many pounds of butter per acre?" This is the true test; not, how much will one particular cow produce? though he should know that, too, of every individual in his herd. In the class for milch cows at the recent Oxfordshire show, the prizes which were offered to the "dairy cow of any breed (not having had more than three calves) which shall give the greatest quantity of milk at two milkings, not more than twelve hours apart." were awarded thus—First prize, Mr. G. Ferme's Ayrshire, 54i pints; second prize, Mr. W. J. Henman's Shorthorn, 44 pints If an old cow is quickly fattened, its meat will be more tender than where the feeding has been protracted. The great difficulty in leading old cows is in getting them to digest large amounts of food. This is best done in sum- mer, when fresh grass, which is the most easily digested of foods, may be supplemented with gradually increasing rations of corn and cake, taking especial care never to give more than will be readily eaten. MOUNTAIN SHREP.—North Lancashire farmers will be interested in reading the following by Mr. Chet. Scott on the wintering of mountain sheep :—" That hill sheep should not be fed until it becomes absolutely necessary, and that it will not pay to do so otherwise. That under certain conditions cake or corn may be advisable, but as a rule should be avoided. That turnips may be given with advantage to wether sheep, but are not recom- mended for ewes. That hay is the best food for hill sheep, but that grass may still further be used with good effect in the shape of ensilage. That on high farms re- moving the sheep to low ground is expensive, but as yet the cheapest method known. That stens are a great ad- vantage to hill sheep, and that by proper management heavy losses through severe winters may be averted." S rRING FOR SHEAF-BINDRRS.—The following letter from Mr. R. Hunter Pringle, Eastmere, Watton. Norfolk, deserves attention ;—" It appears to me that we who work with sheaf-binders during harvest are paying un- necessarily high for our string. Sevenpence per pound was last year's price, 'and this year sixpence-halfpenny is quoted. The least of these is too much. I for one will be glad to give another class of string at a lower price a trial. I believe a sufficietiltly strong twine can be got at 4d. per pound. Any firm desiring to have their , twine tested and reported upon may send, say, one stone of it to my address. Our harvest will be probably among the first begun in the eastern counties, so that there will, be time for me both to test and report." TUMOUR.—East Somerset says :—" I have nine year- ling heifers, one of which has within last month an en- largement quite hard on the side of face between eye and mouth, also on under-jaw. It gets much larger, being size of a fowl's egg, and has been in pasture for past eight months, with shed to run in, and looks as well as the others. Will your veterinary or any reader in- form me the cause and name of disease, also cure, if any ?"—Your heifer has doubtless a deep-seated (stru- t-nous) abscess forming on her face. Thoroughly rub in some biniodide of mercury ointment. This will either cause its absorption, or, which is far more likely, cause it to form matter and come to a point. When it bursts, keep it clean by washing with warm water daily, and apply some carbolised oil with a feather once each day. Should it not gather with one application of the oint- ment, repeat when the scurf caused by the first has cleared off. THE VALUE OF STRAW.—Some discussion has been going on as to the cost of growing an acre of wheat, leading to conclusions that it far exceeds the returns of the crop, or are at least equal to them, in the great ma- jority of instances. There would naturally be a far greater result only in those localities where the straw is of peculiar and exceptional value. There are parts of England where the farmer values his wheat straw far more than the grain. Amongst the Welsh mountains the latter yields a high price for thatch. In the neigh- bourhood of large towns and densely-populated districts straw will usually fetch from £2 to £3 per ton, and near Me Staffordshire Potteries, so necessary is it for packing purposes that as much as £7 per ton has been given for it, when scarce, to serve the object. HAY AS FOOD FOR LIVE STOCR.—As the result of Some experiments made as to the comparative value of good hay for stock it is estimated that 1001 b. of hay are equal to 2751 b. of green Indian corn; 100 lb. of green clover; 4421 b. of rye straw; 3601 b. of wheat straw; 16410. of oat straw; ipoib. of barley straw; 1581 b. of pea straw; 2001 b. of buckwheat straw; 4001 b. of driad corn stalks; 1751 b. of raw potatoes; 5041 b. of turnips • 3001 b. of carrots, 541 b. of rye; 461 b. of wheat; 5911 a. of oats; 451 b. of mixed peas and beans; 641 b. of buckwheat ; 571 b. of Indian corn; 681 b. of acorns; 1051 b. of wheat bran; 1671 b. of wheat, pea, and oat chaff; 1791 b. o mixed rye and barley; 591 b. of linseed; and 3391 b. o mangel wurzel.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1886.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. ANCIENT POULTRY AND POULTRY LORE. (Concluded.) Referring once more to the Romans, we find from the historian Gibbon that there were poultry fanciers even in those days. The following passage will:show that the weak Emperor Honorius deserves this name :—" His subjects, who attentively studied the character of their voting sovereign, discovered that Honorius (about A.D. .400) was without passions, and consequently without talents, and that his feeble and languid disposition was alike incapable of discharging the duties of his rank, or of enjoying the pleasure of his age. In his early youth he made some progress in the exercises of riding and drawing the bow, but he soon relinquished these fatigu- ing occupations, and the amusement of feeding poultry became the serious and daily care of the monarch of the west, who resigned the reins of the empire to the firm and skilful hand of his guardian Stilicho." And the same author, speakinc, of the Emperor Charlemagne, who cer- tainly was not weak, says:—" I touch with reference the laws of Charlemagne (about A.D. 800), so highly ap- plauded by a respectable judge. They compose not a system, but a series of occasional but minute edicts, for th 3 correction of abuses, the reformation: of manners, the economy of his farms, the care of his poultry, and even the sale of his eggs." From this it would appear that the breeding and rearing of poultry in France is by no means of modern introduction. The Russians, under Sv•iatoslav, sacrificed to the dead at night near Borostolum, on the Ister, by strangling sucklings and cocks and throwing them into the river; and at the funeral of a Russian chief—described by Ibn- Foszlan—cocks and hens are slaughtered and thrown to the dead man in the boat. If it be true that the cock was peculiarly sacred to the god Donxr, Thunar, or Thor. this German god must have been substituted for Craosha, or a corresponding god of the intermediary nations. Now, as the northern races, when this novel and strange animal first appeared among, were still in a quite ele- mentary state of consciousness, and could only utter the impressions they received in fumbling, figurative lan- guage, there is no doubt that many new superstitions about the cock would spontaneously fake root and spread amongst them. This practice of throwing cocks or sacrificing cocks has only recently died out in England. Moubray thtfs accounts for the old custom of throwing cocks on Shrove Tuesday, which he quotes from an old German writer, named Cranenstein. "Whilst the Danes were masters of England, and lorded it over the natives, the inhabitants of a certain city, grown weary of slavery, had formed a secret conspiracy to murder their masters in one bloody night, when twelve men had undertaken to enter the Town Hall by stektegem, and seizing the arms, to sur- prise the guard which kept it; at which time their fellows, upon a sienal given, were to come out of their houses, and murder all opposers; but while they were puttine this plan in execution, the unusual crowing and flutterinc, of the cocks, near the place which they at- tempted to enter, discovered and frustrated their plan; upon which the Danes became so enraged, that they re- doubled their cruelty, exercising still greater severity over the English. Soon after, however, the English being freed from the Danish yoke, they instituted the custom of throwing at cocks on Shrove Tuesday, the day of their disappointment, from a stupid and barbarian passion of revenge against the innocent cause of their misfortune, instead of admiring the natural vigilance of the birds, however unfortunately applied in a particular case."

From what has been already stated it will be seen that numerous references to the domestic fowl are to be found in history and literature, as well as in the legends and traditions of almost all countries. Even to the present day in our language and on our buildings we find rem- nants of the superstitions which so far as the more civilised nations are concerned have nearly passed away. Mahomet found in the first heaven a cock of such enor- mous size that its crest touched the second heaven. The crowing of this celestial bird arouses every living crea- ture from sleep except man. The Moslem doctors say that Allah lends a willing ear to him who reads the Koran, to him who prays for pardon, and to the cock whose chant is divine melody. When this cock ceases to crow the day of judgment will be at hand. A cock on church spires is to remind men not to deny their Lord as Peter did, but when the cock crew he "went out and wept bitterly." Peter Le Neve affirms that the cock was the warlike ensign of the Goths, and is therefore used in Gothic churches for ornament. Mention is frequently made of the cock in what may be termed modern literature. Shakspere often uses the figure, as do other writers with less observation. But these it is not necessary for us to go into, especially as some of them, in fact, the greater portion, refer to game fowls and to cock fighting. Everything goes to prove that fowls were at first used not for food or the produc- tion of eggs, but for sacred rites, or for fighting, in some cases the cock fighting being a part of the sacred rites. This, of course, in the more ancient times. But with the decay of the religions which practiced these rites there was no stop to the spurt. Whatever became of them it remained.: The addent of summer, which, though laterhas now come upon us with full power, brings with it difficulties to the poultry keeper, the chief of which is with young chickens, if there be any about. It is most desirable that there be plenty of shelter provided for the fowls, both old and young, and if there is not natural shelter this must be provided artificially. The best thing we know of is to interlace branches through hurdles and put these where they will be a protection. What air there is about can find its way through these branches, and the circula- tion cools the atmosphere. It only needs the exercise of a little ingenuity to make some capital provision of this sort.

The death was announced on Tuesday cf the Indian chief, Poundmaker, who took a prominent part in Riel's re- bellion in North-Western Canada. ATTEMPT TO WRECK AN, EXCURSION TRAlN.—PartiCtll2ll have come to hand of a dastardly attempt to wreck an excur- sion train on the Irish Great Northern Railway. Twelve large stones were discovered on the rails immediately prior to the arrival of a heavily freighted train of pleasure-seek.-rs from Drogheda. The engine•driver perceived the dan- gerous obstacle in time to arrest the progress of his train, aid avert what must otherwise have been an appalling catastrophe.

THR• WORLD'S PRODUCTION OF .FLOUTL—Good judges declare that, taking the flour-producing countries of the world to-day, it is likely that the productive capacity is one-third in excess of the aggregate demand. In Eng- land, Germany, and France, milling plant. has been heavily increased of late years, and in England particu- larly, with the most approved American machinery or its equivalent. In those countries, too, millers have an advantage of cheap wheats which the American miller does not always possess. The English miller can pur- chase Australian, Californian, Indian, Russian, or other wheats, and having samples thereof at hand can supply himself with raw material as the miller of no other country can. An expert, who has recently made a tour of investigation among Continental and United King- dom mills, declares that it wilt not be long when, with the advantage of cheaper labour, the best milling plant, and the opportunity to buy wheat at the bottom prices at all-times, the foreign miller will turn out flour cost- ing him 25c. less per barrel to produce than his American competitor. This may be an extreme statement, yet, in view of the increased production and sales of foreign flour abroad in the face of American, there is evidently an approach to the real situation in the statement. The assertion is made without qualification that the United Kingdom, Germany, and Hungary have as good mills to-day as there are in the world. This suggests a query as to how home millers will be able to further reduce the cost of production. The roll cut it down, it is stated, from 50c. to 35c. per barrel. Cheaper wheat has further reduced it, and lower railway freight rates have con- tinued the good work. It may be replied that cheaper average prices for wheat in the future than in the past may help, as well as lower rail rates. It is only plenty and the necessity of it which will put wheat lower, but many farmers are now looking with moderate satisfac- tion at 60c. per bushel where they ones looked for 90c. Who can say that the bottom has ben reached?—Brad- strifes.

Before the business of the nominations concluded at Northwich on Monday, Mr. Fletcher said he wished, before the High Sheriff, to correct a statement which had appeared In a Liverpool paper that the counting of the votes at the last election for the division had not been legally conducted, and that the ballot papers were not properly mixed. He most emphatically denied that statement. The counting was carried out in a strictly legal manner, and he might even say in a painfully legal manner, and he was sure his friend, Mr. C. J. Hughes, the Conservative agent, would bear out that statemeot.—Mr. C. J. Hughes said he could thoroughly endorse all that Mr. Fletcher had said, and he might add that he was perfectly satisfied with the way the business was conducted.—The Sheriff said he was glad to have the united assurance of gentleman so well qualified to know the facts.

div.head: CANDIDATES IN CONCORD.
div.p: THE CANDIDATES IN CONCORD.

An incident which gave rise to considerable amusement occurred during the nominations at Northwicb on Monday. Inspector Johnson suddenly made his appearance and placed a young man in the dock. The officer was asked whether he wanted to nominate the man as a candidate. The an- swer was very much in the negative: and it appeared that the man was charged with drunkenness and disorderly con- duct. The question then arose which of the two candi- dates (each being a magistrate for the division) would try the prisoner. It being Mr. Brunner's turn, he undertook the task. The Inspector then asked for a remand, stating that two magistrates were required to deal with the case. . The prisoner pleaded gaily, and said there was no occasion for a remand •, and the Liberal agent suggested that Mr. Verdin should sit in conjunction with Mr. Bruutier and die- pose of the case. Mr. Verdin assented, and for a few minutes the two candidates discussed in whispers what the fine should be. and then fixed it at 5s and costs. MR. BRUNNER AT WIDNES. Speaking in favour of the candidature of Mr. Birrell at Widnes on Saturday, Mr. J. T. Brunner, who was enthu- siastically received, said when he first saw Widnes, almost all the land from that place to the station was made up of smiling agricultural fields. (A Voice: "It was.") There is man here who has known me for a quarter of a century. (Laughter, and a Voice: "Hundreds of us."—Cheers.) The workingmen by their labours had transformed those smiling fields into a bowling wilderness, but they had not done the preprietors of those fields any harm. When he knew those fields first they were worth perhaps £3O to £5O an acre; but what were they worth to•day ? They were worth over a thousand pounds an acre. It was not the pro- prietors of the land who had raised its value, but the work- ingmen of Widnes. They had paid for the drains and the roads. They hail bought their own gas and water works, and it was by their labour that they had made the land so much more valuable than it was. (Cheers.) They had been paying every year in their rates and their rents not anly the interest of the money for the purchase of the gas and waterworks, but they bad been paving the full cost of them in the bargain; and what had the proprietors of the land contributed? Not a penny. There was a plot of land from Anderson's corner down to the station that was vacant for many a day. That land belonged to one man, and a very large part of other land in Widnes belonged to him. Into the pockets of that man's family the people of Widnes had put an amount of money which cou:d not be reckoned at less than six figures. They had been robbed of that money, and that was the con- sequences of their having abominably bad land laws. Now, Mr. Birrell was an advocate of the reform of the land laws —(cheers)—and it was because Mr. Birrell was an advocate of the land laws, and of many other things which hurt his fellowmen, that he recommended them to vote for him, as he (Mr. Brunner) meant to do next Irriday. (Cheers.) The main reason for voting against Mr. Moss was that he was on the side of the landlords—(hooting)—Mr. Moss would vote invariably against the people and in favour of the op- pressors. (Hear, hear.) Did they know that Widnes was an illustration of the working of Home Rule? He took a great pleasure in referring to the matter. It was a good many years since he (Mr. Brunner) began to move for the establishment of a School Board in Widnes, and he very well recollected how all the Irishmen voted against him. (Laughter.) He remembered going into the Public Hall, and when man after man came in he was asked how he would vote, and his answer was '• I vote for the Father," and that was all they knew about it. (Laughter.) Since they had had a School Board, and since Protestants and Catholics had worked together to manage their own affairs thee had never been one words of qearrelling. (Hear, hear.) He was happy to tell them that the name of Brunner had a pleasant ring in the ears of their priests. (Cheers.) His brother bad worked for years on the School Board with the priests, and they had found him a friend, and he had found them friends. (Hear, hear.) Now, when they found that Protestants and Cathclics could

work well together in Widnes, which was almost a part of Ireland7--(laugh-ter a:ocl cheers)—would they not tell a man who tried to perso:4cle them that Protestants and Catholics in Ireland would quarrel that they knew better? (Hear, heAr.) They haei been told that the population ef Ireland had diminished from eight to five and a half millions. Did the Pe@Ple le,ave Ireland because they were happy and contented? ('‘ No.") They left Ireland because they were disconten. te:d. He was not going to argue what it was that caused tnat discontent, whether that discontent arose from bat., government, as he believed; but what they now pro- .l;osed to do was to make Irishmen contented at home. (Cheers.) Suppose for a moment that they used their best efforts, and made the Irish content, would they not atop at home.? (" Yes.") He found it very difficult to believe that the Tories, who used the opposite argument, were honest. They were vary much afraid that when Irishmen got their own way they would misgovern Ireland. He contended that they were able to govern themselves, and it would be much better for the Irish members to stay in their own Parlia- ment rather thou to come to England to misgovern English affairs.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING,
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING,

Fruit trees that are grown on the restrictive system— which is decidedly the most suitable for s:nall gardens— will need going over for the purpose of shortening and regulating the shoots. The reduction of the branches whilst the tree:is in active growth directsla; greater supply of sap to those remaining; hence, if we proceed wisely we shall go over the trees at intervals of a week or ten days, making a start with the strongest'shoots at the top of the tree and shortening them within about four eyes of the base. Superfluous and weakly shoots should be removed clean away. In pruning cut close to an eye, or a portion of dead wood will be the result, which will look very shabby at the point of each shoot and show more conspicuously after the tree:has lost its leaves. The above instructions apply to Apples, Pears, Plums, and Cherries, as pyramids, espaliers, or trained to walls in any form. This pruning is usually done with the finger and thumb, as the wood is generally soft enough to be pinched. In a month or six weeks after the shoots are thus shortened others will have grown out of them, and they must be cut off close to the base, which leaves very little to be done at what is termed the winter pruning. Cherries on walls become infested with black aphis just as the fruit is colouring, which they rarely fail to disfigure if allowed to remain long enough. Soapy water, discoloured with tobacco juice, applied-with a syringe, will make short work of them. We find the blackbird already attacking the fruit, and we have hung a herring net over the trees. It may not be generally known that Gooseberries make better gain at this stage of their growth than when fully ripe, which enables us to secure them for All the purposes we need before they are palatable to the birds.

Vegetables will now be giving same return for the trouble taken with them, and Cabbage are fit for use in most gardens, and those who wish to make a fews shil- lings by their surplus should get rid of them and not wait till they have a certain bulk of white heart. As a rule we pull the Cabbage up as they become fit for use in order to make room for other crops, such as peas and broad beans, which are already—tbove ground and will daily require more space. This year the Cabbage crop being thin we shall leave a fair sprinkling of the stumps for a supply of sprouts later on, as other green crops are not likely to be ready at the usual time. Broad Beans will be fit for use a little sooner than they would if the tops are taken off when in flower. Beetroots are suffi- ciently advanced to have the hoe run between the rows, and the plants, where very thick, might have their num- ber reduced, leaving the final thinning later on, when they may be pricked out to fill gaps in the rows or to form another bed.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—An interesting class of plants in flower at the present time is the various kinds of Colum- bines. All have beautiful foliage, and many have bright and striking coloured flowers. They seed freely, and are consequently easily propagated, and we witnessed the other day hundreds of seedlings coming up round some plants that had scattered their seeds last autumn. It is always best to save a few plants annually, as the old ones are apt to die in some soils ,after being planted a few years. Pteonia Officinalis„ the one most frequently seen in cottage gardens, produces immense flowers, which are conspicuous at a long distance, and, though they are rather clumsy for such a place, they look re- markably well when placed in one corner against the dwelling, or the fence, and, as they delight in shade and moisture, and their flowers last longer when so situated, one or two might with advantage be introduced to every front garden. Hesperis Matronalis, or Dame's Violet Rocket, is one of the most useful plants that might be selected for the front garden, as they last for a long time in flower, and their beauty is enhanced by their delicious fragrance; and they may be used for the bridal bouquet or the mural wreath. The plant is unfortunately short- ived in many localities, especially near large to+,vns or smoky districts; but if a few cuttings are annually rooted, which is only the work of a few minutes, a stock can be always kept. . Just as the flowering period is three parts gone, two or three plants may be shortened, and if the weather is dry at the time watered, and in two or three weeks the remaining portion of stein may be cut into pieces and used for cuttings, and, if left long enough, growth will be made on the stems suitable for cuttings. After the plants have made a little growth, in spring a root or two may be taken up and divided, when many of the pieces will have roots attached to them. At lany time they root without any protection beyond the shade of some other tree or bush, and we have frequently seen cottagers insert them on the north Bide and slightly under a gooseberry bush. This Wn•znow.—With more brilliant weather, the win- dow plants will require increased supplies of water, and the pots must be examined twic3 daily, and should any be overlooked and it is found that the soil is shrinking from the pot, immerse the pot up to the rim in a pail of water for a few minutes, and it will swell to its normal state. Water for plants is always best when it has been exposed to the sun for a few hours, and, as most plants are in active growth, some kind of stimulants should be added to it, or a sprinkling of Clay's fertiliser should be applied once a week to the surface of the soil, or a thimbleful to every pint of water, and stirred round with the hand previous to watering, will work wonders on most plants.

FATAL ALPINS ACCIDENT.—ArI accident, involving the loss of four lives, in the Alps, is causing great excitement in the best society in Vienna. The Margrave Alfred Palla- vicini, who is in his 38th year, and the only son of Major Margrete Hypolit Pallavicini, recently left an an Alpine tour, in company with Mr. Cromelin, Secretary of the 'hitch Legation in Vienna, who is likewise 38. On June 25th they started with two guides from Kals, with the in- tention of ascending Austria's biggest mountain, the Gross Glockner, by way of Klein Glockner. Since the last-men• tioned date, however, they have never been heard of. The father of the Margrave Alfred left Vienna on Saturday with a search party, but nothing yet has been heard of his debug;

_ POISONED BT DRINKING BRANDY.-0a Tuesday Mr. F. Price held an inquest at theßechabite Hall, Salford, con- cerning the death of Florence Whinfield„ four years of age, daughter of W. B. Whinfieht On Saturday morning a bottle containing brandy was ,left by the father of the de- ceased on the kitchen table, and hie wife having been re- cently confined, the deceased afterwards got up and went downstairs. She got to the brandy bottle and drank some. She was afterwards found by her grandmother apparently asleep in a chair. The grandmother tried to arouse the de- ceased, but failed, and the child was then taken to the Sal- ford Royal Hospital and Dispensary in a cab, where she died about nine o'clock on Sunday night.—Mr. F. H. Folkes, house surgeon at the hospital, said death was the result of alcoholic poisoning from drinking brandy, and the jury re- turned a verdict ot death from misadventure.

WHOLESALE MASSACRE OF CHRISTIANS.—The " Annales des Missions Catholiqoes " have just been published, and the organ of the great French missionary society fully con- firms the sad intelligence published during the past year of the terrible massacres occurring in the kingdoms of Annan and Cochin China. The report states that 10 mi.sionary priests. 12 native priests, 60 catechists, 300 native nuns, and 30,000 Christians were mapacred ; one large mission, embracing 200 establishments, 250 churches and chapels, 2 seminaries, 40 schools, 70 missionary residences, 17 orphanages, 13 homes of religious communities, 1 printing establishment, and the homes of 55.000 Christians were sacked and burned. Bat while such is the tale of martyr- dom, there is the consoling intelligence of still unabated hope and confidence. During the year baptism was ad- ministered to 19,710 pagans, and 180,966 pagan infante in danger of death.

div.head: MR. ROBERT VERDIN'S CANDI-
div.p: MR. ROBERT VERDIN'S CANDI-
DATURE. MEETING AT LITTLE LEIGH.

----- On Monday evening a meeting in support of Mr. R. Verdin, the Unionist candidate for the North- wich Division, was held in the school-room, at Little Leigh. The chair was taken by the Rev. L. D. L. Bennett and there were also present, besides the candidate, Mr. W. 11. Verdin (late Conservative can- didate for the same division), Mr. J. Verdin, Mr. F. Cooke (Crewe), Mr. T. Ward (Northwich), Mr. W. Bancroft, Mr. J. 11. Cooke (agent), and others. There was a good attendance. The tenettamaae said that if ever there was a time when they as Englishmen ought to do their duty, this was the time, and he advised every farmer and labourer in the dis- trict to vote and to do their utmost to return Mr. Verdin to Parliament. (Applause.) Mr. VERDIN, who had a cordial reception, said that in the first place he must congratulate them on the fine work that Englishmen had done for the Union cause within the pre- vious tow days. (Hear, hear.) He was very pleased to tell them that the Union cause was 101 ahead up to Saturday last. (Applause.) That was an example of patriotism for men who loved their country, and he was sure they would one and all agree with him that it was not a question of politics, but that it was a question of their dear old country —whether the unity of this empire was to be broken up. (Hear, hear.) In fact, it was not a question that WAS solely occuping the minds of England and of people connected with the British Empire, for they might say that the eves of the whole civilised world were upon them, and foreigners in every clime were waiting to see whether Englishmen would be ' true patriots to their country or whether they would dis- integrate this eld empire. (Hear, hear.) He trusted that the people of the Northwich Division would be as patriotic as people in other districts. They found that men were re- turned on Union principles by- both Conservatives and Liberals in a great number of the towns of England, and that in some of the largest towns Unionism seemed to be the strongest. (Hear, hear.) If they once broke up this empire foreigners would want to take advantage of us, and he asked them as Englishmen should that be so? ("No.") Very well ; they said no; but if they wanted to avert that danger they must stand by the Union and vote for seen who were prepared to etaud by that Union in preference to any other thing. (Applause.) For several months past this great question of Home Rule and the Irish Laud Bill had been occupying the attention of the people of this country, and they were now asked to let Mr. Gladstone and the rest ef the world see that with them the good of the empire was before everything else. (Applause.) They might ask what will Home Rule do for Ireland? Well, Home Rule for Ireland would, in the first place, create great stagnation in the trade of the country, because it was considered es- sential, and Mr. Gladstone had said so, that if the Home Rule Bill was passed the Land Bill must also be passed. Could it be possible that if Irish farmers bad to pay for their land they would have any money to spare to employ labour in that c-untry. The result would be that a great number of Irishmen would have to emigrate from that country, and the first place they would come to would be England. The English market at the present time was overstocked, and in fact he believed that there was at we- sent not sufficient work in England for more than four per- sons out of every six. Men were either working short time or out of employment altogether, and it was for them to consider what would be the result if additional labour came to this country. (Hear, hear.) Then there was a question of taxation. In the event of the Land Bill being passed, the majority of the landowners in Ireland would want to sell their land to the Government in preference to leaving it in the kande of Irish tenants, and in that case it was computed that 150 millions of money would be wanted from this coun- try. (Hear, hear.) They had not Home Rule in England, and vet they lived peaceably and carried out the laws, and if Irishmen carried out the laws in the same manner they should never have heard of that agitation. (Hear, bear.) They all knew that in Ireland there were two races—the Celts and the Saxons. The Saxons occupied te a very great extent the northern portion of Ireland, and in that northern portion they very rarely heard of complaints relativa to British laws, and in fact the people there are so satisfied with the present laws that they said they would never be ruled by a Home Rule Parliament in Ireland. (Haw, hear.) And although the land in the north of Ireland was not con- sidered to be so fertile as that in the south, yet agriculture there was comparatively prosperous, and Belfast and the north of Ireland was the centre of manufacture and ship- building. The depressed trade of the south of Ireland was caused by the people there not being so induatrious as the people of the north, and by the prevalence of agitation which prevented people from investing capital. (Hear, hear.) If they gave Ireland Home Rule they broke down the confidence that was wanted, because if they had more confidence they should have more prosperity. He trusted that they as Englishmen would take into consideration what they had handed down to them by their forefathers, and would not giveaway the inheritance of their children, but if they gave to Ireland Home Rule they werqgiving away the inheritance which their children should enjoy, The time had come when every Englishman was expected to do his duty, and he trusted that on the election day the people of that division would do their duty. (" We will," and loud applause.) -

Mr.6.21141111-proposed "That this meeting considers that in all legislation relating to Ireland the following principles must be considered, first, the supremacy ot the Imperial Parliament ;!second,the maintenance of the union ; and third, the protection of the Irish loyalists." (Applause.) Mr. JOHN Hoßrox seconded the propoEal. Mr. T. WARD, in supporting the proposal, said the pro- posed Irish Parliament would not be in existence three months before it was at loggerheads with the English Par- liament. If tilere was one thing clearer than another, it was that the very people who were now clamouring for Home Rule had been clamouring for the repeal of the Union before a great many of them were born, and they would never be satisfied without repeal. (Hear, hear.) What Mr. Gladstone proposed to give Ireland was just a nice bit St what these people had been crying for so long, but not quite all of it, and they never would be satisfied till they get all they wanted. If the history of Ireland taught them one thing, it was that if they granted Ireland one thing more was sure to be asicPcl for, and in fact the agitators would never be satisfied until they got total separation. (Hear. hear, and applause.) The proposal was then carried unanimously, and subse- quently a resolution approving of Mr. Yerdin's candidature was also adopted.

Two children named Brookes were burnt to death at Croy- don on Wednesday night. A flour mill at Carlisle, belonging to Mr. Atkinson was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. Damage £lO,OOO. The Rev. George Bode, vicar of Saddington, Leicester- shire, died suddenly last night. He had hurried home and fell dead on reaching the home. A flour mill at Carlisle. belonging to Mr. Atkinson, was destroyed by fire on Thursday msrning. The damage is estimated at £lO,OOO.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone attended early service at Hawar- den Church on Thursday, and in the afternoon went a long drive in the park and woods. A young man named Chapman was drowned at Brymbe, a boy named Hines in the Mersey, near Runcorn, while from Scotland several cases are recorded. _

The paper mills of Messrs. Cropper and Ce., at Burnside, near Kendal, were burnt down on Sunday. Between one hundred and two hundred hands will be thrown out of em- ployment. Benjamin Stubley, grocer, of New Cross, was committed for trial at the Greenwich Police Court, on Wednesday, charged with personating his father at the Deptford elec- tion. It was stated that the prisoner took the oath and swore to his identity when challenged by the presiding officer.

At the Conference of Chambers of Commerce held in London on Wednesday, bi-metallism formed one of the chief subjects of discussisn. Eventually the Congress carried a resolution tio the effect that the diminishing supply of gold has been an important factor in the depression of trade, and believed that the remonetisatten of silver would afford some relief. _

FIRE AT A BOLTON FACTORY.—At one O'clock OR Tues- day morning a fire broke out at the tobacco and cigar manu- factory of Mr. Thomas Winward, Oxford-street, Bolton, by which a large portion of the premises were gutted and a considerable quantity of valuable leaf tobacco destroyed, the damage being estimated at upwards of £lOOO. An engineer was injured by falling from a window. Mr. Winward is fully insured. Two BOYS DROWNED AT STOCKPORT. -- Thomas Far- rington, aged ten, who lived with his parents in Walton street, and Thomas Davies, also aged ten, an orphan living in Stee-street, were drowned at Stockport on Wednesday night. Farrington fell from a raft on a mill reservoir at Hdigate, and Davies was bathing in the river Mersey at Heaton Norris. In both cases help was at hand but proved unavailing. DEATH PROM THE HEAT.-....The great heat of the past few days has caused several cases of sunstroke in the hay fields in Cheshire. Op Wednesday night. at Wheelock, Mr. Yates held an inquest on the body of William Evans, labourer The deceased complained of the heat, and lay down under a poplar tree. Some hours afterwards he was found uncon- scious, and never rallied. A post mortem examination showed that death was due to the heat, and a verdict to that effect was returned.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

FIGHTING BETWEEN TURKS AND MONTE- NEGRINS. Cameos, MONDIY.—A serious encounter occurred on Saturday evening between Montenegrins and Turks on the frontier. The official Montenegrin version of the affair States that on Friday morning several hundred armed Turks from Kolashis crossed the river Tara into Montenegrin terri- tory anti set fire to some houses in the vicinity. Two Montenegrin captains, while escaping from the flames, were 'takes prisoners by the raiders, who occupied the fortified 'Poets. The alarm having been meanwhile given to the nearest Ydontenegrin frontier guards, the latter attacked the post the following evening. Fighting continued until two o'clock Yesterday morning, and resulted in tbe Turks being driven cut with the loss of many killed. Between 50 and 60 of ibe raiders, however, bad locked themselves up in a block of houses, haying with them the two Montenegrin captain* Who were taken prisoners. The Turks were promised par. don on condition of surrendering the two captured captains. The losses on the Montenegrin side were seven killed, in- dueling a woman, and thirteen wounded. Later particulars *ate that the besieged Turks, taking advantage of a dense fog yesterday evening, attempted a sortie, sided by their comrades on the Turkish side et the frontier, but after severe fighting were driven out of their positions and com- Polled to surrender the two captains. Imre, MONDAY.—The following intelligence has been assiayed here from Zara concerning the frontier fight be- tween 'Parks and Montenegrins. A body of Mussulmans, alleged to be 2000 strong, emigrants from three Montenegrin villages which were fermerly under Turkish rule, but which 'W ere forcibly occupied in May last, attacked Majkoracs on the night of the 2nd inst. They took two Montenegrin asptaius prisoners but were ultimately repulsed with loss. CsTraraz, TUESDAY.—Forty of the Turks who violated Use frontier on the 2nd inst were conveyed this afternoon to Podgoritza under escort. Among them were several Begs from poljanci and Kolashin, a circumstance which is re- tarded here as pointing to the existence of a widespread conspiracy. According to the statements of the prisoners the raiders numbered shout 2.000 men. CHOLERA IN AUSTRIA AND ITALY. Timms, SUNDAY NIGHT.—It is no longer possible to doubt that cholera exists in Austria, although there is still some doubt as to the extent of the epidemic. According to Sae telegram there were eltwee cases of cholera of the Asiatic type at Fiume yesterday. Oa the other hand, smother telegram from the same place places the number of eases at three. Bois, SATURDAY.—To-day's cholera returns from Lad- ino, a small commune in the province of Brindisi. and Trea- dmill& Fontana, in the same province, show that the epi- demic is assuming serious proportions. In Latiano, there Were, daring the last 24 hours, 79 cases and 23 deaths, and at Franc.avills. Fontana the same number of deaths and 18 cases. THE ALPINE DISASTER. YrstrstA, THURSDAY.--A. telegram received from Win- diechmatrei by the President( of the Austrian Alpine Club states that the bodies of the Marna Nave Alfred Pallavicini, Si M. Cromelin, secretary of the thatch Legation in Vienna, and of the persons who accompanied them on their ascent of the Gross Glockner, in which tee whole party perished, have been discovered in the Glocknerkaar, at the foot of Posterize Glacier. FRENCH MONARCHISTS. PAuts, SETNDAY.—At a banquet of journalists connected With the Monarchical Provincial Press this evening. M. Lambert de Sainte Croix, the authorised representative of Ole Comte de Paris. said the Royalist party had the same chief, the same hope, the same object. A powerful aaxili• ary to the cause was to be found in an honest France, in an oppressive Republic and in liberty. SERIOU'S FIRE IN FRANCE. . PAms, WEDNESDAY.—A fire occurred last night at Dun- kirk, in the oil factory of Messrs. Marchand Freres. The building was totally destroyed, and the lose amounts to about £BO,OOO. Two persons are reported missing. In con- sequence of this fire some 500 workmen are thrown out of employment. DEATH OF CARDINAL GUIBERT. PAurs, THURSDAY —Cardinal Guibert, Archbishop of Paris, died this morning. THE NEW HEBRIDES. WELLINGTON, t'ATURDAY.—Tha House of Representatives • has passed a resolution to the effect that, while deprecating :sly French °emanation, and thinking that the islands ought to remain denationalised, yet if her Majesty's Government should deem it necessary to permit the islands to be annexed to Frauce, it should be done on condition that transportation should be altogether discontinued, and that British subjects and trade should receive full protection. Moreover. the /eland of Rape should be ceded to Great Britain, and the labour traffic should be properly controlled. The House also asks that the island of Rarotonga should be brought under British protection. AMERICA. New Yonx, &mei:AL—The Canadian cruiser Terror last evening captured the American fishing schooners Geo. P. Cashing and C. B. Harrington near Shelbourne' Nova Scotia, and took them into Shellaourne. Both belong to Portland, Maine. The seizure of the City Point on the Previous day was due to the fact that two men were allowed to land with clothing bags before the captain had reported the circumstances to the Custom House. The American fish- ing steamer Novelty, which called at Picton, Nova Scotia, for coal and lc-, has been ordered to leave. TUE BULGARIAN QUESTION. CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDLY.—The Porte recently de- spatched two notes to Sofia, the first complaining of the terms of the address of the Bulgarian nation in reply to Prince Alexander's speech at the opening of the session, and the second reverting to the advice given to the Prince to keep as much as possible within the limits of the Turco- Balgarian agreement, in order to prevent any intervention On the part of Russia. The Sultan, however, recognised the difficulties of the Prince's position, and has never ad- drawled any communicatiou of a menacing character to His Highness,. UNSETTLED STATE OF BURMAH, SIMLA, WIZDNESDAY.—A bill is to be introduced in the Viceregal Council to-day, providing for more speedy trial of prisoners in Burmah. It is only a temporary enactment, expiring at the end of the present year. DSSTRUCTIVE FIRE AT THE BRUSSELS UNIVE RSI TY. BRUSiELS, WerreespAY.—A destructive fire occurred to- day at the Brussels University. The whole of tbe right wing, where the laboratories, the library, and the great Academic Hall were situated, was entirely destroyed in less than an hour, though a portion of the books in the library were saved by the students. One of the firemen was severely injured. The damage is estimated at a million francae, none of which is covered by inslsrance. RUSSIA AND BATOUM. Russia, it is announced, has notified to the Powers that, is defiance of the 59th article of the Treaty of Berlin, she is prepared to close Batoum en the Black Sea as a free port. It is alleged, apparently on good authority, that for several years Russia, in contemplation of this step, has been erect- ing strong fortifications at Batoum. By the completion of the Baku-Poti Railway. Batoum has been placed in direct communication with Tiflis, and and all English goods pas- sing over that line en route for Persia will be subject to whatever dues the military authorities at the Black Sea port may think fit to impose. Several of the continental papers comment severely and sarcastically on this illegal act of the Russian Government.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the members of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday, in the Board- room at the Workhouse, Whiston. Mr. John Lowe presided, and there were also present—the Revs. Thomas Chambers, C. W. Wooll. and T. Finegan, Messrs. W. Birchall, W. Tyrer, W. Middleburg, J. Leetherbarrow, J. lienwright, W. Swift, J. Jackson, C. B. Johnson, J. Matthews, J. W. Wareing, W. Gerrard, James Burchal I, J. Ellison, H. Hul me, and James Buckley.—The Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale), reported that there were 419 inmates, against 444 last week and 417 in the corresponding week of last year, vagrants relieved 52, egainet 57 in the corresponding week last year. —A letter was read from the Local Government Board stat- ing that the distfict auditor (Mr. Hazlehuret) had surcharged the late assistant overseer for Woolton (Mr. J. R. Wood) to the extent of £I4BB Ga 91, and asking if the Guardians haa sommunicated with the Guarantee Society.—The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) remarked that they had received £lOOO from the Guarantee Society, and it had been spent. He would reply to the letter.e7The R-v. Thomas Chambers had writ- ten to the Local Government 'Board explaiming that several assistant overseers for Wootton had become defaulters for large sums of money, and the ratepayers had as many times made up deficiencies. He pointed out that an assistant overseer could have as much as £7.506 in his hands at one time, whereas his guarantee only amounted to £l,OOO. On behalf of the ratepayers of Wootton district he urged the Local Government Board to intervene, and require a larger guarantee. The Guardians referred the letter to the Fi- nance Committee.—A letter was also read from the town clerk of St. Helens (Mr. Brewil) appointing Wednesday, , the 14th inst., as the day on which the Health Com.nittse of the Corporat;on would meet Mr. Hartley on the subject of the price to be charged for the admissien of pauper pa- tients into the St. Helens Infectious Diseases Hospital.— Considerable discussion ensued as to the quality of milk supplied to the house by Mr. Ward, farmer. It was stated that he had entered into a contract tosupply it milk with not seYen degrees of cream, but on many occasions come up to that standard. Ultimately it was decided to enforce the terms of the contract and if inferior milk was r e again supplied they would get it elsewhere and debit Mr. Ward with the difference in Price.—Mr. . J. Tal, o the relieving officer for Sutton, was appointed Widnes district and Mr. Fenniugton to the Sutton district. —Mr. Jackson gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the salary of Mr. 0. M. Barton. relieving officer for Eccleston, be increased from £lOO to £l2O —The Clerk asked for three guineas remuneration for coraducting the recent Windle election of Guardian, and one guinea for his services at Speke, which election had been a f allure.— Rev. Thomas Chambers asked the clerk to explain how it was the two last elections at Speke had been failures, but the Clerk said his decision might possibly be impugned, and, be would have to &newer to the Local Government Board, therefore he was was not in a position to give a pub• lie explanation.—Tke Rev.T. Chambers said he was satisfied

NOMINATION OF CANDIDATES. At eleven o'clock both candidates, with a con- siderable number of their principal supporters, were present. Sir George Errington, Baronet, was accom- panied by Mr Charles Pilkington. J.P., Mr G W Raw- lins, Rainhill ; J Prescott, Earlestown ; B Harri- son, P Hall, 0 A Littman, Newton; F Broai- bridge, eleation agent ; while the Conservatives present included Sir Richard Assheton Cross, Mr Mar- tins Brown Westhead, chairman of the Newton Poll- ing District Conservative Club; Mr C B F Barran, Mr W H Brook, Warrington ; -is.
