div.head: TELEGRAM FROM MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: TELEGRAM FROM MR. GLADSTONE.

Sir R. Cross, the Conservative cAndidate, having stated in his speech on Monday night that Mr. Gladstone had changed his Irish policy from fear of outrages, Mr. Maitland, of Rainbill, communicated with the Premier en the subject, and on Tuesday received the following telegram from Rawarden

Not one word of truth in the reported allegation of Cross. Challenge him to prove it. My declaration that this great question was coming forward was made in Edinburgh Nov. 9. See letter to Balfour, when I knew nothing about the

Fenian outrages. GLADSTONII. It was deemed advisable to obtain a prompt contradiction of Sir R. Cross's statement, as the latter had been posted throughout the division. iN On Friday evening AT a meßetUinßgTinos7ppOorr. of Sir Geo. Errington was held in the Church Schools, 'Burton- wood. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Neill, and amongst those else present were the Rey. F. N. Shimmin, Mr. C. Pilkington, Mr* Foulke:3, Mr. Mahers, Mr. Gooding, and kf • . r. Broadoridg e (election agent.) Sir George Errington arrived at the meeting shortly after nine o'clock, having previously addressed a meeting at Havdeck. He was received with much enthus- iasm. Sir Geerge delivered an able address, in the course of which he referred to the Irish question, and also made re- ference to the English land laws. Home Rule, he said, was necessary for the welfare of Ireland, and an improvement in land laws was also necessary for England. At the close of the meeting a vote expressing confidence in Sir G. Erring- ton, vtas passed, and the Liberal candidate was heartily cheered on leaving the meeting. MEETING AT PENKETII. On Saturday afternoon Sir George Errington ad- dressed a meeting at Penketh. where he received a cordial welcome. The chair was occupied by Dr. Gor- nall, and amongst those also present were Messrs. C. Pilkingtou, J.P., G. W. Rawlins, C. E. Parker, T. Dodds, T. Brett, T. Summeragill, J. Jackson, A. J. White, T. Watson, J. C. Routlethre, G. Brandon, F. Johnson, F. Broadbridge (agent), icc. The Cuatasiler, who was well received, said the spirit that ani.nated Mr. John Crosfield at Warrington when he replied to the electors on the previous night animated him, and they were ready to fight again in Warrington, an'd no doubt would succeed next time. (Cheers.) The question of Ireland would bate to be settled by this country, and bat. log been a Liberal all his life, he wee anxious that Mr. Gladstone should have the honour of bringing into Parlia- ment a bill that was to bring peace and contentment to Ire- land. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone was in a manner fighting with one band tied owing to the desertion of his friends. If the Liberals did not win this contest, it was only a question of time, for they must eventually win. He had great pleasure in supporting the candidature of Sir George Er- rington, who happened to be a member of the Catholic Church. He (the chairman) thought that it was a discredit to the Liberalism of this ceuntry that mere members of the Catholic faith had not been returned to the House ot Com- mons. (Cheers.) Sir GEOROB ERBWIGTON, who was on rising to speak greeted with cheers and waving of bats, expressed the pleasure it gave him to meet the electors of the Sankey dis- trict. lie thanked them very much for their kindne3s in assembling at that meeting, in order to make the most of the short time at their disposal, for be could quite understand that it was not without some difficulty that people could assemble. They were quite right to be impressed, not only with the importance, but with the difficulty of the struggle in which they were etogasted. (Cheers.) Surrounded as they were by friends, be bad no doubt that they would be able to make a right good fight, and reverse the decision, which they all regretted but were not discouraged by, which took place at Warrington on Friday. (Cheers.) Instead of being discouraged, they were in one sense encouraged, be- cause it stirred them up to work harder, and he had little doubt that the result would be what they desired. (Cheers) He bad said to them that the issue was a very important and serious one. He did not think that it was too much to say that there never had been an occasion which required more determination on the part of the Liberal electors than the present one. It was a test, not only of the strength of the Liberal party, but of the / honour and the loyalty of the people of Englend—of that honour and loyalty to which Mr. Gladstone had appealed— (cheers)—and to which he would not appeal in vain. (Re- newed cheers.) Mr. Gladstone had devoted a long life to the service of this country ,and bad gained the respect and the love of the whole Liberal party. He bad spent that life in an endeavour, under great difficulties and against great odds, to confer upon the people of this country what might be called the balance o 'power, (Cheers.) 'I hey knew how different things were when Mr. Gladstone began, and there was so much work o fan uphill kind to be done. Mr. Gladstone had devoted h life to that work, and bad lived to see the realisation of it, in so far, at least, that he had placed the power in the hands of the people as aitaiust those who were opposed to all reform. (Cheers.) The present issue was a simple one. Mr. Gladstone having succeeded in this great task and earned the cosfidence of the people, now appealed to those whom he had enfranchieed and placed in power, and asked them to use that powsr in order to confer the same benefit upon their fellow-citzene who were still deprived of it. (Cheers.) They must remember that Mr. Gladstone did not propose anything that could possibly be of injury to the people of England. They had, no doubt, heard many things urged against Horne Rule. It had been said that it would" introduce disunion into the Empire, but nothing could be more ab- surd than that statement. (Cheers.) The pre- sent union between England and Ireland was one of handcuffs, and the union they wanted was the union of hearts. (Cheers.) The union Mr. Gladstone pro- posed to bring about was one of a totally different kind, one of love, fairness, and justice. There were many, and some of them painful, difficulties in this matter. Some of them they expected. There was the opposition, to which they

div.head: TFT E FXA I NEIL SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1886
div.p: TFT E FXA I NEIL SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1886

were-accustomed, of their opponents. rt was an opposition I which possibly was getting weaker, but one whist), so long as it existed, would, they could depend upon it, be exercised with all the force and vigour at the command of their oppo- nents. But there was another and a far more painful oppo- sition, and ens which he thought more blameable, because it was an opposition that earns from within. (" Shame.") It was also more difficult to wantend against, because it appealed not to those feelings that they condemned in the Tory party, but it professed to apoeal to the fairness and honesty of their own people. He could conceive nothing more painful than the position in which Mr. Gladstone had been placed, in seeing men with whom he had been working so long to be now so little in harmony with the true spirit of popular government as to have withdrawn their support, and to be in some cases actively engaged in opposition to the views of what they considered, and he thought justly, was the popular party. These very influential and able men liked to flatter themselves that Mr. Gladstone and his fol- lowers had seceded from them and they themselves were the Liberal party. (Laughter.) They wiebed to make out that Mr. Gladstone Was a seceder. It was rather diffieult to understand how an enormous majority could secede from a small minority. (Cheers.) It was presureptious te say that they, the Liberal party, Mr. Gladstone and the millions, were seceders. (Load cheers.) lie spoke with the greatest respect for Lord Hartington, but he thought him mistaken. He thought Lord Hartingten would sea and regret his mistake' and he was a man of that sourer flat when be did sae hiltmistake be weed make me secret of regretting it. (Cheese.) The wear, hawevir, to whom he would especially allude as having enjewod the high sonfldence of the Liberal party, was Mr. Bright. It was pleasanter te think of Mr. Bright in his early days than of the Mr. Bright of the present. (Cheers.) When they read some of his earlier speeches they could hardly believe that it was the same Mr. Bright who was now taking such an opposite view to what he formerly did. Mr. Bright used to preach justice and fairness to Ireland. Mr. Bright, they would remember. had always been a great power on ques- tions where there was some great moral lesson to instil, er appeal put before the people. He was a man who always appealed to justice, and his great strength was not so mush as a statesman, as with the great moral questions affecting the whole nation. He thought it must be a pleasure is them to turn from the Bright of to-day to the Bright of Previous days. (Hear, hear.) He (Sir George) believed that the people of England were with Mr. Gladstone, and that they intended te carry out his views, and to give to their countrymen in Ireland the power to manage their own exclusively Irish affairs in the same way as English people exercised the privilege they valued so much in manag- ing their own affairs. (Cheers.) The question of Home Rule, if it was followed up, went further than Ireland, and he believed that was one reason why it was so bitterly opposed by the Conservative, classes, or, as Mr. Gladstone put it, the classes generally op- posed to the people. He believed that the reason for this opposition was because these people saw in the scheme the germs of those Spforrne that were necessary for this coun- try. ([Mud sheers.) In the first place it was clear, although the Home Rule question should, and did, occupy the fore- most place ic their programme, it was net by any means the only question before them, and they must not forget that there were other matters of vital importance, and they must also remember that exi long as the question if Home Rule was in the way, these other questions could not be consi- dered. No one whe had sat in the House of Commons of late years sould possibly not be distressed, pained, and even ashamed, to see the utter state of impotence to which the House of Commons had been reduced by this question stop- ping the way, and preventing ordinary work being transact- ed. They were often told that Scotland and Wales did not desire Home Rule. It was true that they did not desire it 1 in the sense that Ireland did, but there was no doubt that one if the greatest questions they had to oonsider was the decentralisation ef power—local self-government—and it was j clear that that very much took the character of Home Hula. (Cheers.) 'There were questions of the greatest and most vital importance which never could be settled until the power to do that had devolved upon local bidies of some sort. The Imperial Parliament, of course, would hive to settle the broad lines to be worked in the different localities, but the first step was to grant Home Rule to Ireland. He believed that it would be for the benefit of Ireland, and for the benefit of the development of the larger Liberal measures in England for which they were now kept wait- ing. The question is which he was particalarly interested, as a candidate, and as a member of this nation, was the great one of land reform. (Loud cheers.) That, he could not kelp thinking, had a future before it upon which would depend, perhapo, the safety of the country, because it was quite clear that the question of land generally was getting into such a position the* groat changes were necessary. Al- luding to a remark made by one of the audience. Sir George said that if his friend referred is what was sometimes said about Mr. Gladstone's proposals to spend money in Ire- land upon the land question, be would explain that matter. Mr. Gladstone, they would admit; was an authority on finance, for it was he who had built up the whole fivance of the country. Even his most bitter opponents conceded that for finance there perhaps never was a genius equal to his. (Cheers..) Mr. Gladstone—though, he might mention, the proposal was withdrawn—had pledged his authority as a financier that the proposal would not cost England one six- pence. (Cheers.) He was not surprised that their oppo- nents said it would cost a great deal. But wou!d they, be asked, prefer the authority of Mr. Gladstone or Lord Ran' dolph Churchill? (Leughter and cheers.) But this question had been dropped, and the principle of Home Rule, the feendatlon of the scheme, alone remained. Their opponents allowed their friends of the rank and file to denounce Home Rule but most of the leaders took good care to keep to generalities, and not de- nounce the principles of Home Rule. The moral he saw in that was that they were golne to play over again a game they had played before. They want:d to "digit the Whigs"— (laughter)—and he was afraid that this time, considering hew many Whigs there were who had seceded from the Liberal party, that these gentlemen would find themselves very much "dished" iodeel. (Loud cheers.) Thev.would Ind that their Conservative friends, after using them against Mr. Gladstone would threw them over, and they would uave had the pleasure of getting the chestnuts out of the fire for Lord R. Churchill (Laughter and cheers.) Briefly refer- ring to agricultural depression, the candidate said that how- ever much the Conservatives might coquet with Protection, or Treat they called Fair Trade, he was sure that they were far too good Liberals to think that any great advantage could come to working-men by having their food products taxed. (Cheers.) A change In the laud laws was necessary; and to keep down the expenses taxation should be reduced— (cheers) —and equitably adjusted as regarded realised property and labour, which really meant the lowering of the rent. (Cheers.) Mr. C. E. PAIMIIIt, on behalf of the Liberals of Penketh, welcomed Sir George Errington. Mr. Pilkington, and Mr. Rawlins. (Cheers.) He then proposed-4 Thet this meet- ing considers Sir George Errineton an eminently fit and proper person to repreeent the Newton Division ef South- West Lancashire in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his triumphant return on Thursday next." (Cheers.) Mr. BAXTER seconded the resolution. which was carried amid cheers, and a vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. PILKINGTON, and seconded by Mr. RAWLINS, brought the meeting to a termination.

I help him—(applause)—and he was sorry it was the last if the election meetings, because, although he had had enough of them in one way, yet he had not had enough of them in that room. They al weys had such a splendid meeting and such enthusiestie and warm-hearted applause, that it wee a pleasure to everyone to address them. (Applause.) He had great pleasure in introducing Sir George Errington. (Cheers.) Sit GEORGE ERRINGTON met 'with a perfect ovation. The , entire audience rose and cheered again and again, while bats and handkerchiefs were waved enthusiastically. He said it was indeed a pleasure to stand before them and re- ceive that enthusiastic welcome. It was not wanting in en- thusiasm, and it would encourage them if they felt dis- couraged, which, however, they did not. (Cheers.) On the contrary, they were certain of success on the following day. (Loud cheers.) They had begun that campaign in that room, and were finishing it that night, and it was going to be so successful that it would long live in the annals of Lancashire Liberalism. (Renewed cheers.) He did net for one moment think they ought to be dis- couraged, for it appeared to him it was beyond question that the power and determination of the true Liberal party in England was never more thoroughly shown then in the present contest. (Cheers.) So far as they had bees able to judge nothing could be more feeble or less con- clusive in the minds not only of themselves, but in all those whom they had addressed, than the arguments brought for- ward by their opponents. (Applause.) They had heard a great deal about patriotism and tke evils the measure if Ness Noe leas going to hiring upon the empire. and . they tonal that the Conservative party claimed to have the only and whole monopoly of loyalty in this country. (Laugh- ter.) It was very easy to make such a claim, but he did not think they would allow such a-claim. (Cheers.) lhe measure of Home Rule would be an honour to the country, it would be useful, and it was necese try for the unity and safety of the empire. (Cheers.) The outcry of their op- ponents was merely one against Mr. Gladstone, and the so- called danger to the Constitution was merely an election cry. They wanted the simple-minded Liberals to believe the stories but their opponents took good care that they neither believed them nor cared to act upon them. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone had spent his life in the sort ice of the country, and he had helped the country by develop- ing the power, first of the Liberal party and Liberal mea- sures, and he had thereby strengthened and consolidated the power of the people. From their enthudasm he believed defeat was impossible, but, whatever the result might be, he should never forget the kindness, generosity, fairness, and the indulgence with which he had been treated by the people, and the Liberals especially, of Earlestown. (Pro- longed cheering.) Mr. E, R. Itussuhh, M.P., who received a hearty welcome, expressed his great pleasure that his ova election was over in time to enable him to say a word or two on behalf of their excellent candidate, Sir George Errington. (Cheers.) He had long had the pleasure of knowing Sir George Erring- ton, who had been a member of Parliament for a longer period than he (the speaker) had, and he could testify Sir George Errington had always been a most usefal and re- Bisected member of the House of Commons. (Cheer...) Sir Richard Cross was a man for whom be had great respect, and Sir George Errington had expressed his opinion to the same effect, but he did not think that Newton Division would lose in the least degree by sending Sir George Erring- ton in his place. (Load cheers.) So far as his observation had gone, he believed the Liberal party was in a sound con- dition. (Apt:datum.) He did not hold it altogether to be a mark of unsoundness that there were members of the Liberal party who were conecietiously troubled on the great question now before the nation—( hear, bear)—and he looked forward to the time when they would again be united. (Applause.) Ireland had been so long repressed and held in chains that they now beheld, he was sorry to eay, some of the noblest examples of intellect amongst us more brutalised than be liked to say by the very habits of coercion which had been so long exercised towards the Irish—(cheers)—and as Liberals they should devote themselves soberly and steadily. but without flinching in the least degree, to that great undertaking of giving justice to Ireland, and the first and best thing they had got to do towards it was to send Sir George Errington as a messenger from that division to sup- port Mr. Gladstone. (Prolonged cheers.) Mr. Tuosees T. HARLEY. of the Protestant Home Rule Association in Ireland, addressed the meeting, and urged that there was very little sectarian bigotry or prejudice among the Protestants and Catholics, He denied that if the Home Rule Bill were passed the Catholics would oppress their Protestant fellow-countrymen. (Cheers.) Mr. CAREW, M.P., alao spoke, and said that whatever might be the immediate issue of the contest, of its ultimate result there could be no doubt. It had already enabled Irishmen to come upon English platforms to state their grievances and demands, and it had done much to efface years of bitter memory from the hearts of Irishmen, while It had done more than 65 Coercion Acts during the last 85 years to bring about a bond of union between the hearts of two nations too long estranged. (Cheers.) To whom did they owe that? To the man who had' led them in the past, who still leads, and notwithstanding the division would still lead the Liberal party. (Loud cheers.) Their duty at the polls was to vote in support of the man who had led them in every reform, and who for 50 years had never ceased doing good, and never would cease until the last day of his lie to bring about peace and goodwill between tbe two peoples. (Cheers.) Mr. KENNEDY (Birkenhead) next spoke, and was greeted with prolonged cheers. He said he could only give them the same advice as he gave them on the last occasion, and that was that England expected they would again do their duty. (Cheers.) At the last election the men of Earles- town and Newton did their duty well, and they bad no complaint to make, except that the enemy was a little too strong. (Laughter.) But it was only a temporary defeat. (cheers)—and now that the time for shouting was past they wanted them to work next day, and they would secure the victory. (Loud cheers.) He ventured to prophecy that they would place Sir Richard Cross in the same position in which his countrymen in Edinburgh had placed Mr. Goschen. (Cheers.) The speakers then left the meeting to catch the last train to Liverpool, and hearty cheers were given for them. The following resolutton was afterwards passed, amid prolonged cheering :—" That this meeting pledges itself to do its beet to return Sir George Errington to Parliament for the Newton Division, pledged to support Mr. Gladstone in his English and Irish policy." The proceedings then concluded. SPEECH AT THE STATION. On leaving the foregoing gathering Sir George Errington was enthusiastically cheered along Earle-street to the rail- way station, where be was followed by an immense crowd. Sir GEORGE ERRINGTON, on stepping forward to address the large crowd from the footbridge crossing the line, was received with great enthtreiastn. He said: Gentlemen, we have only got one moeienf, but I cannot go away with- out thanking you most sincerely, for your kindness, and for the splendid reception which you have given me. (Cheers.) I am sure that is an omen that we are going to win to- morrow. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, you have only to show the same spirit and the same truly Liberal feeling as you are showing now, and we are certain to carry this elect ion by. a splendid majority'. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, once more I thank you. I believe we are certain of success, and with this thought we shall meet again to-morrow. (Loud cheers.) THE CANDIDATES AND THE CONTEST. The second election of a member of Parliament for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire took place on Thursday and, like its predecessor of last December, was the all-absorbing topic of con- versation for a week or two preceding the day of polling. In the contest the Tories had almost every advan- tage. In Sir Richard Assheton Cross, who for 17 years was one of the representatives of the old South-West Lancashire Division, prior to its divi- sion into seven districts, and of which Newton is now the centre, they, possessed a strong candi- date. His own popularity among the Tories of the division, his former struggles to retain in ' himself the representation, his record of undefeated championship of their cause, brought him, as matter of course, into the field to seek the honour of being the first Parliamentary representative of the newly-constituted Newton Division. When it was announced last year that the Liberals intended to bring out a rival to so strong and powerful a champion of Toryism their action was at first considered presumptions, but when Colonel George McCorquoclale of Newton-le- Willows entered lists as the opponent of the Tory Cabinet Minister the result was by no means the foregone conclusion it was at first thought. The details of that memorable fight are stil "resh within the recollections of our readers.

It was admitted that Colonel McCorquodale "fought against fearful odds," and accomplished everything but success after a most gallant attempt to reduce a Tory Stronghold. Out of a total con- stituency of 9,344 voters, there were but 900 ab- stentions from voting, and the result was: Cross, 4,414; McCorquodale, 4,031; majority, 383. The comparative smallness of the majority fell like a thunderbolt upon the Tory party, while it held out every hope to their opponents. This has been evidenced on the present occasion in a re- markable degree. The announcement of the defeat of Mr. Gladstone's Government upon the Home Rule Bill came at a most inopportune moment for the leaders of Liberalism in the Division. At that mo- ment their former candidate, Colonel McCorquodale, found himself unable to again accept the pres- sing offer to again come forward, and the Newton Liberal Council were in the unenviable position of being without a candidate. Nothing daunted, how- ever, the Liberals of the division proved their sterl- ing quality by facing the difficulty, and the sequel was seen about three weeks ago in the acceptance of Sir George Errington, Bart., as their candidate. Sir George, as our readers now know, was then on his way home from a visit to America, but he lost no time in coming into the division, where his re- ception was of a most cordial and enthusiastic character. During the past fortnight the campaign has been conducted and continued with great vigour and energy. This roused up all the Tory organisation, and the most strenuous efforts have been put forth to maintain Sir Richard in ins for\ mer position.

The contest was prolific in electioneering litera- ture. Placards, circulars, handbills, "special edi- tions," and other similar methods were adopted to influence the independent and wavering members of each party. The various posting walls and hoard- ings throughout the division were covered with red, blue, and black placards, while the smaller sheets were distributed broadcast. The Liberals issued a telling placard, which stated "The great question of the day for the electors to decide is whether they will have Gladstone and conciliation, with Ire- land and the real unity of the Empire, or Salisbury and a paper union only supported by 20 years of coercion," while another pointed out the incon- sistences of the Tory party in reference to the Irish question, and concluded with the ex- hortation, "Electors rally round the Gladston stan- dard. In another placard was propounded the question, "What is the Irish question ? " and an answer was found by extracts from the views of various politicians, concluding with the words, "Vote for the Liberals and justice for Ireland." Another effective message was worded as follows: —" Gladstone gave the ballot and secrecy, Cross spoke and voted against it; Gladstone save you your vote, Cross spoke and voted against it. Then show your confidence in the great leader who trusts. you by voting for Sir George Errington, Bart. the Liberal candidate." During the piesent and last week Sir Richard Cross personally visited several of the works and collieries in the district, and atten- tion was drawn to this fact by a placard as follows: "Working-men. Do not vote for a candidate who canvasses you in your workshops and on the pit banks with your employers, managers, or foremen at his elbow. Do vote for the man who asks you to give him your vote of your own free will without dictation or coercion, vote for Sir George Errington." The Conservatives were not backward in this line of electioneering tactics. They almost confined themselves to reprinting portions of ad- dresses and letters of Unionist Liberals, and the Liberals of the Newton Division were asked to " Listen to your leaders," and " Vote for Cross and no separation." Several cartoons reflecting on the respective leaders of the political parties were circulated. THE POLLING. The polling opened at eight o'clock on Thursday morning at the twelve polling places comprised within the division. The total number of voters according to last year's register, and upon which the present contest took place, is 9,344, and they were apportioned as follows : Ashton-in-Makerfield 1,523, Billinge 601, Golborne 744, Haydock 875, Newton (including Earlestown) 1,980, Rainford 536, Rainhill 352, Rixton-with-Glazebrook 159, St. Helens (Eccleston, &c.) 986, Sankey 511, Warring- ton 558, and Winwick 519. The greatest interest appeared to be taken and manifested in the polling for the Newton township --Lthe centre of the division, and containing the largest proportion of the voters. Last December the electors registered their votes at the District Infants School, Market-street, but on the present occasion the arrangements for again securing that building fell through, and the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School, Cross-lane, was used for the pur- pose. Here, when the poll opened at eight o'clock, a fair number of persons had congregated, and a few minutes later Sir Richard Assheton Cross, the Tory candidate, put in an appearance. His opponent did not visit Earlestown until about.noon, when he was received with great cheering, which was how- ever eclipsed in enthusiasm when he paid a subse- quent visit at a later period of the afternoon. Dur- ing the forenoon comparatively few voters had visited the poll, this being no doubt due to the fact that all the works in the district, without exception, were in operation, But many employes stopped for the ;day after breakfast time, while a very large num- ber failed to return after dinner. In the meantime Earlestown had begun to wear a busy and animated appearance. The crowd assembled near the Wesleyan School in Cross-lane gradually increased in proportions until noon, when some hundreds had congregated. During the dinner hour a large number of votes were registered and as many of the men fail-ed to return they assembled near the polling station, thereby swelling the throng to an immense proportion. Party favours were worn by the large majority of those present. who good humouredly hissed or cheered their rivals in political opinion. Both Sir George Errington and Sir Richard Cross visited the neighbourhood several times during the day. Later in the evening the streets became MOYB crowded, but no disturbance was threatened. The removal of the polling station from the District In- fants' School to the WeSleyan Schoolroom in Cross- lane necessitated an alteration in the arrangements of the political parties. The Liberals had taken an unoccupied shop in Grant-street as their central committee-rooms, and it was proposed to conduct heir voting business there, but they were com- pelled to carry out the latter at another shop in what is known as "Workhouse-row," Bridge-street. Here was an excellent staff of Liberal workers. The, Conservatives had secured a shop in Cross-lane as I their committee-rooms. The polling booth for the Warrington district ' was at the Infant School-room in Cairo-street, and each candidate had committee rooms in opposite houses. There were two stations, and the officials were as follows :—Station 1, Mr. M. Jackson, pre- siding officer; Mr. John Roberts, poll clerk ; Mr. G. W. Blair, Liberal personation agent; and Mr. T. B. Cross, Conservative personation agent. Sta- tion 2, Mr. J. 11. Houghton, presiding officer; Mr. John Heaton, poll clerk; Mr. S. Dunbobbin, Liberal personation agent; and Mr. Ralph John- son, Conservative personation agent. Police- Sergeant Cox was stationed at the booth. The can- didate* visited the booth during the day, and were i I 0s cheered by their respective supporters. In the morning Mr. Peter Rylands, the newly-elected mem- ber for Burnley, registered his vote in, it :is pre- sumed, the interest of Sir R. A. Cross. He was cheered by the Conservatives present. There were not many vehicles brought into use in this district, but, judging from the favours worn by the occu- pants, the majority in use appeared to be on the side of the po atoelrlConservatives.stnh en the al i t NiotsToary d rriactoiflis t cr iecst, Bwerery n st a re- quiredttTehn eti td, 052 t poll oeNI t the Golborne contingent at St. Thomas's Church Schools ; Haydock at the Colliery Schools, Hay- dock; Billinge at the church schools, Billinge ; Very little excitement district Rainhill at the National Schools, Rainhill ; Rixton- with-Glazebrook, at the National Schools, Hollin- lare ; Sankey, at the Board Schools, Great Sankey ; and Winwick, at St. Oswald's National School, Win- wick. The crowds gathered about the streets of Earlestown anxiously inquired of visitors how the polling was going on in other townships. It was considered an established fact that at Haydock, Ashton, and Golborne--the working-class portion of the constituency—a great majority of the elec- tors were in favour of Sir George Errington, but it was admitted that the weak points in the Liberal armour were St. Helens, Warrington, Billinge, Croft, &c., where the squires and the parsons have considerable local influence. The St. Helens polling district of the Newton Division comprised the township of Windle and Ec- cleston (urban and rural), Parr, and Sutton. There are 980 voters on the register. The polling stations were at the Cowley Schools, College-street. The Conservatives claimed two-thirds of the entire num- ber, and boasted they could give Sir Richard Cross a good majority. St. Helens being looked upon as a weak point of the division for the Liberals, and the 'fact that they worked at a disadvantage in the matter of vehicles, did not augur well for the suc- cess of Sir G. Errington. Nevertheless, the leading Liberals of the district worked hard and did their best to bring up voters. In the Rainford district there are 536 voters, but during the morning the polling was exceedingly slow, it being a colliery district, more anifnation was manifested after three o'clock, when the colliers had been drawn up from the pits. The polling stations were at the church schools. At both places the Conservative supporters wore blue, but the Liberals in St. Helens had no colour, and at Rain- foad only a red card with the portrait of Sir George Errington was exhibited. The only addition to the mural literature was a small bill bearing the words, "Cross for ever." The polling closed at eight o'clock at all the stations, after which the ballot boxes were sealed up and conveyed with all possible speed to the New- ton Town Hall, where it had been announced that the counting would take place and the result be de- clared the same evening. Shortly after the conclu- sion of the poll at Earlestown, Sir George Errington, who was greeted with prolonged cheers, addressed a few words to some thOusands of persons who had congrecrated round the Liberal committee-rooms. Ile 'briefly thanked those friends who had voted in his favour, and those who had worked so hard in his behalf. THE RESULT.—GREAT EX'JITEMENT. After the closing of the polls at eight o'clock, crowds of people went from Earlestown, Ashton, and Places in the vicinity, to Newton, where they as- sembled in front of the Town Ilall. Great excite-
ment was manifest for some time before_ the result

Majority After the declaration the scene in front of the Town Hall was one almost beyond description. The several thousand persons assembled cheered and counter-cheered, hissed and groaned, for several minutes, but 'gradually something approaching , quietness was obtained. Sir R. A. CRoss then appeared at the window, and addressed the crowd. He said: Electors, you have won a great victory. (Cheers and groans.) You have won a great victory. We have been fighting in the cause of justic—(cheers, mingled with ' hisses)—and in the cause of freedom. But you have fought a good-humoured battle and I have ; had a most honourable opponent. (Loud cheers.) ' We have fought it with al our mights. We have I fought for the prinaiples which we hold so dga.a, but we have fought as men, and, although we huys been fighting this great battle, now that the ! battle is over we are all friends. (Cheers.) The first thing I had to do aftar the : poll was declared—and I did it with the 1 greatest pleasure—was to shake hands with my ; honourable opponent. (Cheers.) Lancashire has spoken out. (Cheers and groans.) Lancashire has ! told the Prime Minister that he has made a great ! blunder. (Cheers, groans, and counter cheers.) They have said that they would have justice to Ireland. So say we. We will have justice to the whole of Ireland and not to a part of it—to those who can- not help themselves as well as to those who have tried to tyrannise over others—and it is because we have been fighting that battle of freedom and of liberty, of order and of good Government, that I again stand , before you as your representative in Parliament. (Cheers and groans.) I will not detain you longer here to-night. I advise you to go home and be friends. You have sent me once more as your re- presentative to Parliament and I thank you for the honour you have conferred upon me. I thank you heartily far all that you have done to-day, not for myself, but for the cause of justice and of freedom. (Cheers.) Sir GRORGB ERRINGTON, who was received with , cheers and groans, said: We have fought a great battle, and if you are not discouraged, I certainly am not. (Cheers.) We have not run away. We have stood up against considerabledifficulties, from which we have not run away, and we shall live to fight another day. When that other day comes I shall be at your service—(cheers and groans) and I cannot ask for any more loyal, and more friendly, and more cordial sup- port than that which I have received in this contest. (Cheers.) The moment that you call upon me again I shall be ready to come forward. (Cheers and hisses.) We will fight this battle again, and we shall succeed. They who defeated us to-day are not the popular party in this constituency. I told you that the contest would be between the classes and the masses. This time, unfortunately, the classes have prevailed, but we shall reverse that decision. (Groans and cheers.) I appeal, therefore, from this decision of the classes, to the people, who I am sure will reverse it. I shall ask no more loyal honourable, and cordial support than that I have received this time, for which I thank you most cordially, and which I shall never forget. (Cheers.) We shall fight this battle again and we shall win it. (Cheerg An d groans.) The people will win it for us, against the classes that have defeated us this time. (U_proar.) Gentlemen, I thank you. Our opponents will not allow us to be heard, but, gentlemen, the time will come when this decision shall be reversed. (Cheers and groans.) Shortly afterwards Sir R. A. Cross thanked Mr. Brighouse and the other gentlemen who had acted in an official capacity, most cordially for the way in which they had carried out their duties. lie also I thanked the Press for the care they had taken in reporting the speeches during the election. (Cheers.) Sir GXORGE ERRINGTON, in a few well-chosen words, endorsed the remarks of the successful can- didate. (Cheers.) Mr. BRICatoVsB, in reply, said that if both candi- dates had been satisfied, he and those associated with him felt that they had done their duty. (Cheers.) The proceedings then concluded, but a consider- able time elapsed before the crowd assembled out- side the building dispersed.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

After a grandly fought-out game on the Old Trafford Ground, Manchester, the first of three representative matches between England and Australia ended, on Wednes- day, in a victory for the Englishmen hy four wickets. The contest produced splendid cricket all through, and the win- ning team are to be congratulated upon a very fine perfor- mance. Barlow scored 68 runs for once out, made three good catches, and in the second innings of the Australians took seven wickets for 44 runs. The English fielding was ; smart and brilliant throughout. After a good attempt to save the match, Cambridge were beaten at Lord's ti.ound, on Wednesday, by 133 runs. The match Derbyshire v. Surrey was concluded at Derby on Wednesday, Surrey whining very easily by 157 runs. A. defeat for Derbyshire seemed probable from the state in which the game was left on Tuesday evening, as there was little likelihood of their getting the runs off on such a I wicket. Lancashire has put fre=h hope into her supporters by gaining a couple of signal victeries—first over Oxford Uni- versity, and then over the champion county of the South, Surrey. The Preston and St. tielens teams met at West-cliff on Saturday, to play their return game. The weather was be 4u- Wally fine, and an enjoyable afternoon was spent. Tug visitors turned up with a weak team, the result being that they received a severe defeat.

div.head: MEETING AT MARTINSCROFT.
div.p: MEETING AT MARTINSCROFT.

On Saturday evening a meeting in support of the candidature of Sir George Errington was held in the Schools at Martinsoroft. There was a fair attendance. Mr. S. Barlow (Warrington) acted as chairman, and amongst those also present were Messrs. T. Flood, Kilduff, and D. Wilcox (Warrington). The CHAIM:RN explained that Sir George Errington, hay- ing so short a time at his disposal. was not able to be pre- sent at that meeting. He thought that, without a shadow of a doubt, Sir George Errineton was the best of the two candidates before the electors of that division. Mr. Glad- stone, whom toe Liberal candidate was prepared to support, did not appeal to the upper classes, but to Vie people—to the men of sense who had bad the power to voie given to them by the same man who now made tots appeal. He deprecated all religious animosity, and said that the great troubles of Ireland would eease were she allowed to govern herself. What was wanted was the union of love—the Irish and the English peoples hand in hand.—Mr. T. FLOOD also spoke. In this great contest they were piloted by Mr. Gladstone, a man in whom millions had confidence, and, if he did not lead the party to victory, he would have been piloting a holy and noble cause. English statesmen, he claimed, after referring at length to the history of Ireland, had misjudged the Irish character, ad had been mistaken in viewing the wants of Ireland from an English standpoint. The old union between England and Ireland was an unlawful and unholy alliance. and had borne fruits of retribution t) the English.—A few remarks were also made by Mr. KILDUFF, and a vote of thanks was passed to the Rev. Father Walsh for the use of the room. ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. The most enthusiastic and successful meeting held during the campaign took place in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on Wednesday night, when the large room was thronged to its utmost capacity with a demonstrative audience. The meeting was announced to commence at eight o'clock, but it all- an-hour before then the place was full, and the time was whiled away in the singing of popular Liberal songs, interspersed with cheers for Sir George Errington and the " Grand Old Man." The entrance of Sir George Errington and his friends was the signal for tremendous cheering, which continued for several minutes. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., and among the gentlemen on the platform were Mr. E. R. Rus- sell, M.P., for Bridgeton division of Glasgow; Mr. Carew, M.P., for North Kildare, Ireland; Mr. Thos. T. Harley, of the Protestant home Rule Association, Ireland; Alderman T. Cook (St. Helens), Rev. H. J. Ward (St. llelens), Rev. P. N. Shimmin (Earles- town), Mr. Samuel Barlow (Warrington), Messrs, B. Harrison, G. W, Rawlins (Rainhill), J. Taylor (llaydock), J. Prescot (Earlestown), Keegan (hon. secretary Earlestown branch of the Irish National League), F. A. R. Neill (Bold), G. Ratcliffe, L. T. Foulkes, F. Broadbridge (election agent), and others. The CHAIRMAN, wh6 was received with loud cheers, said it was with minded feelings he took the chair that night. He need not tell them how glad he was to see such a meeting as that to welcome Sir George Errington for the last time before the day of polling and the friends who had come to

div.head: SIR RICHARD CROSS'S CANDIDATURE. DOWNALL GREEN.
div.p: SIR RICHARD CROSS'S CANDIDA- TURE. DOWNALL GREEN.

On Tuesday evening Sir R. A. Cross addressed a Unionist gathering at Downall Green. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Crompton, and the candidate was supported by a number of friends. In his address Sir R. A. Cnoss again refuted accusa- tions that he had failed to carry out his promise to pass a bill through Parliament giving power to miners to appoint their own checkweighmen and power to relatives in cases of fatalities to examine witnesses. (Cheers.) Alluding to Mr. Gladstone's Irish proposals, whicn he strongly condemned, he said that , they had it on the authority of a Cabinet minieter that Mr. Gladstone was forced into his present course of action through fear of tbe Irlsh•American party. Ile Richard) wonld not be so coercod—(cheers)—but he desired to give Ireland the same laws as the remainder of the United King. , rium had. Ile believed the Irish were a high-spirited &MI generous race, capable of loving and of being loved, and if properly treated he had no doubt that they would be loved ind lovable. But they had been Misled by agitators, who had got them under their control.—A resolution in support of the candida,ure of jrS R. A. Cross was afterwards passed.

div.head: MARTIN CROFT.
div.p: MARTIN CROFT.

On Monday evening a meeting in support of the candi- deture of Sir R. A. Cross, Bart., was held in the Catholic School, at Martinecroft. Mr. William 11.)yston presided. Sir Richard Cross wrote expressing regret that engagementa in other parts of the division prevented him from being present. Captain Nicholson, Warrington, proposei—" That this meeting heartily thanks Sir Richard Assheton Cross for again offering his services to the constituency, ex- presses the greatest gratification that he will oppo.e any attempt to break the union between Great Bri,ain and Ireland, and pledges itself to use every lezitimate en- deavour to secure his return to Parliament." Speaking as a Catholic, Captain Nicholson said be advocated for Ireland a fair, liberal, and proper treatment, but he advocated " No surrender" in the way of giving up the control of that country to an indepenient Parliament for Ireland.—Mr. Rosman' PIERPOINT seconded the motion, and it was sup- ported by Mr. JOSEPH Devtgs, and carried without opposi tion.—A meeting was afterwards held at boffin Fare, when- Mr. William Smith presided. The speakers were the same as at Martiescroft, and a resolution similar to that already quoted was carried with enthusiasm. BURTONWOOD AND RAINHILL. Sir R. A. Cross addressed a meeting of his supporters at Buttonwood, in the Church School-room, on Monday even- ing. Mr. Selby presided, and theta was a good atten- dance. Sir R. A. CROSS. having referred to the miners' question, spoke upon Ireland. There were, he said, about live mil- loos of Irish people, and two millions were about the most loyal people under the man. These loyal people asked th it they should not be handed over to the tender mercies of the other three millions. Mr. Parnell and his crew have been rul- ing Ireland with the greatest tyranny that any country was ever subjected to. The National League ruled Ireland with rod of iron. The law of the land was merciful, but the Irish National League showed no mercy. In that morn- ing's papers was a correspondence between Mr. Gladstone and one of the members of the late Government, and now was revealed the secret why Mr. Gladstone had brought forward these bills. He was afraid of the Irish Americans. Two millions of Irish people were begging and preying for mercy at their bands. He did not appeal simply for jus- tice, but for mercy for these loyal people. (Cheers ) Would they hand over these loyal people to the Nationil League, and take from them that which was their birthright and foundation of their liberty, and that for which their forefathers had fought for centuries and had now obtained. They had got what no other nation in Europe, had—the protection of such a Parliament as the United Parliament of G.teat Britain and Ireland. (Cheers.) What lad been the answer to the policy pronounced by the Prime Minis- ter? The metropolis had gorie against him, and so had the vast majority of the barougles, la Lancashire there had been 35 borough contests, and 30 of those constituen- cies had answered the Prime Minister—" We won't have either you or your bills." He was quite sure that in that division they would give a similar anewer, and say, as they did in 1888 and 1885, that they would have neither Mr. Gladstone or his measures. (Cheers.) A resolution in support of the candidate was passei, on the motion of Mr. Webster, junr.. seconded by Mr. Brisco. and a vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meet-
ing,. The same evening Sir R. A. Cross addressed anothQr meeting at Rainhill. where he was well received. A res'Au- tion of support was carried.

- LORD HARTINGTON is, as the Arnericahs say, "coming along ; " he moves slowly, but he does move. Speaking at Crawshawbooth, on Monday evening, he said No doubt I have on previous occasions given evi; pression to much doubt whether in the preslf., condition of Ireland a large extension of se, government will be for the advantage of Irelant; herself, and whether it would not make the task a. the government of Ireland still more , difficult; I have long ago acknowledged that on that point was not in agreement with the bulk of the Libers+ party, and I am perfectly willing to admit that al.ti reasonable desire for extended self-,government 143 Ireland must now be considered. There is a large admission in these wordi--- an admission which may well make the Con- servatives on the one hand, and the Liberals- !on the other hand, ask themselves -what' does this mean. and whither is Lord HART" INGTON going ? People have been accus- tomed to say that his lordship was the onlY politician who was immovable on the question of Home Rule; but can this be said after the statement of Monday night? We are all pretty familiar with the Tory and Whig argu- ment that nothing can be done in the way of granting local self-government for Ireiand until the people of that country show less disposition to resist English rule—until they bring forth fruit\ meet for repentance; but here is the Chief Apostle of that doctrine confessing that he has been wrong. He 111. continently drops the contention that the conferring of larger powers on the Irish people would not be for the benefit of Ireland herself, and expresses himself as "perfectly willing to admit that any reasonable desire for extended self-government must now be considered." But what is extended self-- government for Ireland but Home Rule int' one form or another? And if this must be granted—for the mere "consideration" of the subject will but aggravate the sit uation--- why not grant it in a form that will be accept- able to the Irish people? What is the use of going to the trouble of preparing a sump- tuous repast unless there is some reason to believe that it will be to the taste of the guests? Or to chanze the figure, whY waste time and money in setting up a piece of machinery when those who are to work it say it is not what they want; that it will not serve the purpose ; and that theY will decline to supply the motive power? Whatever faults of construction certain political tinkers think they can see in Mt.- GLADSTONE'S proposed legislative machinery for Ireland, there is this to be said of it—that it is the outcome of an experience which unrivalled, and that those who have to bring it into operation belicAre it will work, and work well. Can this be said of any other design, or plan, or scheme? Lord HART- ; INGTON offers nothing; he has only just been brought to see that something must be done, and yet he has been spoken of by Aft. BRIGHT as a wise man because he has hitherto proposed no remedy for an admitted evil. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has had two or • three plans, but none of them have secured the approval of Mr. BRIGHT or Lord HART- INGTON—to say nothing of their being ac- ; ceptable to the people of Ireland. Mr• BRIGHT'S scheme is the latest that has been , placed before the people, and it is certainlY the least. It is not original, but that wouid. be of little moment if it could be said of it that it was good. It is simple—very simple; he proposes that the Irish members should constitute a Grand Committee, to discuss and re..shape or amend Irish measures, after•tbe first reading, with the understanding that 1 after they have left the Grand Commit- tee, the House of Commons, at the ~ stage of a bill known as "the report" should be at liberty to re-discuss and re-shape and further amend the bills which had been , before this Grand Committee. Now if the relations between Ireland and England were of a normal and harmonious kind—such for instance, as those existing between Wales '• and England—we can well believe that a proposal of this kind would be of some service in relieving Parliament of a consider, able amount of work; but with Ireiana hostile to English ru!e, and torn by On' tending factions, Mr. BRIGHT'S scheme pre- sents itself to us as ridiculously inadequate. To begin with, it would not acccmplish what even Lord CARNARVON thinks should be aimed at—it would not in any degree satisfi the aspirations of the Irish people. gr* BUTT, when leader of the Home Rule part).', gave his consent to trying a scheme of Lb?! kind; but it was not thr he thought it wouia secure the end he had in view, except, indirectly, by showing that it was rniSerablr abortive of legislation for Ireland. But let of us suppose that the Grand Committee

div.p: Ireland wzs now at work; and that in view of the threatening language of Ulster Orange- men a bill was submitted having for its object the re-enactment of a portion of the Crimes Act. Is it likely that, with, say, 18 Ulster mem- bers on the Committee, the discussion would be of a kind to promote peace and good-will amongst the Irish members? And when the minority were out-voted, is it likely that they would accept their defeat? Would they not appeal to their Tory comrades in the House of Commons? And what would be the result when the S 5 finally found that they Were in a minority? Surely it is not too Much to say that the last state of that House Would be worse than the first. Mr. BRIGHT'S scheme will not do, for his Grand Committee would have nothing grand about it but the name. Ireland does not want a Debating Society; she wants a Parliament of her own on College Green.

ft The defeat of the Liberai candidates at Warrington, St. Helens, and at Newton, is undoubtedly disappointing ; but it is not so discouraging as it would be if there were / , reason to believe that -there was anything in , ,the nature of a Fory reaction. The Con- servatives are gaining seats in many places, but this is not because of their inherent . strength, but on account of Liberals being !. Weakened by being divided. Successful Con- servative candidates willingly acknowledge their indebtedness to Liberal voters; and,there- fore, all that would seem to be required for the Liberals to win is that they should fight . the next battle as a united host. Bad as their plight may be, they are not yet reduced . to having to depend for success upon bring- ing Conservatives to their side. There is • every evidence in the polls, thus far, that they , will be sufficiently strong, when they are united, to drive Toryism to the wall. But a • house divided against itself cannot stand; , and it must be confessed that Liberals have , shown themselves too prodigal of their power jo hoping, -as they have hoped, to win, whilst 2truizgling with the enemy and with foes of ' their own household. The Liberal Unionists , !ill surely, ere this, have begun to see that they are being used as so many cat's-paws to Pull Tory chesnuts out of the fire. Another • lesson they will have learned is that the , great mass of the Liberal party is strongly in favour of Home Rule in some form or another being given to Ireland. So long as ' there was any doubt on the subject, dissentient -Liberals were justified in, at any rate, insist- ing that the question should go before the country. The great mistake they have made we have said all along—that they have brought about a General Election at the worst time and in the worst way. There was every- thing to gain by giving distracted Liberals time to think over, and discuss, and adjust , their differences. Mr. GLADSTONE sought to , provide this interval by suspending the Home , Rule Bill after getting it through a second reading; and we cannot but deplore the folly 1 of the Unionists—particularly the CHAMBER- LAIN section—in refusing the reasonable corn- Promise that was offered them. So far as they were concerned, there was, in the last ; !nstance, no question of principle involved ; , it was a matter of expediency. Mr. CHAM- "'MAIN himself was prepared to advise his friends to abstain from voting rather than Vote against the bill ; but he allowed the rashness of hasty men to overcome nis better judgment. A decision was taken to v&e against the bill; and thus on the narrow issue whether the protest against the bill should be in the form of abstention or t,4t giving an adverse vote, the Chamberlain l• section defeated the bill, and precipitated the conflict which is proving so disastrous to them as to the rest of the Liberal party. What we have got to do now is to mark on our charts the rock upon which we have split, and avoid it for the future. The Home Rule question is to the front, and with nine-tenths of the Liberal party pledged to it as a Policy, and four-fifths of the people of Ire- land insisting on it as a right, there is no keeping it back. It awaits—it demands a Settlement; and if Liberals are wise they will sPeedily re-unite and settle it, and thereby do justice to themselves and to the noble tra- ditions they inherit.

MR. PETER RYLANDS has crept in as mem- ber for Burnley with a majority of 4.3. He tflay not now be "a crawling delegate" of the Liberal party, but we are not prepared to say that he is in any better position as the elect of the Tories of Burnley. There is a story told of a certain PETER whose Saturday night supping often caused him to be late for Sun- day service. He entered church one Sunday just as the Minister—who was preaching on the apostle's denial of Christ—exclaimed-- "Sneaking PETER !" This was too much for the conscience-stricken sinner who was raakinrY his way to his seat, so he looked re- Droachfully at the minister and said—" I didn't sneak in." We cannot help won-. dering if Mr. PETER RYLANDS will, Simi larly, feel a twinge when reminded of his large Tory vote and of his small Majority. There is one direction, by- the-bye, in which it will be prudent for him to cease to do evil and learn to do well, and that is in abstaining from declamation against Mr. GLADSTONE. It is simply absurd to say, aS he does, that he has been "fiercely at- tacked by Mr. GLADSTONE." The PRIME MINISTER is not in the habit of fiercely at- tacking anyone, and he has had something better to do than make more than a passing reference to Mr. RYLANDS having "gone to the bad." And what does the member for Lumley mean by speaking of the sacrifices be has made "in supporting measures which be disapproved" in order to keep Mr. GLAD- STONE in power? It would seem that he Would have people come to the conclusion that the PRIME MINISTER was not grate- ful; but how if they were led to think that Mr. RYLANDS was not so sctu- . Pulous as he might be, seeing that ac- cording to his own statement he often acted "against his own convictions? " There is a rumour in circulation at Burnley that the hon. secretary of the Liberal Association received, lon the 2.Bth Januuary last, a letter from Mr. kYLANDS, which was laid before the Liberal Executive ; and that that letter would, if it Were made public, show that the aspiring rnember for Burnley would have had nothing to say against Mr. GLADSTONE, if he had been given a place in the Ministry. We let the rumour go for what it is worth. It is certain that Mr. RYLANDS objects to the letter in question being made public. Had he nat better be quiet and let sleeping dogs lie?

div.p: TOUCH AND GO." The electors of Widnes are just now on tenter- hooks; they have polled, but they will not know until about noon to-day who has won. Mr. Birrell will be the member for the Widnes Division, if an unusually large number of Liberals have not gone wrong; but at present nothing is certain—but un- certainty.

_ In the Northwich Division, Mr. BrMiller is hav- ing a hard fight. Tile Tories, conscious of being bard hit intellectually, have been attempting to re- tort physically, after the old, bad fashion. The struggle, as will be seen from the various meetings announced, waxes keen and hot. But if working- men do their duty by the Working-man's candidate they have in Mr. Brunner, they will be able to spare the weaklings who drift to the other side. The Northwich Division of Cheshire is free, and they must keep it free.

By way of celebrating the victory of Sir Gilbert Greenall, the bell was rung on Friday night at the Parish Church, Walton, where both candidates re- side. It is due to the Vicar, the Rev. L. J. T. Dar- well, to say that this was done without his consent, and that he took an early opportunity of informing the defeated candidate that his, wishes had been disregarded and his instructions violated. After the election last year, the vicar refused to allow the church bell at Walton to be rung; but it appears that last night week one of the wardens took upon himself to admit the men. Now, as the vicar has sole control over the church in a matter of this kind, it is obvious that a serious offence has been committed. It is a disgrace to the church to ring the bell in connection with party warfare ; and it is a disgrace which wouldbe felt if it resulted in somebody having to go to gaol. It would be interesting to know if Sir Gilbert Greenall was aware of what was being done. Per- haps he would be as oblivious of everything regard- ing the matter as he was as to the action of his agent, and gamekeeper, in trying to stop the foot- path at Morley Common. He would kear what the vicar said on Sunday as to the discreditable inci- dent, and it would be wiell if he and others pro- fited by the homily.

People are asking, who supplied the free drink which was to be had amongst the Conservatives during the election campaign. One Tory hanger- on confessed at the police court yesterday that when he threatened a certain Liberal he had had nearly three quarts of liquor. It is said that the Warrington Conservative Club was an "open house." There seems to have been a" mixture" of people as well as of liquors ; but whether it was " judicious" or not is very questionable.

After the declaration of the poll at Warrington, a boisterous mob, in Hall-street—excited by elec- tion liquor—broke into the premises of Messrs. Sexton, and did damage amounting to over .E3O. Ringing the church bell might satisfy the Tories of Walton ; but it was not enough for the roughs of Hall-street. How loyal—how law-abiding are the Tories! We suppose Liberal ratepayers, amongst others, will shortly be called upon to make good the damage done. Or is it possible that the police will set about searching out with a view to punishing the offenders?

Sir Richard Cross has polled 112 fewer votes than at the last election. He has not had the benefit of the Irish vote; but he has been helped by Liberal Unionists. The abstentions on the part of the Liberals have been numerovs but this is'rto proof of a, Tory reaction.

Mr. T. Sexton, one of the most prominent of the Irish Nationalists, has stormed and taken West Belfast. What becomes of the twaddle abcut the power of Ulster in resisting Nationalist sentiment in Ireland, when they cannot hold their own in tne ballot box in a single province?

-- This is how " Punch" hits off Mr. Bright's remedy for the ills of Ireland : DR. BRIGHT'S BOLUS. I've loved those darling Irish all my life, I watch their woes with sympathy and pity; And so, to settle all our life-long strife, I'd give them—yes, I would—a—Grand Committee

Mr. Chamberlain must have been• in a bad frame of mind when he made his Welsh speeches. The matter and manner of his references to Mr. Gladstone were alike of the Churchill type. What could be worse than the statement that the Clime Minister had placed himself in a position to ascertain the opinions and receive the suggestions of the Irish Americans Mr. Gladstone gave the statement a flat contradiction ; but we do not see that Mr. Chamberlain has had the decency to apolo- gise. Nor did he say the other week, as he ought to have done, that he was glad to find that he was under a misconception in suppos- ing that Mr. Gladstone had joined in the sneer at his having a Mayoral mind. -- Pressure, it appears, is being put upon Cheshire tenants to vote against the Liberal candidate for the Eddesbury Division. But the law is justly severe in dealing with those who practice intimidation. Why not allow the Tory magnates to apply the territorial screw; and then pIA.-sish them after the elec- tion by giving ttirn a turn of the legal sct ew An insurance agent, of Manchester, has had L 2 zs. zd. to pay at St. Helens for damage done to a railway carriage, through his opening the carriage door, and leaving it open after the train had stated. He missed the train, after all, through being late, and he will think it would have been a good job if he had been too late to open that carriage

door. Mr. Seton-Karr, after the manner of suc- cessful Tory candidates just now, thanks the independent Liberals who have put " coun- try before party." By " independent Liberals," he means, of course, those who have voted for him. flow could they be independent, or have any regard for the country, if they voted Liberal ? Umph As Mr.. Bright once said, "the audacity of the Tories is measureless."

The historian who wants to discover the patriot who at this crisis "put country before party" will turn to the correspondence be- tween Mr. Gladstone and Mr. A. J. Balfour. He will then see that the Grand Old Man, with characteristic disinterestedness, as far back as December last offered to assist Lord Salisbury's Government in the settlement of the Irish question on non-party lines. But the Government refused; they were " inde- Dendent" • but who will say that they "put country before party?"

A Tory candidate, Mr. George Kynoch, said the other night that, "when there was a possibility of the loyal people of Ireland having to appeal to force of arms against Mr. Liladstone's Legislature, he was prepared to contribute within forty-eight hours of neces- sity arising, ten thousand as good rifles as were ever made, and two million cartridges from his own stock for the support of the

loyal people of Ireland." Wonderfully "loyal," truly, to take up arms against the Crown ! But is it not time to let some of these blud- veon-men know that there is such a thing as law, and that it is strong enough to punish them?

The following capital story is being told at the expense of Lord Randolph Churchill. It is so good that it must be true : A true blue, old-fashioned Tory, crossing the threshold of a polling-booth in South Paddington, was accosted by a smart young electioneerer with, "You're not going to vote Tory this time, sir ? " " Tory ? why, yes, of course. I always vote Tory, on principle, sir!" "But have you read this ?" inquired the young man, producing a copy of Lord Randolph's address. The old gentleman deliberate- ly put on his glasses and perused the document. " What ! Lord Randolph said that? Well, that's not kind, that's not gentlemanly: in fact, rin -- if I vote for him now." And the old man went straight away and voted for llopps.

WELSH WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anniversary services were held on Sunday, when the services were con- ducted by the Revs. Hugh jonee, of Hatddfrynond Edmund Humphreys, of Chester. TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN, V. SITERDLEY AMATEURS. —This rounders match was played at S. lielns on Saw- day, the visitors winning by 29 runs. Scores :—Trinity, 77; Sherdley Amateurs. 48. Crime' theencn, WEsTote PoiNr.—The anniversary of the National Schools, Weston Point, was celebrated on Sun- day, when the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, BA , incumbent, preached two sermons in aid of the school funds Saw LIGHTSHIP TOR RUNCORN.—Mes.rB. Brundrit and Co., ship builders, of Runcorn, have received an order from the Mereey Docks and Harbour Board for the construction of a lightship for the, Mersey. The ship will he designed by Mr. J. S. Trotter, of Wineford. when each ser- vice was well attended, and the collections amounted to £lO 3s. ROUNDERS.—WIDNES V. ADMIRAL (LevaarooL).—This match was playete on the grouod oe the Admital, on Satur- day afternoon, in very best weather. The visitors Went in to bat and made a grand stand, knocking up a total of 55. The home team next handled the willow, but made a very poor stand against the Widnes ca!etain. who howled in grand style, Keenahan holding him in grand form, only one man being missed in the innings. which ceised fur 28. Being 30 runs behind, the Admiral had to fellow on, their secoud attenipt only realising-39, runs, which left the visitors 10 runs to get, to. win, which they got by their first three !lieu's 11 itting.• They finished the round, and keecked off 30 runs for the loss of two men, thus winning the match by 20 runs and 9 men to bet. Score :—Widnes (two innings), 87 ; Admiral (two innings) 87. . . BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES —On Sunday the Sunday school anniversary was celebrated. Special sermons. were preached by the Rev. W. E. Taylor, of Sr. Helens, and the collections amounted to £4 16e.--On M rirlaer night a chorus, comprising the choirs of the St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, and the Baptist Chapel, Widees, rendered the cantata "Jesus of Nazareth," aided by a string band. IThe yerious choruses were performed with conspicuous sue- ! cess, while the excellence cf some of the solos and duets was such as to elicit hearty encores. The soloists were Miss Jones Miss Simkin; and Miss Birkett ; Messrs. Richard Morrie and A. Fox. Mr. B. Brown occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. It. Yeatman. The choitewas conducted by Mr, I. Fdwards, and the pianoforte accom- paniments were played by Mr. J. E. Bates. LAUNCH AT RUNCORN.—A tine new river flat was launched on Monday afternoon, front the shipbuilding yard of Messrs Brundrit and Co., Runcorn. The fiat has been built to the order of the Widnes Alkali Company, and is in. tended for the trade of that firm between Widnes and Liver- pool. The flat is 74 feet in length, 19 feet 6 inches in breadth, and 8 feet 6 inches in depth. She is framed and planked with English oak throughout, excent flat of bottom and bilges, which are of American rock elm. Toe flat is in every way strongly built, and eminently suitable for the heavy trade of the Mersey. She has been built from the designs of Mr. J. S. Davies, drauglitcran for Mess's. Brundrit and Co., and every cere has been taken in her con- struction to preserve the high reputation of the firm. The fiat was christened the " Edward " by the grandson of Mr. G. H. Bolton. In the evening the workmen had a jovial time at the Anchor Inn, Brunswick-street, Mr. Bolton hav- ing sapplied funds for their enjoyment. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTNCRITY.—The fort- nightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Lieutenant Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs J W N Tanner and J Lockwood, arid Messrs Hadfield, Knowles, Brandreth, Aaron, Hall, Linaker (cletk), W H Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr Adams (medical officer of health), and James Farriogton (inspector of nuisances). A letter was read from Messrs Linaker and Davies, architects and building surveyors, Frodsham, with reference to the nuisance from an open drain at Weston Point. The writers recommended that a new 9-inch sewer should be laid down the road leading from the bridge oppo- site the Dock Hotel, emptying into the culvert communica- • tiog with the old basin. To this the Weaver Navigation would not object, arti it would afford a very good outfall.— A complaint having been made by the Daresbury Highway I Board that several grids had been removed and several cess- ! pools filled up at Stockton Heath, and it being stated that! tßere was a danger of the roads being flooded in conse- quence, a committee was appointed to confer with the ; Highway Board.—There was no other business of pnbli I interest.

RUNCORN BOLILDOF GrunDuaNs.•—Lieut .Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting on Tuesday. Present: Toe Heys. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Leek- wood; Messrs. J. Weir, P. Speakman, Fisher. Aaron, I Brandreth, Knowles, Hadfield, IL Linaker (clerk), ! and W. IL Linaker (deputy clerk). A letter was read from the Local Government Board in reference to the bathing accommodation for the girls and 7-ranger chil- dren in the Workhouse. The Board attached great import- arms to the regular bathing of the children and thought, in I their opinion, proper facilities should be provided for this purpose, so that no inducements should be offered to officers or attendants to bathe too many children in the same water. —Mr. Speakman said it appeared that there were 38 girls in the house, and these girls had to go and wash in the bath. room erected for the boys, the boys during this time having to keep in another place. Moreover, the boys' room I is not large enough for the girls, and he (Mr. Speakman) thought a room such as the one soggestPol at the last meet- I ing should be erected. The estimate (£75) was prepared by 1 Messrs. Linaker and Davies. Mr. Speakman gave notice that at the nest meeting he would move that the resolution already carried should be rescinded and that tenders be i advertised fer.—ln reply to Mr. Hadfield, the Clerk said that each member would receive notice of the motion.—The Bev. J. Lockwood said that when any money was to be I spent there were always a lot of members present, but , whenever anything of a merely routine character was to be -transacted, although it might be of equal importance, they were generally away.—Mr. Weir supported Mr. Speakman's views—There was no other business of importance. Sr. HELENS AND WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.— The regiments of volunteers hitherto known as the St. Helens and Warrington Volunteer Rifles, other- wise the 9th and 21st Lancashire, have just ex- changed a territorial for a Royal designation. Her Majesty has commanded that in future they shall be called the Ist and 2nd Battalions Prince of Wales Volunteers, South Lancashire Regiment. Mn. GLADSTONE AND SIR RICHARD CROSS.—Mr. Gladstone's attention having been drawn to a state- ment by Sir Richard Cross that his policy had been ( forced upon him by Irish rebels, telegraphed as fol- lows to Mr. Maitland, of Rainhill :--" Not one word of truth in the reported allegation of Cross. Chal- lenge him to prove it. My declaration that this ! great question was coming forward was made in Edinburgh; November 9 (see letter to Bright), when I knew nothing about Fenian outrages." THE BIRKENHEAD SHow.—Entries for this show, which comprises horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry, pigeons, dogs, cheese, butter, , horticulture, and machinery, close to-day (Saturday). The show is to be held at Birkenhead on the 28th, 29th, and 30th days of the present month, and prizes to the amount of £l,OOO are to be awarded. It will make the 44th exhibition. Prizes well -Worth competing for are offered, and, according to the number of entries already received in the various classes, an excellent show will result. Complete arrange- ments have been made both for visitors and ex- hibitors. The band of the Royal Irish Constabulary will perform selections of music each day,

A LOVE QUARREL AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. G-. Pilkington, John Sadler, clerk of works at the New Town Hall, and Thomas Sherratt, a teacher of music, were charged with assaulting Charles William Cooper, manager of the boot shops in Widnes trading under the name of "The London Boot Repairing Company." Cross summonses for a like offence had been issued against Cooper. —Mr J W Knowles represented Cooper, and Mr H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, represented Sadler and Sherratt —The facts, as stated by Mr. Knowles, who characterised the assault as , a cowardly and brutal attack upon his client, "a mere boy," were to the effect that on the evening of the Ist inst. lie was returning from a walk, when a dog belonging to Mrs. , Sadler began to chase his dog, which snapped at its pursuer. Mrs. Sad lee thereupon called bins a fool, a scamp, and a rascal. Cooper replied, "Any one would think from the way you talk you had been reared in a pigstye." Later in the evening Cooper, accompanied by his Im:l4:Brady's son Stan- ley, saw Sadler and Sherratt near Dr. O'Keeffe's residence, sod Sadler asked, "What do you mean by saying that my wife was brought up in a pigstye ?" Sherratt jomped about in an ex- cited manner and 5110Uted "Why, why, why." It was at leged that Sadler would not listen to any explanation, hut attacked Cooper, who had both his eyes blackened and his nose injured. Sherratt, it was stated, aidPd his brother-in- law. Mr. Knowles informed the Bencb that Cooper was the accepted lover of a young lady whom Sidler's wife wished her brother Sherratt t) have. Theeung lady had rejected Sherratt, and `-hetice a grievance against Cooper.—En-
deavours to settle the matter amicably_ were made without i

_ avail, and the evidence was heard. The above statement was spoken to by the complainant, and Thomas Stanley, of Vine-street.—Mr. Riley contended that the case was of such a trifling character that it came within the class which the law said could be dismissed by the Bench. Having regard to the fact that there was a spite between the parties, it was only natural that the words used by Cooper should heighten it, and it was not surprising that Sadler should as him whether he did think that the lady members of the family with which he sought to ally him- self did betray the way of the pig stye. (Laughter.)— Thomas Sherratt, one of the defendants, stated that Cooper Put his face near to Sadler's face in an insulting way, and Sadler pushed him away. He then ktrack Mr. s.adler on the left ear, and a fight ensued. Stanley went to aid Cooper, and then Sherratt interfered.—Dr. Olieeffe said he saw Sadler and another young man boxing. Immediately after- wards Sadler was attacked by another man, and then Mr. Sherratt went to his assistance, and all four were fighting.— The Bench dismissed the summonses.
