MTh. BRUNNER'S MEETINGS.--A Mass Meeting of working-men supporters of the Liberal can- didate for the Northwich Division will be held this (Saturday), afternoon on Runcorn Heath. Mr. W. Summers, the new M.P. for Huddersfield, will be amongst the speakers. The same evening there will be a meeting in the Central Hall, Northwich. On Monday evening there will be two gatherings in support of Mr. Brunner—one in the Market Hall, Winsford, and another in the Middlewich Centenary School. Mn. VERDIN'S MEETINGS.—Three meetings are to be held on Monday in support of the candidature of Mr. Robert Verdin, "the Liberal Unionist," one in the Drill Hall, Northwich ; a second in the Public hail, Runcorn; and the third in the Town Winsford. FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH CHOIR TRIP.—The annual outing of the adult mernhers of the Frodsham Parieh Church choir took place on Thursday, when, favoured with splendid weather, a pleasant day was spent in renewing acquaintance with the various places of_ interest in and near Southport. LACEY-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.— The anniversary was celebrated on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. Ebenezer Jenkins. of London. in the after- noon Mr. Wm. Oul ton, J.P., of Liverpool, delivered an ad- dress to the scholars. Special hymns were eung on each occasion, and the collections realised upwards of £7O. MAIN OF BOWLS AT RUNCORN.—Mr. W. Jaekson, pro- prietor of the Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, on Thursday opened the bowling green attached to his house with a I main of bowls. There were 48 entries, and the crack j bowlers of the district. and Warrington and Northwich, competed. The first prize, worth £2, was won by Mr. Gleave, of Warrington, and the second by Mr. Forster, of North wi ch. FAILURE IN THE. CHESHIRE SALT TRADE.— A petition has , been filed in the Naetwich and Crewe County Cou. t on be- half of Joe.ah Frith, of Chester and Winsford, salt man- ufacturer. The gross liabilities are over £lO,OOO, the greet bulk unsecured. The assets, excluding the debtor's house- hold furniture, amount to £370. The causes assigned for the failure are depression of trade and unremunerative prices of• salt. There are over 100 creditors. ALLEGED PASSING OF COUNTERFEIT COIN. John Williams, who said he came from Liverpool, was on Tues- day at Widnes Police Court charged with utteriag a counterfeit half-crown to Mrs. Atkinson, who keeps a stationer's shop in Victoria-road, and one to Mrs Outram, of the Swan Inn, Waterloo-road. 'The prisoner, when appre- hended, had also a base coih in his possession. He was re- manded for further inquiries to be made. BATHING FATALITY AT Ruercorts.—A boy named James Hines, stepson of Felix McConn, labourer, Mersey-street, was drowned in the Mersey at Runcorn on Tuesday night. Hines, who was nearly 16 years of age, was t.athing at Pickow Rocks, when he dived beneath the water. He did not reappear, and on ae search being made the youth was found by a man named James Atherton, unconscious. Every effort was made to restore animation, but withoet success. An inquest was held on Thursday before Mr. J. E. Worsley, and a verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned. SAD BATHING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Thomas Rollin- son, nine years of age, son of Edwin Rollinson, wheel- wright, of 6, Arthur-street, Widnes, met with a sail death by drowning on Tuesday evening. With several other boys he was bathing in a pit in Pulheuee-lane, when he sank. His companions raised an alarm, and `.7illiam, Beesley, a lehoprer, of Foeter-etreet, dived fate the water and brought up the boy alive. Every effort' to restore animation failed, and the boy died. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned at the inquest on Wednesday. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Thursday afternoon Mr. Fred Lea, of the firm of Messrs. Lea and Sons, painters and plumbars, met with a serious accident. He was taking part in the painting of the outside of Mr. Matthew's shop in Victoria-road, and tor this purpose was standing on a scaf- feld about ten feet high. A ladder leaning against the wall near by was blown down by the wind, and in its descent struck Mr. Lea on the head, and knocked him to the greund. He Was attended by Drs. O'Keeffe and MacLennan, and afterwards removed to the accident, hospital, where he lies in a precarious condition. PROPERTY SALE AT FRODSHAM.—OD Tuesday, Mr Har- rop held a sale by auction at the Commercial Hotel, Frod- sham, when the following lots were offered, viz. :—A field close to the Frodsham Railway station containing la Or 35p, was sold to Mr George Sharrock for £l9O. Twenty shares of £1 each fully paid up in the Frodsharn Gas Company, Limited, were knocked down to Mr H Clough, for LI 17s 6d each. The mowing grass on "The Elolpoot " meadow, con- taining 25a 3r, situate on Frodsham Marsh, was purchased by Mr Joseph Enema for forty guineas. There was no offer for two semi-detached houses in Frodsham, lately in the occupatiou of Mr Cameron and Mr Fairhurst. The " Hol- pool Meadow," situate on Frodsham Marsh, and containing 25e 3r, was withdrawn at £l,OOO. ATTACK ON Mn. BRUNNER.—On Wednesday, while Mr. Brunner, the Liberal candidate for Northwich, together with Mrs Brunner and others, was enjoying the hospitality of the Vicar of St. John's, Over, an excited mob of non- voters assembled outside. When Mr. Brunner and his party drove out of the grounds an attempt was made to upset the trap and drag the coachman from his seat. Both attempts having failed, mud-throwing was resorted to, and the party were profusely bespattered. Stones were also thrown though no one was injured. Mr. and Mrs. Brunner have again been victims of AD eutrageous assault. On Thursday night as they were driving from an opsn air meeting at Moulton, where the works of the Unionist candidate are situated, a gang of ruffians pelted them with seot, mud, clods, and old shoes. Mrs. Brunner was struck violently on the breast with tine missile. 'Frantic efforts were made to Irighten the horse, but fortunately without success. SCENE AT THE WIDNES MODEL LODGING HOUSE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, a woman named Min- nie Lynch was charged with assaulting William Roberts, manager of the Model Lodging House in Lugsdale-road. On the 2nd inst. the woman, who had been lodging at the "Model," complained of a beef stake Roberts bad cooked for her, and threw a 71b. weight at him. ' He took no notice of that because he thought it was a hit of a joke. (Laughter.) She then took possession of the house, and would not let him attend to his duties. The defendant was also charged with threatening Mr. Alfred Bronchemite, the proprietor of the lodging house. She had broken a win- dow of the house, kept in wait for him with a glass bottle, and had threatened to take his life. She was a wicked woman, and would use either imife or revolver.—The woman was fined 103 and costs in the first cese, and a war- rant was issued for her apprehension in the second. CONSECRA.TION OF A NEW CEMETERY AT HALTON. The consecration of the Church of England portion of the new cemetery at Halton took place on Saturday by the Right. Rev. the Lord Bishop of Cheater. A procession was formed at the vicarage in the following order :—Members of the Burial Board; Messrs. .1. Barrow, J. W. Haddock. R. Elrighes, J. Looker, H. Rowe, J. Rutter, and J. S. Jeacock, secretary to the Board ; Messrs. J. Rutter and J, Stokes (wardens); J. Ackerlev, W. Nixon, and A. Woodier (sides- men ; choir, men and boys. Clergy: Revs. Canon Heron, M.A., rural dean of Bowdon; Canon Greene'', M.A., rector of Crrappeohall, and rural dean of Frodsharn ; Edward Marsden, M.A., vicar of Aston ; William Preston, M.A., , incumbent of Holy Trinity, Runcorn ; W. Fielding, 8.A., curate of Aston ; T. Manton Armson, curate of Runcorn ; and Robert Edwards, curate-in-charne of Newtown Mission Church, Runcorn ; the Bishop and his secretary (Mr. Richard Farmer.) On arriving at the cemetery, the pro- cession formed on each side the rcad, when the Rev. J. Lockwood, as chairman of the Burial Board, unlocked the gates, and on the arrival of the Bishop at the entrance, handed to his lordship a humble petition from the Board on behalf of the parishioners of Halton, to consecrate the por- tion set apart and appropriated for the burial of deceased persons according to the rites and usages of the Church of England. The procession then formed again, and proceeded round the ground, the Bishop and clergy repeating alter- nately the verses of the 40th and 90th Pselins, after which his lordship's secretary read the sentence of consecration of the burial ground, which was afterwards signed by the Bishop in the presence of the people, and aiso by the Rev. Thomas tireepall, M.A., rector of Orappenhall, rural dean of Frodsham ; the 12,v. George Hero,' , rural dean of Bowdon; and attested by Farmer. The hymn, "Brief life is here our portion," was then sung, and the proceed- ings were brought to a close by a few prayers and the bless- ing. A large crowd assembled both inside and outside the cemetery. Sir Richard and Lely Brooke and family were present at the ceremony. The procession was again formed in the reverse order, and repaired to the school, where a substantial tea was provided. The contractors, Messrs. William Ashley, John Howard. and T. Sinipkin, of Run- corn, present at the proceedings. Mr. Siinkin, n masona,O'f RE:tricorn, has • kindly presented the Board with e were ls two slabs of Aberdeen granite, which have been sto placed on the entrance pillars. On the one in bold gold letters is " Halton Cemetery," and on the other " Consecra- ted 3rd July, 1586." On Sunday morning the vicar preached an interesting sermon from the striking and suitable text, taken from Genesis xxiii, 4th verse, "Give me a burying place that I may bury my dead," which was attentively , listened to by a good congregation.,

div.head: METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. NEW SUNDAY SCHOOL. _ .
div.p: METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. NEW SUNDAY SCHOOL. _ .

Under most favourable atmospheric conditions, the , memorial stone of the new Sunday school in course of erection in connection with the Zion Chapel, Oakland-street, Widnes, were laid on Saturday afternoon. A conviderable audience, consisting of members of the congregation and other friends of the cause, assembled to witness the inter- esting ceremony. On the platform which had been erected were the Rev. W. \rause, the resident pastor, the Rev. J. D. Tbonue, Congregational minister, Runcorn, Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, Birkenhead, J. Houghton, and the chapel choir. The school, w,hich is to adjoin the Chapel, is to be 53 feet in length, by 31 feet 6 inches in breadth, and is estimated to accommodate 300 persons. Mr. Thos. Sadler is the builder, and 'anticipates to conclude the contract by September. Devotional exercise having been engaged in, The Rev. W. VAUEIe gave a 'few facts relative to the posi- tion of the congregation. About thirteen years ago, he said, the building on his right was erected to serve the purposes both of a school and chapel, but one part of that building was occupied by pews. During these thirteen years there had been a considerable increase in the number of scholars, and the building was new no longer large enough for them. There were up,at the books 272 scholars and 35 teachers, and it is has therefore become necessary for them to erect that new building, which was to serve the purposes of a school only. A year ago the:, had not a single penny to- wards the new building, but during the winter their friends had been bard at work, and their efforts had been very suc- ceesful. About three months ago they held a bazar which reale.ei over £100; they had a harvfst tha.nkseiving lest autumn that produced between .£23 and £24 ; and by :neans of sewing meetings held from week to week, about £4O had been secured. Tuey had therefore about £l5O or £l6O towards the new school. He did not suppose that the school would cost much less than £5OO, so that they were still open to receive as mach as they were eireparel to give. Mr. \rause then presented a trowel, with a suitable inscrip- tion to

Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, who laid the first stone. In a brief speech 11l said he should always be happy to do anything he could to show his sympathy with the people of Widnes and anything which was lot .the good of the town. (Applause.) Mr. Robert Shaw. of Runcorn, should have laid the second stone, but he was unable to be present through a had cold. He forwarded a letter of apology and a cheque for five guineas. his place was taken by Mr. Birkenhead, who suitably performed the functions required of him. Mr. Vause remarked that Messrs. Gossage and Timmis had given him £lO towards the school, and he had received five guineas from Mr. Shaw and three guineas from Mr. Deacon ; sa that they had made a good start that afternoon with £lB. A collection was then made, and the proceedings concluded with a rote of thanks to Mr. Deacon and Mr. Bir- kenhead for their services, carried on the proposition of the Rev. J. D. Thomas.

div.head: THREATENING MR. 11.
div.p: THREATENING MR. 11.

At Warrington Borough Court, yesterday morn- ing, James Shaw was summoned for using threaten- ing language to Henry Whitham, on the day of the polling for the Warringon borough election. Mr. A. Browne appeared in support of the summons, and Mr. Fox represented the deendant. Before the case was gone into, Captain Reynolds, one of the magistrates on the bench, asked if it arose in re- gard to politics; if so he should not care to take part in deciding upon it. Mr. Browne, in reply, said that although the threats were used on the day of the election, they had nothing to do with politics. Captain Reynolds thereupon retained his seat, and Mr. Browne, proceeding with the case, said that it arose out of a trade dispute. Several years ago a strike occurred at the works of Messrs. Rylands, where complainant and defendant both worked at that time. Since then there had been always some difference between Mr. Whitham and certain of the men, which culminated on the elec- tion day in defendant using the threats complained of. Mr. Whitham was personation agent for the north-east polling station in John-street, and, whilst he was at the door waiting for the arrival of voters, 'defendant came up. In the presence of a number of witnesses., defendant used offensive language to the complainant, said "lie would take it out of him, and, "if he would only came out" he "would give it . He also said that he would give .£5 if complainant would come into the street, and "let . take it out of him," and that complainant was ruining the trade. Evidence was then given in support of this statement by Hy. Whitham, 170, Manchester-rd. ; Benjamin Farrer, assistant manager at Messrs. Rylands' works ; P.S. Cox and P.C. Bracewell, of the Borough force.—ln defence, Mr. Fox contended that the prosecution was a frivolous one, and called witnesses.—The defendant, who was first called, said that he took a man to the booth on Friday, and told him to put his cross to Greenall's name. Complainant took hold of his arm and pushed him. Defendant then told him that if he pushed him again he would knock his head off. He did not mean to do any injury to Mr. Whitham. In answer to Mr. Browne, he said that when he got outside he started to curse Mr. Whitham. lie had had soinething to drink, in fact he had .seven gills of ale, three lemonades, and two "lemon dashes." (Laughter.) Mr. R. W. Francomb, chairman of the North-East Polling nistriet, said his atten- tion was called to the disturbance, and he put an end to it.—The Mayor asked whether there was any possibility of amicably settling the case, by both parties shaking hands.—Defundant said he was willing to shake hands with anybody. (Laughter.) —The Mayor: Are you willing to shake hands with Mr. Whitham ?—Defendant : Yes, I am willing to shake hands with him, if he will shake hands with me.—Mr. Whitham said he would be willing to shake hands under ordinary circumstances; but he considered it would only be a farce to do so on this occasion.—The Mayor then .said that the proceed- ings were not calculated to increase good-feeling between the parties. The language used by the de- fendant was undoubtedly calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, even if he had not used threats. Considering the excitement of the election, he thought the justice of the case would be met by binding the defendant over in Jiis own recognizances of -1-70 to keep the peace for six months.

THE ELECTIONS.—On Monday Mr. Webster, bar- rister, stepson of the Rector of Warrington, Mr. Quekett, was returned as a Conservative for St. Pancras, receiving 2,327 votes, as against 1,826 for his opponent, Mr. T. E. Gibb. Colonel Hamilton, who has some connection with this district, was also re-elected for Rotherhithe. OCCASIONAL COURT.—At an Occasional Court held yesterday, at the offices in Bank-street, four men named Thomas Sanders, John Haydock, Isaac Kirkham, and John Wilkinson, were charged with assaulting Martin Cawfield and Martin Barnett, at Little Leigh, on the 3rd inst. They were remanded to the next Petty Sessional meeting at Dares- bury. Lvir BAND.—A number of brass instruments, for the members of the Lymm Church of England Temperance Society Band, which has recently been formed, arrived a -few days ago from the well- known firm of Messrs. Besson and Co., Euston-road, London. The instruments will be the property of the Church of England Temperance Society Com- mittee, who will have the band under . their con- trol.

KILLED ON THE RAILWAY AT Moong.—On Satur- day. an inquest was held ar the Red Lion Inn, Moore; by Mr. J. E. Worsley, deputy coroner, as to the death of Hannah Dunbobbin, aged 28. Deceased was the wife of a platelayer employed on the Lon- don and North7Westlrn Railway. and had been in the habit of carrying her husband's dinner to him. On Friday she was returning from this errand when she was knocked down by an express and killed instantaneously. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

BOWLING HANDICAP AT PADGATE.—On Saturday the new green attached to the Stocks Inn, at Pad- gate, was opened by a handicap main of bowls, open to all England. Owing to the short notice that was given, only 32 players competed. The green was in fair condition, and the weather being all that could be desired for this popular summer game, some well- contested games were the result. The proprietor (Mr. J. Hayes) gave a copper kettle, and the players subscribed is each. The following are the results:- 1, James Bridge, kettle and lOs ; 2, T. Holbrook, Ss; , 3, T. Lee, 4s; 4, G. Ball, sen., 4s; and B. Tomlinson, G. Ball, jun., W. Bolton, and C. Littlewoodt, is Cxl sii. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, July 3rd, 1886.-The mean temperature was 60 Fahr., and therefore 3-4 deg. warmer than the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 71 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 6th inst., and the minimum temperature, 49 Fahrenheit, on the sth inst. The rainfall measured nil. The general direction of the wind was N. During the week, which was the 27th of the current year, 41 births and 17 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19-07 per 1,000, against 19.9, th e average of the previous four weeks, and against 20-5 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from aptha, 1 from old age, 2 tubercular disease, 3 brain disease, 2 phthisis, 3 lung disease, 2 cancer, 1 heart disease.—Jxo. H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

CROFT BURIAL SOCIETY.—The quarterly meeting of the above society was held at the registered office of the society, the General Elliott. Hotel, Croft, on Saturday. Mr. James Shaw, a member of the committee, was appointed chairman. The Secre- tary, Mr. Alfred Dixon, stated that he had for- warded the particulars required for the quinquen- nial valuation of the above society to Mr. William Somerville, of Birkenhead, who was appointed the actuary to complete the same at the last quarterly meeting of the society, and that the work was in progress, and he hoped to receive a duplicate copy of the actuary's report in a few days, when it would be necessary to call a special meeting of the com- mittee, trustees, and officers to adopt the same as soon as received. . He had written to the Registrar of Friendly Societies informing him that the valua- tion was taking place, and that the result would be torwarded to the central office as soon as completed. —lt was resolved that 500 copies of the actuary's report on the condition of the society be printed and distributed by the secretary and collector.

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE PARTY VIOLENCE AT
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE PARTY VIOLENCE AT
WARRINGTON.

An outbreak of party violence of a very discredit- able and destructive character took place in hail- street, Warrington, about midnight of Friday last week, the day of the, borough election, The suf- ferers from the violence were Mesers.. Sexton Bros. merchants, who, being Irish voters, seem to, have been suspected, like most of their compatriots, of leaning to the Liberal side of politics. About twelve o'clock one of the Messrs. Sexton was returning home along Hall-street with a horse and shandry, when he was set upon by a crowd of people, many of whom seemed to be very much under the com- bined influences of drink and .excitement, and the horse was sorely maltreated. The horse and vehicle were with considerable difficulty got into the yard behind Messrs. Sexton's premises, but a determined attack was then made upon the gate of the yard, which was ultimately broken down, and much damaged. The yard was then inundated with people bent on mischief or plunder. A large dog which was chained up, and therefore , could neither defend itself nor make an es- cape. A fi .vas beaten by a number. of cowardly ruf- fians till it appeared to be more dead than alive. Others made an attack on a wooden structure which is used as a stable, and after pulling the front of it down and doing other damage, turned the horses out into the yard. Messrs. Sexton being large im- porters. of eggs,. a great quantity of these were stored in crates in the yard, and large numbers of them were destroyed; and, indeed, the mob, which evidently contained a good deal of the roughest element of the town, was as maliciously destruc- tive as it possibly could be. It is estimated that before the premises were finally cleared of the law- less aggressors, something like £4O worth of damage was done to Messrs. Sexton's property. We have not heard that any of the police witnessed the scene of violence, but, there can be no doubt. the in- stigators or leaders of this entirely inexcusable out- break of lawlessness should be severely dealt with, if for. no other reasons than to maintain the credit of the town and to prevent similar occurrences. .The sense of security of the town at election times would be ,severely shaken if it was thought that partisan attacks of this description on peaceable tradesmen might pass unheeded and unpunished.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Moanae—Before the Mayer (Alderman Harrison) and Alderman Davies. Diateritemnas.— Sarah Ellen Wilkinson was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on Satur- day evening. She WAX released from prison on Saturday morning, met some friends at Manchester, with whom she had drink, and on reaching Warrington met other friends and had some more drink. She was allowed to go.— Martha Cottam was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Church-street on Saturday night. She said that she was excited awl shouted " Greenall for ever "—it was an exciting time. (Laughter.) She was ordered to pay ls, the lock-up fee.--Mary Scully, cherged with being drunk and disorderly on Seturday night, was ordered to pay the loce-up fee.--Patrick Fillhurn, for being drunk in Win- wick-street the same morning, was fined 2s 6d, including costs.—John Conway was charged with being drunt and disorderly in Dial-street and was fined 5s and costs ; and Binary Hines, charged with being drunk and disorderly on Town Hill, wan discharged with a caution. The latter de• fondant caused some amusement by referring to Chief Constable Hunt and the Mayor as " love." On being die- mimed she remarked " God bless you, Mr. Harrison, six times over "—(lanahter)—and anethemetised a constable as she left the court. DinralrDlNG TITS RAILWaT COMPANY.—lhomaa Pittick and Michael Finnan, Irish farm labourers. were charged with riding in second-class carriage- with third-class tickets on the London and North-Western Railway, from Heady to Warrington.—Mr. Ferrand appeared for the rail- way company and said that on arriving at Werrington de- fendants refused I. pay the excess fare, saving that they bad been told to go into the carriage at Heatley.—The magistrates fined them 2s dd each, including coves. I:LIaD/Y.—Before Alderman Davies and Mr. F. Monks. WIFZ ASSAIILT.—Jovn Hardy was charged with having assaulted his wife Ellen Hardy, on the 3rd July. Com- plainant said that on Saturday night she followed defend- ant for his wages when he struck her twice in the face and kicked her. For lout teen weeks she had only received 23. from defendant. On the other band defendant affirmed that his wife was always drunk on the Saturdays and Mon- days, and in fact was the 'drunksnnest " woman in War- rington. He was fined lOs and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. TRURSDAT.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. Snuartwo Our —James Johnson. Edward Sauce, Bridget Lally, and Elizebeth Nutt, for sleeping out in Arpley fields, were sent to prieee for seven days' each. R7nrUsING TO Wonx.—John Woods, for refusing to per- form his task of work while a casual inmate or the vagrant ward at the Unicat Workhouse, was sent to prison for four- teen days. Assarnr.—Ed ward Sauce was charged with assaulting Margaret O'Brien in Academy-street, on the previous even- ing, was sent to prison for two months.. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Captain Revrolds, and Alderman Burgess. AssenneeNG A Moerisn.—John Welsh was charged on a warrant with aeseulting his mother, Bridget Welsh. He was ordered to be bound over, himself in £lO, and one surety in £lO, or go to prison for a month. Soate TIRED.—J4mes Burns was charged with being an absentee from her Majesty's Liverpool Regiment since ten o'clock on the previous night. He was apprehended by P.C. 16, and on the way to the station remarked that he had only nine week,' service, and was tired of it. The magis- trates directed that prisoner sheuld be handed over to the military authorities. MAINTENANCE Cass.—John George was ordered to pay 24 a week towards the maintenance of his grandchild, Milly tieorge. THREATS.—AIice Welsher WAS summoned for using threats to Alice Denmain, on the 13th ult. The case was dismissed. —Catherine Carey was summoned by Martha Davies for a similar offence. Dismissed. Aesertr CAPES.—Elizabeth Pritchard was summoned by Elizabeth Shaw for assaulting her on the 3rd inst. She was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to eay the costs of the case.—Sarah Massey was summoned for aesaulting Thomas Bailey and Margaret Clifford on the 3rd inst. It was stated that defendant assaulted Mrs Clifford, and threw a steno at that person's husband, which, however. hit Bailey, who was stand• ing near at the the time, and made both his eyes black. She was fined £l, in all £2 2e, or 14 days' imprisonment. She signified her intention of taking the alternative of imprisonment —Jas. Tarpy was charged with assaulting Mary Tarpey on the 3rd inst. It appeared that defendant had regularly subjected his wife to ill-treatment although he lived on her earnings. lhe Bench theuglt the case an aggravated one, and sent elefeo- •dant to prison for three months, allowing the wife a judicial -separation.—Kate Kelly was summoned by Louisa Mallet for assaulting her on the 3rd inst. The case was dismiss-d. —Martha Talbot was charged with assault on the corn- plaint of Mary Coburn.—Dismissed.—Ann Jordan was summoned for assaulting Celia Loftus. The case was dis- missed.--John Denton WAR charged with assaultinc Geo. Lang, a foreman in the employ of the Warrington Carriage Company. Defendant Was in the employ of the company, and on Monday he left his work without notice. On Tues- day he returned and asked complainant if he had got stopped. and the reply wes that he had. Defendant then struck him. The Bench imposed a fine of 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprieonment. WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WinentsPer.—Sefore Messrs. P. Stubs, R. Houghton, J. Tinsley, and W. F. Gooch. ASSATTLT.—James Hudson and Samuel Kninht were sum- moned for assaulting Edward Lawless, and Harriet Hudson for assaulting JAlllrs J. Brooke, on the 13th June.—Mr. A. Browne appeared to prosecute, and said that complainant Brook was a farmer at Rixton, and Lawless was a labourer in his employ. On the evening of the day in question Law- -less was working in the fields, when Hudson and Knight 'commenced throwing stones at him. He complained to his master, who, in the evening, went to the house where the fiudsons' lived to ask the reason why they had thrown stones at his labourer. Thereupon Mrs. Hudson rushed at him and struck him on the eve. The defence was that provocation had been received.—They were each fined 5s and costs. , CHAIM' AGAINST A PCSLICAIf —Samuel Kilshall WAX charged with permitting drunkenness on his licensed pre- mises at Burtonwood—the Elm Tree beerhouse—on the let of last month, and Patrick Mul.nev was charged with being drunk on the premises. P.S. Carnes proved the case. —Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of the defendants, and said that Mulaney bad been to Newton races, where he had bad drink, but was by no means intoxicated. IHe was ac- customed to read the newspapers at Kilshall's house to the company present, and en the evening in question did so by the light of a eendle.—The cases were dismissed.

div.head: GENERAL ELECTION.
div.p: THE GENERAL ELECTION.

At Huddersfield Mr. Summers, at one time the expected Gladstoniau candidate for Burnley, has secured a Minis- teriAl triumph over Mr. Crosland (C). Mr. Talbot and Sir Hussey Vivian, who have been re- turned unopposed for Mid-Glamorgan and Swansea Dis- trict respectively, now support the Irish policy of Mr. Glad- stone.

Serious disturbances occurred at Cardiff after the declara- tion of the poll at midnight on Wednesday. A large num- ber of persons were more or less seriously injured, and some 20 casts were treated in the infirmary. Mr. Gladstone will not return to town till early next week. A meeting of the Cabinet will be summoned for Tues- day or Wednesday, when a decision will be arrived at as to the course the Government shall take in view of the result of the general election. It war rumoured a day or two ago that the return of Mr. Duncan (Liberal) for the Exchange Division of Liverpool was to be petitioned against. It is now stated that the re- quisite money deposit has been lodged,and that the petition is to be proceeded with. On Wednesday Mr. Gladstone telegraphed that the state- ' meet made toy Mr. Chamberlain in Wales that Mr. CAMp• bell-Sennerman had asserted that the Prime Mini.ter had placed himself in a position to know ti.e opinions of the Irish-Americans and receive suggestions from them is abso- lutelv false.

A New York correspondent telegraphs that money con- tinues to pour in for the Parnell Fund from all quarters. Fifteen thousand dollars have been received within a week, the largest sum yet subscribed in the same time. The American papers look upon. the temporary defeat of Horne Rule as certain now, but conshier its ultimate triumph as inevitable; no other solution they think being possible. Such was the extraordinary prosperity that Ireland reach- ed under Grattan's Parliament that, although the popula- tion of Ireland was then as large as at present, yet Ireland found employment for her owp people without emigration, and without sending Irish labourers to compete is the Eng- lish labour market. Such is the testimony of Lord Clare, an impartial witness, since be was one of the most unscru- pulous authors of the Union. Mr. Malcolm Mac Coll asks :—"ls it net morally certain that a similar cause would produce a similar result now ?" Chelsea borough has never been so closely canvassed as during this election, and the result has been that Sir C. Dilke (M) has been beaten by Mr. C. A. Whitmore (C) by a majority of 176. sir Charles has had a bard fight, owing chiefly to the unworthy use his opponents made of the un- fortunate social scandal with which his name is connected. So cowardly and manifestly unjust were the means resorted to, that several ladies were urged to action by it, and during the last three days of the contest canvassed unceasingly for Sir Charles. At most of his meetings Sir C. Mike was re- ' ceived with enthusiasm. A remarkable result took place at Ashton-under-Lyne, where Mr. J. E. W. Addison, Q.C. (C), and Mr. A. B. Row- ley (L) each bad 3,049 votes recorded. The casting vote of the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Walker, a Conservative) was Riven to Mr. Addison, who was declared elected. Result of last election :—Addison, (C), 3,164: Mason. H. (L), 3,118. It is said that on the last occasion 294 Irish votes were given for Mr. Addison. On this occasion the Irish vote went solid for Mr. Rowley, and his victory would have been assured but for the defection of some Liberal Unionists, estimated at 60 at the outside.

Sir John Swinburne, Gladstonian candidate for Lichfield Division, Staffordshire, has issued the following instruc- tions to his bailiff:—On the polling days give each Parlia- liamentary elector in my employment a reasonable time for polling, and every man his wages as if he had b.en at wore all the day. (2) Abstain from asking them for whom they are going to vote. (3) Do not advise any of them upon petition). matters. (4) If any of my workmen or labourers speak to you on the subject, inform him that I hope every man will vote according to his own convictions. (5) If any workman or labourer asks you about the ballot, assure him it is quite secret. At Grimsby, where Mr. Heneage (U L) was elected over Mr. Sutherst (M) by a majoriry of 333, an extraordinary scene occurred immediately after the declaration of the poll, which was made from the balcony of the Town Hall.—Mr. Heneage, on coming forward to spiak, was met with cheers, groans, and hooting, continued for a minute or two. He moved a vote of thanks to the mayor' as returning officer, and exoreesed his thanks to those who had voted for him.— Mr. Suthere, who was also received with mingled demon- strations. after seconding the vote of thanks, declared the election had been won by fraud. The Tories had combined with the weak-kneed Whige, but the true Liberal& would yet drive Mr. Heneage from the borough or right into the I arms of the Tories. He concluded by calling for three cheers for Mr. Gladstone, which were heartily given. Lord Randolph Churchill having stated at Paddington that the Premier was spending a large amount of secret service money to aid the reture o;) candidates favourable to his policy, Mr. J. kilbournerof Walsall, wrote to Mr. Glad- stone on the subject, and has recei-red the following reply: "Downieg-street, Whitehall, Jul", 2. 1886. Sir,-1 am desired by Mr. Gladstone to acleaowledge the receipt of your letter, calling attention to a passage in Lord R.. Churcbill's recent speech on the totbject of Secret Service money. The statement there made is a gross untruth. Mr. Gladstone has nothing to do with this monev.or its adrainis- tratioe, but it is true that 1.5,0001 have been paid to the Secretary of the Treasury of the present Government and £7.500 to the Secretary of the Treasury of the party to which Lord R. Churchill beloegs.-1 am air, your obedient servant, a W SPaNCER LYTTLETON." At Liverpool several disi,raceful scenes were witnessed during the election. Oa Friday night a Liberal gentleman. a member of the Reform Club. accepted the invitation of a Conservative friend to go to the Conservative Club, in Dale street, to await the return. of the day's elections.. Dur- ing the temporary absence of his. friend the gentleman was pointed to in jeet by a Conservati-ae as a Radical who bad voted for Sir T. Brassey. The visitor was sitting at a table at the time, and behind him was standing a Conservative member of the City Council and a magistrate. Without any warning whatever, the latter seismi the visitor and sung him violently to the ground. When the victim rose-from the door he was suddenly attacked by several members of the club, aided by the magistrate, and again thrown to the _

ground. He endeavoured to escape, but was overtaken on the stairs by his assailant, who lien invited him to go up stairs and have a bottle of champagne to make the filarrel up. On this invitation being refused the assailant en- deavoured to shake his victim's hand. Failing in this, the magistrate rrffered to send him a written apology, besides subscribing £5O to some local charity. We understand that this offer was refused, and that the gentleman who suffered the injury is contemplating the advisability of taking legal action against the magistrate. In West Derby Division, immedittely after the declaration of the poll on Friday night, a crowd, numbering upwards of 500, headed by a fife and drum band, paraded the streets, and in passing the Liberal Association rooms in Lowhill smashed the windows with stones which they had collected in the neighbourhood. A similar outrage was perpetrated at the south end of the city on the &Imo" night. Fights have been numerous in the lower parts of Toatett..-park, and as a result the medical staff at the Southern Hospital have been kept very busy, between 50 and 00 cases being treated on Saturday and Sun- day, most of which were caused by faction fights.

MR. GLADSTONE AND MR BRIGHT. Mr. Gladstone has written the following letter to Mr. Bright :—" Hawarden, July 2nd, 1880.—My dear Bright,— lam sorry to be compelled again to address von. In your speech you charge me with having successfully concealed my thoughts last November. You ought to have known that this was not a fact, for in reply to others from whom this gross charge was more to be expected than from you. I pointed out last week that, on the 9th November, in Edinburgh, I told my constituents that if the II ishelections went as was expected, the magnitude of the subject they would bring forward would throw all others into the shade, and that it 'went down to the very roots and founda- tions of oar whole civil and political constitution.' , (Midlothian Speeches, 1885, p. 44.) Do you now adhere to your accusation ? (2) You say I have described a conspiracy row existing in Ireland as marchinrt through rapine to the break-up of the United Kingdom. This also is contrary to the fact. In 1881 there was, in my opinion, such a conspiracy against t`le payment of rent and the union of the countries, and I so riennbtql it. In my opinion there is no such conspiracy now, nor anything in the least degree resembling it. You

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1888.

put into my mouth words which, coming from me, would be absolute falsenood. (3) You charge me with want of frankness because I have not pledged the Government to POMO defined line of action with regard to the Land Purchase Bill. A charge of this kind as between old colleagues and old friends is, to say the least, unusual. Evidently you have not read the bill or my speech ea its introduction, and you have never been concerned in the practical work of legisla- tion on difficult and complicated subjeets. The foundation of your charge is that on one of the most difficult and most , complicated of all subjects I do not, in the midst of over- whelming work, formulate at once a new course or method of action without consulting the colleagues to whom I am so much bound, and from whom I receive invaluable aid. It might, I think, have occurred te you, as you have been in the CeDinet, that such a course on my part would have been indecent and disloyal, and I should greatly prefer to bear all the charges and suspicions which you are now un- expectedly the man to fasten upon me, for you state Iyou are convinced it is my intention to thrust the I Land Purchase Bill upon the House of Com- mons. If I am a man capable of such intention I wonder you ever took office with One so ignorant of I the spirit of the Constitution and so arbitrary I in its character. Though this appears to be. in your opinion held by my countrymen in general, you quote not a word ;in support of your charge. It is absolutely untrue. Every oandidate, friendly or unfriendly, will form his own view and take his own course on the subject. We must con- ! eider to the beat of our power all the facts before us, bat I certainly will net forego my right to make some effort to amend the dangerous and tniechievoce Land Purchase Law passed last yeatior Ireland, if such effort should promise to I raeet approval. 1 have done what I could to keep out of eontroveray with you; and, while driven to remonstrate ; against your charges, I advisedly abstained from all your etatemeete, criticisms, and argumente.—Always yours ain- , , eerety, W. E. ULADSTONB." Mr. John Bright nag addressed a letter to Mr. Gladstone, . in which he states that he has done what he could to keep out of the controversy with the Prime Minister, and ab- stained from speaking in public until he was in the face of his constituents, but to them be felt bound to explain his 1 opinion and judgment on the Irish bills. Ho stands by what he has said, and says he shall be surprised if the new Parliament be more favourable to the Irish measures than the one Mr. Gladstone has thought it necessary to dissolve.
WEDNESDAY.

RAILWAY COLLISION.—A serious collision, occurred on Monday mornine on the Caledonian Railway near Holy. town, between the ten o'clock express from Edinburvh to Glasgow and he eleven express from Glasgow to Euinburgli. Tee Glasgow train was ascending an incline when the axle of the locomotive broke, and the train lett. the metals and crossed the road to the other line, at Fulwood Junction. where the Edinteirgh train, coming down the gradient, smashed into it. The E:linburgh engine was wrecked, and the sides of several carriages were crushed in. The engine driver had both legs brokol, and other persons were in- jured. The CHAIRMAN, who is a very popular gentlemen, was received with ringing cheers, said he came there to evince his intense interest in the great inns now before the coin- try—(hear, hear)—and his deep interest in the candidature of his friend Mr. Birrell. (Cheers.) The question now be- fore the country was one of the most momentous ever placed before a nation, either in the chequered history of tbis country or of any other country. They, as Widnes electors, had it in their hands to say whether they would send a member to Parliament to assist Mr. Gladstone, their great leader, in passing that 'beneficent measure, that mes- sage of peace which he brought forward in the last Parlia- ment—(" We will '')—er whether they would send a Tory —(cries of "Ito," and hooting)—to help Lord Salisbury so that he might try to give them twenty years of coercion. ("Loud groane.) He eaid "try," because in his own opinion. coercion was as deed as a door nail. (" And always will JA.") It was for them to say whether they would let Mr. Gladstone peas that beneficent measure' which had his (Mr. Gladstonee) hearty approval, from a desire to let Ireland become a happy member of the United Kingdom, or whether they would let Lord Salisbury and his friends bring forward a measure on the earns question, considering that they would do it as enemies and as grudgingly as they could, and certainly spoil it. If they sent Mr. Sim!' to Parlia- ment he would vote for Mr. Gladstone, and they would have a measure passed which 'would certainly give peace to Ire- land, and give tleent a real, and not a paper union, as there had been for the last, eighty years. A fortnight ago Mr. Birrell came to them comparatively an unknown man. Since then their admiration for him had grown upon tern. All those who had' had the oppoitunity of listening ,to that admirable :wimp of speeches which he had delivered to them must feel attained that he was the right man. (Loud cheers.)_

Mr. BIREILL, who was greeted with loud and prolonged cheering, said the great question which they had to consider was whether they could safely put the measure of confidence in the Irish peop/b which Mr. Gladstone, their great leader —(epplause)—thought they could? (Hear, hear.) It was admieted by both parties. and not enly so, but by all three parties—the Toriesethe Liberals, and the third party, which was neither Liberal nor Tory, nor fish, flesh, fowl. nor good red herring—(laughter)—and who, calling themselves Unionists now, would soon call themselves Liberals and vote for Tories next week—(" shame ")—he said it was ad- mitted by all three parties that the whole and simple ques- tion was whether Mr. Gladstone was right in trusting the Irish people as he had proposed. (Cries of " Tea.") Lord elehsbury had said it was an act of folly and direct wicked- ness to place confidence in the Irish peep's. The noble lord had-said that the lush were no more fit for self-government than litatentots. (Laughter, and groans.) That was a most offensive thing for any man to say of a people; and even if he believed it was true, it was imprudent to say so. He asked what wasethe use of the Tories saying that their object was to maintain unbrokes the union between the two countries,, and then to insult the people who they said formed an integral part of the empire. It was not the way to make the relations between the two peoples amicable, and it was only stirring up discord te say that one nation was no more fit for self-government than Hottentots. It so happened,. however,, that in our colonies we bad granted self-government., and the Hottentots of South Africa had exercised those rights which were now to be denied te our Irish felloygoountrymen, who had for centuries enjoyed Parliamentary represestatios. Therefore. when Lord Salisbury and his friends denied to Ireland the privileges of self-governownt they were denying to Ireland that which they- bad already- extended to all ranks, classes, and religiens which composed our vast colonial system. When people told them that the Irish were incompetent to govern them- selves, thiry must prove that charge, which on the face of it was ridiculous and absurd, because the Irish who had large- ly emigrated or had had occasion to leave their own country and had goneeto the colonies were now found occupying prominent place and taking a leading part in the self- government which their opponents said they could not carry out in their own conntry. Was an Irishman less in- terested in the future and the good fortune of Ireland than in that of any other country ? ("No.") Was he not far more likely te,de all that in him lay to maintain the for- , tunes of his country, and to show that the assertions of the Conservatives-were nothing more than foul and false libels, nothing more than mere idle words to say in the faee of the plain historical fket,in the face of the position Irishmen had gained in one colonies, thist they were incompetent to govern thereselves. (AViplauee.) The Liberals now naturally asked their Conservative friends why they were unfit to perform the simplest functions any nation was called upon to perform, and they were told that they were not fit be- cause some-were Catholics and some were Protestants. (Laughter.) • What were we in this country? Were not we divided in oto religious opinions? ("Yes," and cheers.) And yet we were able to put an end to onr religious distinc- tions and to govern ourselves without the intervention of religion at alt. (Cheers.) To say, therefore. that Ireland could not govern herself because of her religious differences of opinion was to,ray what was simply rir:iculous. These excitable Protestants in the North said that if the Govern- ment was given:to the Irish people they would go in danger et their lives., (Laughter.) They were told this by the Ulster men who Inbebited the large cities on the north-east of Ireland, .and by the Protestants, who formed by fir the majority in-the north. And yet when they inquired in the south they: found that the Protestants, who formed the minority, never expressed a fear as to the Catholic ma- jority. They also found that many of the Irish leaders in the past had been Protestants, and Mr. Parnell was a Pro- teetaot. It was idle to cantend that this was a question be- tween Catholic and Protestants. (Hear, hear.) Each one had an interest in the matter, and he for one believed that if they restored that which the Irish held until they were robbed of, it by what Mr. Gladstone termed a nefarious transaction'—the Parliament of which they were once so proud, and which they could still make an organ for good in their country—they would make Irishmen have but oze object in view and one endeavour, namely, to restore and maintain friendliness and love between us and their own country. (Loud applause.) He was not ashamed to Bay that nothing had given him greater pleasure than to see the friendly feeling which bad been extended towards the great leader of the Irish peonle by the audiences that he had ad• dressed in England. Now was the time for the people, and if th.:A could carry this measure through the House of Core- morassby a.suliScient majority, the House of Lords would be wits in their generation and let the measure pass. He thought they had lived in hate and animosity long enotegh, awl. he hoped that Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchmen would he of one mind, and then the policy which Mr. Glad- stone had proposed would lead to the coaciliation of Deland and the establishment of a union of love between the two ceuntries. (Great cheering.) He came there in search of men, and it was-in Widnes, the home of busy industry, that he had found the men whom he mought--(eheere)e—a large indus- trious population living by the, sweat of their brow, all of whom possessed thanks to the untiring exertions and en- thueiastn of Mr. Gladstone—(cheers),--and in spite of the bitter opposition of Lord Salisbury and Mr_ Goselien— (groans)—now possessed the franchise and had the rieht an I were able to make their voices- heard in the Councils of the nation. (Cheers.) Heewas fighting this contest and would go to the poll as a Liberal. (Hear, hear.) He was faithful to the traditions of the-past. IT; was a Liberal in the same sense as those men were Liberal who broke the chains of the slave andestruck•the tax. off bread. (Cheers.) He veuerated the memories of, those Liberals of the past who waged an tincessing_wasfaree against monopoly and prieilege,and he asked them to return him to Parliament for that division in order that he might, according to his humble cipecity, continue- that contest. (Cheers.) They were sometimes told that the people often made mistakes. But he appealed to history, to wove that the mistakes and follies of the people. were wisdom—wiedom personified— crying aloud in the streets, as compared with the traditional folly and blind bigotry and obstruation of the House of Peers. (Cheere ) Years-out and, years in that enlightened assembly, who had enjoyed all the-advantages ot birth and education, had persistently, "done those things which they oeght not to have done, And, left undone those things they ought to have done" in this matter of Ireland. (Cheers.) • The record of the House of Lords was one of criminal stupidity. The wrong_ whion the Liberal party were at present engaged in, righting, and the crisis which they were now confronting, would not have existed and might have been spared us bad the House of Llards- only acted in vests gone ;by with common humanity,. (Hear, hear.) They had now I ' to censider what was- the immediate and present state of affairs. Were they to be governed by a junta composed of Tories and renegade,Libeeels?, (" No," and cheers.) Was Lord Salisbury to reign over them—(hooting)—by the Divine permission ,of Mr..Chamberla.in ? (Renewed hoot lug.) Was Lord Randolph Churchill to govern India— (gruans)—that vast province and integral portion of our empire— on the recommendation of John Bright? (Cries of "No.") This etnnatural alliance could not long last; the Liberal dissentients would soon End that the residuary legatee of Liberal dissension was Tory rele; they would find their labour hare been. spent in behalf of restoring to the country .a government which they were eager in sup- porting Mr. Gladstone in removing at the last election; and they would find the- nesepens which they once employed were now being turned against themselves. (Hear, hear.) For he confessedeae,a loyal Liberal, it had been with some malicious pleasure he had read recently in the Tory press the statement which ho- thought was perfectly just, that the victory which the Toeies fancied they saw before them was one wbich they alone would shaie; they told their Liberal dissentient friends who were voting for them that they must not imagine they were fighting the cause of Lord Harting- ton. "No," they said,. the "'victory isours ; Lord Salisbury is the man ;,you will- have to subject yourselves to his rule and support his, ministry." (Cries of "Never.") Were the Liberal electors of Widnes prepared to de that? (" No.") They !mew what Tory rule meant. (A Voice: "We know to °us sorrow," "Hear, hear," and cheers.) Having referred. to- the various Lineral measures of reform which were urgent, but which could not come to the front until the Irish qu.estion was settled, he said they might as well expect to see the roses growing on a heap of phosphate as to see the roses of Liberal legislation flourishing during the time the Tories were in power. (Cheers.) The British .lemocracy dentandea that they-should have an English Government capable, ready, and willing to deal with those reforms which were near and dear to them. They were not 'prepared to keep all those questions hungup for an indefinite period simply that one party or another might retain office. (Cheers). They meant to have these tenestions settled, and anything which stood in their way most be speedily re- moved. (Hear, hear.) He alluded in condemnatory teerne to the speech of Mr. Chamberlain at Cardiff, where he ap- pealed to. religious prejudice. He cried "shame" on Mr. Chamharlain—(booting)—who seemed to be coming cot in a most disgraceful light, throwing off those colcars Cf leberelism which he long wore. He seemed to be an Orangeman without even the excuse of the Orangeman hing fervent in his faith. Mr. Chamberlain bad as much religion in his composition as they would find La a free- thinking blackbeetle. (Loud laughter, and cheers.) To try, as he bad done, to play upon the religious feeling of others, and to try to make them feel an excitement which he was quite incapable of feeling, was not condtezt for a man to pursue at a great cris'et like this ; and he (Mr. Birrell) rei,iced to believe that neither the Protestant.) of Scotlend nor Wales would believe those slanders directed against their Boman Catholic knew-countrymen by Mr. Chamber- lain. (Cheers.) He felt pretty confident what the result of the electien would be so far as Widnes was concern. (Loud cheers.) He appealed not like his opponent to the cupdity, prejudice, and fears of the electors, but to their courage, their generosity, and their faith in God. (Cheers.) It was he who stood there as a Unionist candidate, not Me Moss, tor some time private secretary to Sir Richard Cross —(a laugh)—it was he (Mr. Birrell), and not his opponent. who wee pledged to do all that in hint lay not only to main• tam n and preserve the Union as it at present existed betweee the two countries, but to create a real union, one of hearts, of rei%le; teitbe aed affection—a union which would ie.

div.head: SPEECHES.
div.p: SPEECHES.

Mr. John Morley, addressing a meeting at Newcastle, on Saturday night, said he thought that a good many Liberal Unionists were abstaining from voting rather than Vote for Tory candidates. He wished the electors to note that in Manchester 21 000 veters—almost exactly half of the toral poll—went for self•government in Ireland. He 4lso pointed to the case of Leeds, and asked how me, who thought seriously of the future politics of the country were to get over facts of this kind. The artisans of Leeds and Man- chester were, he said, the men in whose hands the fortunes and the destinies and the future of the country must inevit- ably lie. _

Mr. Parnell was present at a meeting at Hackney on Saturday evening. He said the concession of 11.4nie Rule was enevitable, and whether it was conceded now by the Liberal party and Mr. Gladstone, or next year by Lord Salisbury and the Tory party, conceded it would be. The people must take care they did not let the Tory party twist into office, far they might depend upon it it was not coer- eion they would give when they got into office, but an Irish Parliament. The Irish party were not a bit afraid of Lord Sa.isbury on this question. He believed the Land bill was dead, and that they would not be troubled about it any more unless they let the Tories come into power. As to Mr. Bright's proposal to establish an Irish committee. so far from such a scheme enabling Parliament to deal with the affairs of the working people of the country, there would be ten times more obstruction than now.

Speaking on Saturday morning. at Stockport. Sir Horace Davey (Solicitor-General), one of the defeated candidates, said: It is too early to speculate upon what the causes of oar defeat may be, but if one of the causes be—and in MY opinion it will turn out to be the principal cause—that the Tory canvassers and the Tory csmiidates have endeavoured to inflame the race prejudice of the British workmen against his Irish fellow-workmen, I don't envy them a victory ob- tained by that means. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, the present members for Stockport are fond of calling themselves Unionists. (A Voice: " Paper." and laughter.) I wonder if it is proof of their claim to that title that they have ob- tained their seats at Stockport by inflaming sectarian big- otry between people professing different relieious creeds, and by appealing to the prejudice, or rather, I should say, creating prejudice in the minds of the British woraing-man against his fellow Irish labourer? Ishould rather say that they have sown the seeds of a jealousy, suspicion, distrust, and prejudice which did not exist—(hear, hear)—and I venture to say that those seeds will germinate and will grow into a plant which will not be very pleasing to our friends. (Cheers.) Lord Hartington addressed at meeting on Tuesday night in support of his candidature for the Rossenciale division of Lancashire, in the Co-operative Hall, Bacup. The hall was crowded. In the course of his speech the noble Marquis was frequently interrupted, and had to pause occasionally for two or teree minutes until order was restored. On a vote of confidence being called for, the show of hands was found to be in opposition to Lord Hartington. Mr. Newhigging addressed a crowded meeting at Rawtenstall on Tuesday night. Mr. Devitt, who spoke in support of a resclution, pledging the meeting to support Mr. Newbigging, said that between the concession of a domestic legislature such as would satisfy the national aspirations of the Irish people and a policy of repressive legislation there was no medium course which would settle the Anglo-Irish difficulty. The resolution was carried, with one dissentient. —On Wednesday Lord Hartinet on addressed a large meeting of electors at Waterfoot, held under tba presidency of Mr. E. Ashworth, of taehills. They were willing to give their attention to any well-considered measure for the extension of local solf.goveenment* consistent with the real unity of the empire and the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament. A resolution in support of Lord Hartington was passed. Mr. Newhigging also addressed a meeting at Crawshawbooth and was heartily received. The polling takes place to-day (Saturday).

div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

Soft and low.—A dissipated dude. The best thing out—An aching tooth. l'aons.—At the Zoological Gardens. She: "If the lion were to break out, which would you save first—the children or ma?" He: "Me." " Look here, judge," said the burglar; ain't so bad as you think I am. Only give me time and I'll reform." And the judge gave him fifteen years. A Szerous FAIILT.—At the bric-a-brac dealer's: "Oh! what a delicious little vase. It is very old, isn't it?" "Iso, madame, it was made recently." " Ab, what a pity! It is to beautiful." "I must have order in court," sternly commanded a justice of the peace; "I must and will have less noise and confusion here. I have already disposed of three im- portant cases without being eele to hear one word of the evidence." CONNUBIAL CHlllllS.—Httsband: How much do you lack of being a fool ?—Wife (sweetly and meaeuring the distance betweea them with her eye): At present I sin within about three yards of one. ()Ivrea To GT...assns.—Mies Keene: Why, Mr. Blondbang, what has caused this change in your appearance P—Mr. B.: I presume it's my glasses, doncher know? I've just begun to weah them.—Muss K. Well, you should always wear them. You've no idea how intelligent they make you look. I scarcely know you. "I can't get up early," said a poor victim to his doctor. "Oh, yes, you can," was the reply, "if you will only follow my advice? What is your hoar of rising?" "Nine o'clock." "Well, get up half an hour later every day, and In the course of a month you will find yourself up at four in the morning." A lady who bad just returned from her first visit to Italy was asked by a friend how she had been pleased with Venice. " Ob, very well on the whole !" she replied. "But there was one drawback. We had the misfortune to arrive just at the time of a serious inundation. The whole place was flooded !" Little Johnny has a habit of waking up in the middle at the sight and demanding something to eat. At last his ' mother said to him, "Look here. Johnny; I never want anything to eat in the night." "Well," rejoined Johnny, "I don't think I'd care much to eat anything either in the night if I kept all my teeth in a tumbler of water." div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1886.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Blackhurst, Jolly, Bonnell, Brown, Woods, , Isherwood, John Houghton, William Houghton, Hibbert, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Harrison, Strange, Eckersley, Gibson, Mackie, Wright, Forster, Kilshall, and J. C. Sutton (clerk), / HOUblit COMMITTED. The minutes of this committee were read, and stated that the dietary table revised by Dr. Spinks was produced and read. The committee found that the Dr. bad increased the quantity of tea and coffee for the use of the inmates taking tea and coffee by SI per cent and 50 per cent respectively. and they did net think this could meet with the approval of the authorities —Mr. Bows said the dietary table of that Werk house was much itt excess of the average of the dietary tables of Wier Unions. lie would recommend that they apply to the Local Government Board to suggest te them such a dietary table as they in their wisdom thought ap- propriate for the inmates of that bouse.—Mr. BLACKHURST asked how the matter of the dietary table had been brought forward.—Mr. Bnowa said that the inspector bad men- tioned it and Mr. haalehnrst, the auditor, had written to the Local Government Board about it. fie (Mr. Brown) found that ten years ago the dietary table was supplieel with permission to use it for twelve months only, but in coolie- quence of the old guardians leaving the Board and the new ones knowing nothing of the matter the thing bad gone on till this day. It WAS only the vigilance of the London authorities that had brought it to the front.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded Mr. Brown's proposal that the Local Government Board be applied to for a dietary tahle.—This was agreed to, and the minutes passed. THE sCHOoLS COMMIT-TM—A WANDERM. The Padgate Schools Committee reported that the boy, John Warrington, bad again absconded from the schools, and having been before Liverpool magistrates, was sent back to the school. The medical officer reportcd the health of the children to be excellent.--The Cuarumare' in moving' the confirmation of the minute', said that the lad Warring- ton was so mischievous that he was not fit to be with younger children, and it had therefore been resolved to put him uoder the charge of the tiilor at the Workhouse.—Mr. Joutty said that the lad told the inspector of polioeat Liverpool that he would soon be there again. The lad said that he rode to Liverpool on the buffer of a railway engine. —Mr. BROWN thought that was a bit of romance.—Tbe CLERK mentioned that Warrington had 'oeen deserted when an infant and brought to the we, khouse. It Was thought that he had been left by some gypsies, but they could not find out where he had been born.—The minutes were agreed to.
MANUFACTURERS OF DECORATIVE AND ART FURNITURE

SCHOOL YENS COMMITTER. The Committee reported that tees had been granted in 88 cases, 15 of which were new, and 73 old.—On the motion of Mr. BLACIEHURST the minutes were adopted. TUB WARRINGTON VACCINATION OFFICER. A copy of a letter sent by the Local Government Board to Mr. Holford, vaccination officer for Warrington and Latchford, was read. It stated that the Board had had under consideration the letter of Mr. Holford with regard to the arrears of vaccination in the district, and the Board learned that he.was employed as a commercial traveller. It appeared LO them that that fact was sufficient to account for the defective discharge of his duties, and they intimated that unless he was prepared to give up his employment AS commercial traveller, it would he requisite that he should resign his office as vaccination officer.—The CLIME said that all they could do would be to await the result —Mr. RATCLIFFE asked if it was necessary that Mr. liolford should give up all other employment.—The CLuttx said it was not, but the Local Governmeot Board evidently thought that a commercial traveller Was so much taken Dern his district that he could not attend to the duties of the office. —The subject then dropped. A DBILATYD ACCOUNT. A letter was read from the Local Government Board ad- verting to the appeal by Mr. Brown against the surcharge of the sum of £3 78 7d made by Mr. Hazlehurst, the district auditor at his audit of the Guardians' accounts for the half- year ended Lady Day, 1886. It appeared that the dates in the invoice of the goods supplied and work done in respect to which the sum in question was paid had been altered by the erasure of the month originally entered and the eubsti- tution of the word "June," but there was no evidence at present to show by whom the alteration was made, but the Beard would b• glad if the Guardians would investigate the matter and ascertain.—With regard to this matter the House Committee reported that it had bad the letter of the Local Government Board before it. The Master of the Workhouse (Mr. Mackay) explained that seeing that the account had not been rendered by Mr. Hedgcock in time he made the alteration eo as to save as he thought asy trouble as the work had been done and the money was due to Mr. trouble, CLARK said that was a matter be- tween the Local Government Board and Mr. Mackie, and ths matter then dropped. TUE BAND. isc. An application was read from Canon Dodd, Etretton, asking that the Board would again allow the school band to attend the annual school treat and sports. Granted —Mr. WOODS also called attention to the fact that the school trip was to be held next Thursday, and he invited as many of the Guardians to attend as possible. TEE CONDITION OF TEE TOWN. In reply to Mr. Harrison, Mr. Ilannotranz, relieving officer, said that the amount of out-dour relief at the present time averaged about .£5 a week-more than in the same period last year.—Mr. ileassasosr inquired if there seemed to be any material diminution of distress.—Mr. fisanoultrat was sorry to say that there did not; he had never before found It so bad at the time of this year.—The CHLIRMLN : From what I hear I do not think the public-house returns are any less.—Mr. 'TARSI:MYRNA said he did not think there had been much drunkenness in Warrington in connection with the. election. The relief cases were then proceeded with.
