_ THE WALTON COMMON FOOTPATH. Sir,—l eould like to call the attention of your readers, and particularly those who were interested in the contro- versy which took place in these cclumns some montlfs ago f:l,it the above subject, to the fact that for the last few months the footpath has heen impassable owing to its muddy con- dition. the tine weather that we have had for the last fortnight it still remains in much the Fame ' atato. I would like to ask the queition as to whether this ii entirely due to natural cauSes, or whether it is kept pur- posely flooded by interested parties with a view to suppres- ajng the public LAC of it. The latter seems to me to be the most probable cause, for I have made frequent use of the path to cross the commAn for the last five or six years, and this is the first year I hare found it impossible to cross with comfort.
Trusting that this will occasion some inquiry to be made into the matV,r,—l rermin yours resuectfully. • EDWARD CEIAPMAN.
A WORD TO LIBERAL UNIONISTS.

, Sir,—From the result of the elections so far as they have gone, Liberal Unionists, like myself, may derive a useful lesson. To understand this let us first of all consider what the aims and objects of Liberal Unionists are. Liberel Unionists do not, and in truth cannot, deny thatlrelend is /Suffering from political maladies which must have a Peet- inent of one kind or another. They did not differ from Mr. Gladstone because be proposed a remedy, lent because the remedy he proposed, in their opinion, was rash, inadequate, and one from which very pernicious consequences might spring. Hildmg that opinion, it was their duty in Parlia- ment to do what they could to prevent that remedy being applied, and it is now their duty in the conetituencies to 'do what they can to so constitute the new Parliament that their own proposals with regard to Ireland may be enferced with the greatest weight. And how can this best be done ? Clearly by balancing as far as possible the onpoeira• hosts of Miniaterialsts and Conservatives in the House of Commons, that neither may, in union with the Parnetlites dominate the House. By simply lessening the number of Ministerialists that are returned' the Liberal Unionists do not accomplish their purpose, for if so large a number of Consereatives are elected that, in combination with the Parnellites. they can pass any measure they like, the Liberal Unionists may find thernaelves out of the frying. pan into the fire. Such a combination is clearly one of the possibilities of the friture; the transactions between Lord Carnarron and Mr. Parnell will warrant us in assumirg that much at the very least. Now, keeping those considera- tions in mind the lesson which I said might be derived from the result of the elections so far as they have goes is this. It is now clear beyond doubt to my mind that the inis- terialists, even if combinA with the Parnellites, will not. he so numerous in the coming Parliament that they will be able to force any measure obnoxious to Liberal Uniooists through the House. But it is not so clear that the Conservatives, assisted by the Par- nellites, may not be numerous eneneh to do this. Therefore it is incumbent upon Liberal Unionists in consti- tuencies such as the Northwicb Division, which have not yet been polled, to keep their obj,ct clearly in view, and to vote accordingly. At first their object required that they, ahould do their best to prevent the Ministerial lets from be- ing too nnmerous ; now their object requires that they 'should seek to prevent the Conservatives from being too numerous. It was their proud boast that they preferred principle to their own party, they must now take care that they do not prefer a party which is not their own to the 'detriment of the principle they wish to see prevail. A LIBERAL UNIONIST.

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTION.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTION.

Sir,—Now that the Warrington Tories think there is no 'fear of the Irish Harp dropping out of the Brilsh Flg (as •if there ever was !) they have raised a span new fl4g in which the Harp is printed extra deep, and it has been float- 'lng from the fligstaff At the Tory Club since last week. "Where is Dr. Mackie this election ?" is the universal exclamation of WarrirgteniAns just now. Yes, "%' her Oh, where is he? "—Yours, &c., IQUIRER.

Sir,—Wartington has once more decided to be reprsvented by a Tory ; it has, by i:s choice, declared against progres- sive legislation and prefers that so far as this town is con- cerned the great question of Irish independence shall receive its quietus. But I vesture to assert that neither the man of their choca, nor the majority, has the power to stifle the aspirations of the lonst-soffering people of Ireland:

Freedom's hattte ones begun, Bequeathed from bleeding sire to son; Though baffled oft Is ever won. Now,sir, there has been a good deal of capital made out of ; the split in the Liberal party. Illnstrioos names like John Bright and others of the party of defection have laeen claimed and made as common as that fourth-rate pelitician (and Parnell named "political gutter sparrow.") Lsrd Ran- . dol ph Churchill. Cannot these Tories see the impossibility of welding together the various elements that compose the party of progress with the political dead-heads of the Tory party?• We, the Lih,rals and Radicals, are one, so far as agreeine, - to grant to Ireland some different system of government to the Dublin Castle Rule, and there can be no doubt • that cut of the many schemes proposed by our party for the settlement of this great question some plan will be adopted ' which shall have the approval of the Irish representatives. The desire to do justice to Ireland is acknrwledged by all men of advanced thought; the only difference is in the method. Now let its see if the Tories are prepared to do anything, but out again in force the policy of failure, viz. :—Coercion, a policy whose effect has been to alienate the aff-ctions of the Irish from the English people, a policy that has driven . away from their native land thousands of their race, c,rry- ing with them bitter recollections of oppression and wrong ; . 3 policy, which, while it has upheld the so-called rights of preperty. the greater part of which was obtained by fraud • and retained by force, has failed to recognise the right of the people to live upon the soil. Workingmen of Warrington. believe not the clap-trap of • rich Whigs and Tories, but look around you and see the effects of the evil government of Ireland in the overstocked labour market that you have to contend with. With Ire- land contented, declining industries would revive, and new ones he established, and so bring relief to the English workman. The character of an Englishman hap hitherto - commanded the respect of the civilised world; he has shed his blood and spent his money to free the slave from bnadag:e, and his sympathy has ever been on the side of the opnressed. ' Then why make an exception in the case of Ireland? Her cry for relief has been met in most instances by measures of repression. Remember, charity begins at home; these peo- ple are our people; they have fought with Us the world over. They have held the foremost positions in the Sta'e, and as a whole have been loyal ; and yet, forsooth, because .s few have been guilty of dastardly outraes, the whole race is to be condemned as one not fit to bs trastEd. Re- move the cause, and the effect will cease. „ Now history proves that a wrong Ge4:l.ernm-ent always finds' A vent fn murders arid Outrages, and I trust the elec- tors of Warrington at the next election, which cannot he far distant, will reverse the deciiiion arrived at. so as to he in the van and not in the rear in the settlement of the great question of self-gsvernment for the Sister Isle —Yours, . T. EDEN. • 53, Lythgoes-lanP, Warrington. AFT 1,11 THE BATTLE. Sir,—l can fancy how the Conservatives are latighin-, over theirVcrorv. If I happenefj, toogrie in chet:k, by any chance, to ha one who bellevea in "things as they , are," i als) should laugh, and should keep on swallowing the oysters jot long as,that poor gullible mortal, the work- jpran,lioUd be kind enough to procure them for me. , The dukes issue blank cheques, to be filled up to any

amount; Bedford, Westminster, Norfolk. Argyle, and a host of noble lords rally to the standard, and at once command the slavish adelation of a nondescript animal known by Ithe name of "a Conservative workirg-rnan." Don't cross the last line out. Mr. Elitor ; lam not in an ill temper. I know Home Rule is bound to come, and that soon, so that I can afford to keep cool. When application was made to the Duke of Norfolk by Mr. Mundella's agent for the loan of the Sheffield Corn Exchange, it was refused on the plea that "the present crisis is of such an extraordinary nature," and that the "building must be restricted to the use of the supporters of the Union of Great Britain and Ireland." This noble duke, who is so ably supported by the poor, helpless Tory work- ing-man, and whose brilliant effusions are to be read by every one, keeps in his own hands the whole of the Sheffield market tolls. If the • working-men wish to bold a meeting in the only open space in the town they must pay £3. Agriculturalists pay heavy tolls for merely taking their produce to the Great Northern Railway Station. The fact is, this noble patriot, the Duke of Norfolk, is receiving commerce. of the working classes to drive out of England its the help radea The stupidity and hostility of the upper classes causcs them to resort to such means to gain their ends, that one stands amazed at the blindness of the masses. No doubt can exist that the election through which we are scrambling will find us at its close very much mixed, but workmen sbould see that. as Mr. Gladstone states, if we "do not wish dukes and earls te over-rule the nation and wreck its fortuDes," we must cease to be gulled by their plausible tales of separation. No one can fairly say that Mr. Gladstone is at all timid, and yet he has found it necessary to forewarn the people that "men of outrage might supersede the Parliamentary Nationalists in case of serious delay." This indeed we must expect unless the wish of Ireland is graciousty responded to. The Liberal patty in Warrington differs very little from the Liberal parties in other towns. All have an up-bill fight; all have the same influences to conleod against. For a number of weeks money and beer have been within the reach of men who are usually known as loafing idlers. Organisation with the Tories has now become a fine art ; legal bribery is practised the year round. Their agenti in the polling booths openly state that at the last election they received 7e 6d per day and refreshments, and at the present election they receive lOs per day and find their own refresh- ments. S:avcely a Tory worker but chaffs the Liberal worker with working for a poor party. This has been done to such an extent, that Liberal workers have been beard to declare they would work no longer. We must have canvassing done away with, meg must be prohibited from dragging up their fellow-teen, thrusting them into the booth and shouting out "go in there and vote for Gilbert." Cases Celine under my own eyes of men brought up by publicans forgetting the candidate's name, and bawling out that of the publican's instead. My own opinion is that Sir Gilbert represents the well-to-do classes and the illiterate drunken class. Another class may be added, and it is, I think, the most dangerous class—that is the large number of people directly or indirectly connected with Corporation•officialdom ; men whose sole object is spending/ratepayers' money, and who consider the'present state of things the best that could be devised. CLIFFORD DIX.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The ordinary monthly meeting of this body was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present—The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair; Aldermen Web- ster, Chandley, Holmes, Davies, and Burgess; Councillors Sutton, Dr. Mackie, Wright, Francomb, Jolley, Greenall, Taylor, Fleming, Ashton, Bolton, Hutchinson, W. Pierpoint, and Tinsley; Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Mr. Longdin (borough surveyor), and Mr. Chorley (borough treasurer). CORRESPONDENCE. The MAYOR said that since the Council sucaraanses were issued he had received a communication from Dr. 'Mackie saying that three months ago he was honoured with a request from a number of ratepayers to present a memorial referring to a late erection in Buttermarket-street. He (the writer) was then informed that it would be referred to the Sanitary Committee for their consideration. Last month he inquired alyant it, and was officially informed that the me- tnorial had not been received by the committee. He now wished to ask what had become of the memorial, as he felt hound to inform the gentlemen wbo signed it what had been its fate. The Mayor, after reading the letter, said that probablysAlderman_Burg.ss wauld give an answer. . . .
AlClerman BURGESS : I do not think it should be thrown npon me. That memorial was addressed to you and the Council.

The MAYOR said that he had instituted an inquiry into ths fate of the memorial, which was now in his possession. He had been inform,A on undoubteJly goad authority that it was taken to the Sanitary Committee, and eras delivered. He was further told that Alderman Burgess Was preseut at the time. Whether his information WAS correct or not, of course he could not say. Alderman BURGESS: That is so, Mr. Mayor. The subject then dropped.
WATCH COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were adopted on the motion of the MAYOR. seconded by Alderman WEBSTER, were not of public interest.

div.head: FINANCZ COMMITTBS.
div.p: FINANCZ COMMITTBS.

The minutes were approved the motion of Councillor GEEENALL, seconded by Alderman WnstsTaa. They con- tained a reeolution that the sum of thirty guineas be voted to the Borough Auditors for auditing the accounts of the Borough Treasurer for the year ended 25th March, STREET ThipROVEmENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that the following Wails be approved :—Plan of new entrance gateway to premises in Golborne-street, for Mr. Edward Connor; of alterations to property in Bewsey-street, for Mr. Thomas Forster ; of warehouse, for Messrs Joeeph Croefield and Sons ; of house in Longferd-street, for Mr. George Sheldon : of new street, leading from Arpley-street, for Messrs. J. White, Maclver, and Co. ; and of seven cottages in Cartwright-street and oetock-street, for Mr. C. Longsbaw. The committee re- solved that the sum of £2OO he paid to Messrs. Skelton for a strip of land in front of premises proposed to be erected in Horsemarket-street, the premises to be set back to a line drawn from the corner of the Old Coffee House to the corner of the B:ue Bell Inn. Councillor SUTTON proposed, and Alderman CHANDLEr seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Macre moved as an amendment that the minutes be passed with the exception of the resolution referring to the purchase of land in Horeemarket-street for £2OO The time for widening. Horeemarket-street was so remote, he said, that be did" not see any advantage in buying the pro- perty at present. '1 rade was in anything but a flourishing condition, and there were many who felt the depression. One branch of trade appeared to he in a very critical post- tion, and that branch bad since 1853 been a very prosperois one. There waa Bridge-street still on the la-anda of the Street Improvement Committee, and there were other things on the bands of the Corporation, including the Gas Works. He thought that the proposed expenditure should be deferredl until a more prosperous time. The amendment was not seconded. Councillor MACKIE expressed his pleasure at the oppor- tunity of purchasing the land having beri taken. It was the first etep te what in the long run must be a considerable improvement in the town, and was also a necessary one. Councillor JoLLI4T thought that the purchase was a very judicious one. Councillor SvrroN said that he was satisfied that no one looking at the plan, or the property its-of, would have any difficulty in coming to the conclusion that it would be very wise to acquire the property. The minutes were confirmed.

Aldirman BurtoEss proposed the confirmation of the minutes. The deputation mentioned in the minutes, he said, found that the material they had at Longford was capable of being turned intO a very useful product very much to the interests of the borough. They bad a large amount of debris, the result of the burning of the Wa,te refuse taken there. They took to Longford from 170 to 180 tons a week, and they would have a renidual of froin 50 to 80 tons. It was proposed that this residual, instead of cost- ing £l5O a year to get off the premises, should be ground, and by the addition of a given portion of cement, one-fifth or one-sixth, to produce flags or tiles, to lay down floors in hack-yards, flags in the streets, and anything of that des- cription. There was a floor now being pnt down at the northern dept in Lythgoe'e-lane entirely of the material to which he had referred. It was being m anufactured by themselves, and they would let the Council know what it cost in proportion to what it would have cost had they used the material they would otherwise have been compelled to use. (Hear, hear ) The machinery that would he required , would be the moulds, in which the flags would he made, consistine. a timber about four feet square in proportion to the size, and about the depth of the flag—two or two and a half inches. That was the only machinery, unless they had 1 a pan for mixing the material. Councillor SuTroet seconded the proposition that the , minutes be confirmed, which was carried. At a meetin;,-;:f—the -a-b—eve comMittee held on the 28th Jane, the "Chairman of the Finance Committee called at- tention to a report of the Elective Auditors, relative to the payment of the sum of £6 14s 6d, the expenses of the Mayor in attending the Jubilee of the Association of the Municipal Corporations in October last, and, cn referring to the minutes of this committee, it was found that the Mayor was duly appointed by the committee to attend the Jubilee." _ _
The minutes were approved on the motion of the Neras, seconded by Councillor FRANCOMB. GAS COMMITTILL—THS dAS WOUZS

The Gas Ceminittee recommended payment of accounts (including £5,670 13s for half-year's annuities and interest), amounting to £6,729 is. The report of the committee for the past year was submitted for approval. In presenting the report the committee reminded the Council that the past year had been ode of unprecedented difficulty it, the management of gas works over the whole kingdom. The continued depression in trade and the consequent diminu- tion in the increase of consumption, together with the great and rapid fall in vales of the residual products, bad each oontributed to the grave anxieties of the situation, and in many places an advance in the price of gas became ab- solutely necessary. The committee, however, up to the present time had not resorted to that expedient, but had endeavoured by the exercise of the strictest care and economy to make all ends meet without increasing the cost to the consumer, and the subject is still engaging their attentive consideration. In the mid-winter of 1877, when the works were taken over by the Corporation, the maxi- mum output of gas in 114 hours was 663,000 cubic feet, and the maximum storage power was 600.000—the annual make being 128,284,000 cubic feet. In 1881, immediately prece- ding the opening of the new lorks at Longford, the annual quantity made was 164.42,500 cubic feet, being an increase in round numbers of 36i millions. The works in Mersey- street had thus become altogether inadequate to meet the increasing demand. The completion ot the works at Long- ford, however, had not only removed these complaints, but had proved of considerable financial benefit to the Corpora- tion—thus, in the case of coal and cannel the saving was 1.350; in coke £283; in tar £6l; and in the saving of labour £242. The reduced working expenses and the increased facilities for gas manufacture had resulted in the saving of upwards of aOO per annum cf•expenses, an amount which would more than cover any extra charges consequent on the temporary duplication of the works, and whicn in future years would be still further developed. It was to be *rider- stood that all future extensions would be made at Longford, but there being comparatively little at the Mersey-street works that could be transferred, their abandonment while in good working order, and the entire removal of the plant to Longford would have involved a sacrifice and loss too serious to be contemplated, but as they become worked out and useless, removal to Longford would gradually take place. Tne increase in the manufacture since taking over the works is 64,311,300 cubic feet, or 27,612,000 beyond the total generating power of the Mersey-street works. They had taken into consideration the question of undertaking the manufacture of sulphate of ammonia and Mr. Paterson had devised a temporary arrangement of plant at the Long- ford works. The manufacture was commenced in May taste and the result has proved to be eminently satisfactory. after purchasing the atnmoniacal liquor from the Corpora- tion at its full market valve, and the payment of all other expenses connected with the working, there remained a profit of £479 12s 11d. Thus, instead of realizing £748 19s 4,1 only, by the sale of the liquor to a contractor, there was plus £479 12s lid, equal to £1,223 12s 3d, as the result of our manufacture. The reduction in the value of tar had been remarkable, and no very satisfactory cause had been a.signed for the extraordinary fall in its products. They found it more profitable to consume it in furnaces for beat- ing the retorts instead of coke, and the success achieved by using the, tar as a heating agent was highly satisfactory. The profit and loss account for the past year presented many features of importance. There was a saving in the coal and cannel used and a small increase of about seven million cubic feet in the make of gas, but the residuals have only realized £4,786, instead of £8,202 as for the previous year, and .£7,040. for 1883. Besides this loss of revenue, the increae Aexpenditure had been very considerable during the pstiOe year, arising from the testoration and re•distribu- Lion of mains, paving of Gas-street, renewal of steam boilers, lea, whielr might be considered to some extent normal. The total cost of gas for the year had been 2s ' 9•21 d, or about ld pee 1,000 cubic feet in excess of the pre- VW. us year. Alderman HaLME3 proposed the adoption of the minutes of the committee, briefly; referring to the report of the work of the committee, and Alderman Winsren seconded the motion.

Alderman BURGESs said that it was very laudable and desirable tnat every economy should be used in the melting of Ras, but last week it ceme under the notice of the Sani- tary Committee net the Gas Committee were breaking the law ey producing a dense.hlack smoke. It would, perhaps,. be their painful duty to summons the Gas Committee- before the maeistratee. (Laughter.) Alderman Devies said that when the gas works were purchased, Mr. Fell, Alderman Holmes, and himself pre— pared a scheme of the prospective working of the property, and be thought if that scheme had been followed out the gis works would have been a better success than they were. He asked when a plan showing the course of the gas mains, the appearance of which had been long expected, was going to b 3 laid on the table, and was informed in reply that it , was in course of completion, and would shortly be ready her the use of those who might wish to see it. Councillor DIXON asked how was it that the town waS in darkness on the evening of Walking Day? Alderman BURGESS said that at the Borough Court on the morning following Walking Day Mr. Hunt told him. that he had sent to the Gas Works, and had received a reply from the person in charge that Mr. Patterson, the manager, had given instructions that the gas should not be laid on that night. If the reason was that of economy, it was one that should not be put into practics, as the gas should be lit during the night as a means of' protection rather than say- tbing.elee. It was false economy. The 'MAYOR said that on the morning following Walking Day he rece,ved a note from Mr. Hunt informine him that not one of the public lamps waS lighted on the previous night, the streets being in darknese. The police on duty during the night had -to keep more in the centre, in the street!. instead of being spread over the whole borough. It tees understood that a gentleman in connection with the Cie's Committee, holding an important position, suggaeted tha?,:as"the nights were light there was no necessity for lighting the gas, which would result in a saving. Counpilior W. PIEAPOINT said that in the report the total quantity of gas made was stited. They would render the report very complete if they would also state the amount of miftone of feet that they sold. He had no idea that they sold rather more gas than they made. ,(Laughter.) Alderman HoexEs: The amount we make and the amount we sell are furnished in the tabulated report. With regard to the gas not being turned on, it was a matter ,which shall not occur again. The minutes were then coxfirtned, and the meeting shortly afterwards ternanatecl.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF NORTEIWICII
div.p: REPRESENTATION OF NORTEIWICII
DIVIsION. THE POLLING ARRANGEMENTS. _ _

The following are the polling- --arrangements for Runcorn and the immediate neigh bourhoqg : RUNCORN SOUTH POLLING DISTRICT.—The poll- ing place is at the Board Schools, Greenway-road, Runcorn, and voters in the townships of Clifton and Runcorn, and numbered K 1 to K 450 poll at No. 1 stution,-and voters in the townships of Runconi and Weston, and numbered K 451 to K 913, poll at No. 2 station. _

RUNCORN NORTH POLLING DISTRICT.—In this district there are four polling stations at the Mar- ket Hall, Bridge-street, Runcorn. Voters numbered J 1 to J 630, polling at station No. 1; those numbered J 531 to J 1,056 polling at station No, 2; those num- bered J 1,057 to J 1,621 polling at station No. 3; and those numbered J 1,622 to J 2,773 polling at station No. 4.

ASTON-BY-SUTTON Polling District, for Totem whose qualifications are described as being situate in the townships of Aston Grange, Aston-by-Sutton, with Middleton Grange, Dutton, and Sutton, and whose numbers in the register are from Al to AllB inclusive. The place of polling is at the Board School, Aston.

HALroN Polling District, comprising the town- ships of Halton, Norton, and Stockham, and the register numbers D 1 to D 251. The polling place is at the Parochial School, Halton. The poll opens at eight o'clock on Tuesday morn- ing, and closes at eight p.m. In consequence of the riot that took place at Northwich on the last occa- sion, the -votes will not be counted until Wednesday morning. MEETING OF IRISHMEN LAST. NIGHT.

Last night a meeting of the Irish electors in the Runcorn polling district was bald in Bethesda Schoolroom. The room was filled to its utmost capacity, and the proceedings were very enthusias- tic. Dr. O'Keeffe, of Widnes, presided, and on the platform were several prominent local Irishmen and English Liberals. The CHAIRMAN, who bad a cordial reception„said they were met at a time of political excitement. If it had not been fur a number ef Judas Iscariots amongst Mr. Gladstone's chief supporters, he said distinctly that there would not have been an election to-day. 'taw, hear.) He had just come from Widnes, where an exciting contest was being carried on in a friendly spirit between the Liberals and the Conservatives. He must matte a remark about the Liberal Unionists. Very few of thew dared to show their faces. (Appl-aise.), It was not bemuse they were afraid, hut because they were ashamed. (Applause ) Ha denied that if Ireland got H,otne Rule they would want separation. hear.) He was authorised to say as any n3ember of Parliament that Ireland had no wisSand no desite, in the present, or woulal, have in the fltture, to separate herself from this grand Empire. (Cheers.) Mr. Fox, of Widnes, moved—" That this meeting is of opinion that the establishment of an Irish Parliament would in no way imperil the supremacy of the Crown, the integ- rity of the empire, the security of private propertyoe the protection of the Protestant minority; and recognieee in the Home Rule proposals of the Right Hon. W. E. (ad- stone a righteous intention to do justice to Ireland on the basis of conciliation instead of coercion." (Cheers.) Mr. Tox said a nation was not made of territory, but of men and' women. The present connection between England and Lae- land was not a union and never had been. It 11733 disunion. (Chreere.) If Home Rule were granted, instead of mom money being taken out of Ireland there would be moae money spent there, more work for the people, who would 2 stay at home contented, and the Eeglish labour markets would not be flooded with competitors to the semis extent as they were now. (Cheers.) In conclusion M. Fox appealed to all present to vote for Mr. Brunner,. who would do his best to improve the condition of the villages and towns, and who would devote • his time and energy for 'the benefit of the working classes and the masies of In-lend. (Cheers.) Mr. T. WILLIAMSON seconded the resolutiOn in a brief speech, and dealt with the allegation that Home Rule meant sepafation, which be denied and disproved.. Mr- MASON BARRY, a representative of the Irish Protes- tant Home Rule Association, supported the resolution. There was, he said, no cause for fear on the part of Irish Protestants of their Roman Catholic brethren. He geoted I.tters and gave facts to prove that these fears were ground- less, and said perfect confidence exilted on the part of Protestants with regard to :heir Catholic brethren. (Ap- please.) 'llse resolution was carried unanimously.

Mr. H. HILL proposed 'That this meeting approves of the consistent support given by our late member, J. T. Brunner, Esq • to the Irish policy of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, and pledges itself to use every legitimat4 means to secure his rout') to the next Parliament. (Cheers.). Mr. Hill criticised the Irish speakers at the Unionist meetlng on Thuredby evening., and caused much laughter by his witty remtrks.
Mr., Wo. D. I:vivo seconded the resat utio.n. which was carried! with «n • h CliaBo3. - MR. ROBERT VERDIN AT RUNCORN.

A meetipg of the supporters of Mr. Robert 4ir.erdinethe Unionist candidate, was held in the Public Hall on Thurs- day evening. The building. was well filled, the audience in- cluding many ladies. The proceedings were conducted on the whole quietly and peaceably. One old gentleman was , " turned' out," and when, Mr. Richardson was reading. hiee speech eronsiderahle interruption took place by some yonthse at the end of the room. Ml. Evans, agent air Richard.' Brooke; preeided, aid on the platform were the RemWePres-,1 ton, Reer R Edwards, Rev _Dr V White. Dr MeDougall, Messrs- Robert Verdin, W if Verdin, Goret (.reiverpool), W Sheppard Allen, • W Shore, Alfred Backe Thomas Ward (Forttowich), W, Whittaker, John Brunner, J;P, 7red Cooke, Jr B Cooke (Winsford), and Williena Bancroft', Dr Joyneore, _W Deakin, W Patin (all of Northwich)e J. G Knight, .I Oekleston, Salkeld. Summerfield, Guest, F Samene, W H Rogerson, J W Lightburn, J Burton, atc. Mr. J. H. Cooke read several letters of apology. The first was from Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., who hoped the Union- ist candldete would be returned. Dr. Robinson, of the Belve- dere, declared OW he should vote against the Gladstonian candidate wherever he had the opportunity. Mr. Beckett Chedwick, J.P.. hoped the Northwich Division would fol- low the good example of Chester, and assured Mr. Verdin of his sympathy and support. Dr. S:eele wrote in somewhat similar terms. Mr. Charles Haelehurst, J.Pe explained that he could not be present to take the chair that evening, and added that his views Coincided with the 'Unionist can- didate and the Conservative party generally. He wished Mr. Verdin every success. Mr. Peter Rylands (whose name was received with loud cheers) regretted that he could not sssist Mr. Verdirt, and he Sincerely tweed that the Union- lets of Northwicn Division would make every effort to return, Mr. Verdin. Conservatives and Liberals might well sink all minor diffierences of opinion, and he- trusted that, as in oilier parts of the country, united action wouldeerove successful in the Northwich Division, and that the representative of the division would add another, vote against Mr. Gladetone's dangerous policy. Other letters. were den received. The CHAIRMAN, aiter a few brief remarks, called upon Mr. Receettus, who moved "that this meeting, considers that in legislation relating to Ireland the following prin- eiplee mese be maintained: let, the supremacy of the len- nerial Parliament; 2nd, the maintenance of the Union 3rd, the protection of the Irish Loyalists."' (Cheers.) Speaking as an Irish Loyalist from the south, Mr. Richards said that the Home Rule Bill if it were passed would be their death knell. (Hear, hear.) He had been much struck with the cool way in which the leader of his natty, Mr. Glacietoie, regarded the Irish nation. He entirely. left out, of sight about two millions of the five millions of the Irish netion. When Mr. Gladstone and his followers spoke of the. Irish nation they simply meant the Nationalist party, or as they in Ireland preferred to give them their real name, the IWeel Party, for rebels they were and rebels they would he, as England would find to their cost some time. (Cheers.) Mr. GORST, a Conservative of Liverpool, secended the re- sol aticin.

Mr. SREPPLIID Amen*, formerly mx: for Newcaatlee under-Lynre in supporting the resolutiou, said he was one of .Ibetfiret members in the House of Commons that spoke neainet Mr. Gladstone's Bill, and he voted against it. For 20 years he had been a consistent supporter of Mr. Glad- stone. He supported the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and the Irish Land Bill; but when Mr. Gladstone brought forward the Irish Government Bill, he'fah that he should be false to him convictions andffalse to his country if he voted for it. He hardly knew what Dish grievance there was at the present time. (Eleareheer, and cheers.) The Rev. Dr. Winne said he appeared before them as an Ulster Presbyterian. (Applause:), The grievances of Ire- land were not the laud laws, were Rot the land- lords, however bad, were not Unequal laws, and were not cauteel by density of population.. The one great evil of Ireland was want of credit and want of capital. He did not care what any man said to the contrary, the object of the promoters of Home Rule was :—First, the total, absolute, awl complete separation of Ireland from England ; second, the expuleion from Ireland of every man, woman, and child of the Saxon race. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They bal been told that they were a nation of monvrels, that tbey were not Irish, that their grandmother wee a daughter of John "Xnox, and that their grandfather was a druitner in Cromwell's army. (Laughter.) He was pre,ud ef his genealegy—(cheers)--and so long as there wee the blood of John Xnox in their veins, and so long as. there was the bone and muscle of Oliver Cromwell in them they would never submit to tyranny like that. (Cheers ) The resolution was carried with only a few dissentients, Nr lionzter VETAITN., who was received with cheers mei hooting, said the resolution had been proposed by a loyal Irishman from the south, seconded by a Coneervativeesup7 ported by a Libra), and again supported by an Ulster Pres- byterian. He appeared before them that evening as a Liberal Vnioniet—(cheees)—and he &eked for their support in order that, in conjunction with othertre be might work to- wards the accomplishment of the .objects mentioned' in the resolution. He was pleased to find that the spiritof patriot- ism bad made such rapid strides in Runcorn during the last fortnight. (Cheers.) Tears ago, a prejudice existed in the minds of Englishmen against Irishmen, and be regretted to say Abet Englishmen had made bad laws for 4teland. That within the last 20 or 30 years their Jegislitors had legislated for Ireland, in a generous spirit, and had given quite as much atteutiou to the affairs of that etrautry is to tiose ot,j

England. Ireland had been granted Dieestabliskment, and the Roman Catholics in no country enjoyed gi eater privi- leges than did the Roman Catholics of Ireland. They had perfect religious liberty. They bad also given a land law system which vras much superior to the system enjoyed by the English farmers. He contended that they would not hear a single complaint from English farmers if they had such a perfect system as that of Ireland. The passing of the Home Rule Bill would de- stroy confidence in the country. It would destroy confidence in India, and the result would be that the Hindoos would also expect separation. Russia was on the borders of India, and on the passing of the Houle Rale Bill it would be an easy thing for that Power to send intriguers to endeavour to disturb their subjects in India against the rule of the Imperial Parliament. He appealed to them to be patriotic enough to support the unity of the Empire. (Cheers.) On the motion of Mr.W. J. Shore, seconded by Mr. Rich- ardson, and supported by Mr. Hopkinson, of Manchester, and Mr. Thomas Ward, of Northwich, a resolution to support Mr.Verdin was carried, about half a dozen bands being held up against.
The proceedings concluded in the customary fashion. iIEETINCi, AT ACTON BRMGE.

Mr. Verdin afterwards aelift:e-s;e-ti a meeting at Acton Bridge, at which there was a good attendance, amongst tbe audience being a number of Irish labourer& Mr. E. L. Clarke occupied the chair, and there were also present, be- sides the candidate. Mr. J. Verdin, Mr. W. IL Verdin, Mr. J. H. Cooke, Mr. F. Cook, Mr. Burton, Mr. T. Ward, Mr. J. 'lowland, Mr. E. Gandy, and others. Mr. 'l'. Ward maraed a resolution condemning Home Mule in terms similar tathat given above, and Mr. J. H. Cooke said as a friend of' Ire- land, and one who had travelled over the greater part of the country, he had great pleasure in seconding the resolh- tion which had been moved by Mr. Ward. The thing he wanted them to think about was this: they had been ap- plauding very mnola that night the•7ritne Minister of Eng- land, the gentleman who had imprisoned so many of their fellow-countrymen during the last two or three years. He never knew they approved no much of what he had done. (The Irishmen at this point left the rcomin a body.) He did not know that anything he could have said would have had such an effect upon them. (Laughter.) A gentleman had said that night let them try Home Rule. That was a very good suggestion no doubt, if they could possibly believe it would do good; but before they began to try experiments they sl•ould think what the effect of thew. would be. They had already tried two or three experimenta In Ireland—the disestablishment of the Church. the Land Acts, ix., but that country was 8.4 far from being satisard'ais ever she was. (Cheers.) The bills which had been passed by Mr. Gladstone had had the contrary effect to what was intended, and instead of the country being better for them it was worse. That being so, be :toped that gentle- men who wished them to try Home I%le would admit that it would be dangerous to attempt another experiment —that of granting a separate Parliament to people who were not disposed to be on the most friendly terns with England. (Cheers.) His opinion was that it would. be a most disastrous 'experiment, 'oath for Eng- land and Ireland. (Cheers.) The resolution we, thee put to the meeting slid carried unanimously.— Mr. R Verdin, who was cordially received, then addressed( the meeting in similar terms to those he made use of at Little Leigla..—Mr. James Burton proposed, and Mr. M. Gandy seconded, a resolution in favonr of the carciidature of Mr. R. Verdin, and on the motion being put to the meet- ing it was unanimously carried with acclamation.—The meet- ing aftelwaeds closed with the singing 0, the INAtiuma/ Anthem.

div.p: THE REPRESENT ATIoN OF WIDNES
DIVISION.
NOMINATION DAY AT WIDNES.

A stranger entering Widnes yesterday; would never have imagined that a contest frauglffi -with gteat results and viewed with excitement by the whole of its pOpulation was proceeding,. TN-town ' was as quiet as OD any, ordinary day.:, The vehicles engaged in the election, not very nuraereussort either side, were scarcely to be distinguished from those engaged on the usual errands of; blisine3si, while the customary avocations of the inhabitants were pursued as usual. A glance at the walls of the ad- vertising stations might have dissipated- the ignor- ance. Birrell and Moss were disOtyed with, as much profusien as though they were talismanic charms; but the legends attached were vastly different in their colour and meaning. !‘Justice fOr Ireland" and "The true Union of the Empire" were, of course. prominent features in- Mr. BirreWS mural ' literature, but beyond these were numerous pos- ters calling attention to his claims on,the suffrages of the electors., " Birrell ,and popular control of , the liquor traffic," "Birrell and reform of the land laws,' and other motteB of the LiberalirefOrna were displayed broadcast, along with, extracts from Mr. Gladstone' s eloquent speeches on, the question of the hour. • _ _ .

Ye§terday morning a placard 'signed "A member of the C.E.T.5.," was put forth to ,estranige the tem- perance vote from Mr. Birrell by- attempting to show that the Liberals, with .Mr. Gladstone at their head, had been the enemies., of, teetotal reform, and that, on the contrary, the TCtr,iBB . had been its warmest advocate. In reply, an "appeal to the workers in the great cause of-Wmperance " was is- sued, and asked them not to, be-led astray bpany party feeling that ''.as not consistent with their temperance principles; but votefor the party who would, support popular control of the 'drink traffic. Temperance men 'Ncere implbred to vote for Mr. Bind!, because he.had promised to use his Utmost endeavours not only to advocate Sunday closing; but, also to help to cam? Local Option, The Union Jaclt was the most profuse and imporbant emblem of file Conservative caadidate.. Every advantage, how- ever, was taken of the letters addressed to hiimby Mr. senr., and Mr. John Brock, two gentlemen of position and wealth who have timid themselves unable to agree with the Home Rule proposals, and have gone over to the enemy-I, and they were Pbtcarded all over the division iu large numbers.

Since he was accepted as the Liberal candidate three weeks ago, Mr: Binell has visited every part of the division, and he has worked unciesingly to gain the:votes of the electors. The people of Wid6. nes have had the opportunity of listening to his eloquent tones on no less than three °evasions, and on each occasion he has been received with a cordiality and enthnsiasin that, has shown how, greatly he is appreciated. His view's on the Irish question have been given with no uncertain somd. The wrongs a Ireland have been displayed lay him in their true light, and his appeals for justice and love have been made with ap eloquence and power that have ever called forth a hearty response. .."(1 THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH trislON OV THE COUNTY OF OHEEITER. large and influential body of Unto.. ;hers jonlst. I have pleasure in My Liberal prin.., " but all other considerations and ervient to, and overehadowed by, the ere the country, namely. the supremacy of t.. 'Dement, the maintenance of the Union between Greau - and Ire- land, and the protection of the Irish Loyalists. The serious effect the measures proposed by Mr. Gladstone will have upon this country and upon Ireland has not yet been realized. If such proposals are carried out. I believe that the wealth and capital invested in Ireland will leave that coun- try. stagnation of trade will follow, by which the labour mar- ket in England will be overwhelmed, to the great and serious detriment of our werking classes. It has often been stated that there is no intermediate course between the Government proposals and the policy of Coercion, yet it must be obvious that the support accorded to Mr. Glad- stone's Bills undoubtedly meant coercion of the worst charac- ter, namely, the coercion of the Loyalists of Ireland. The Protestant communities of Ireland, comprising the Episcopalians, the Presbyterians, the Wesleyans. the Primi- tive Methodists, and the New Connexional Churches, have shown their sense of the injustice sought to be committed by condemning the Irish Bills. These proposals wuuld never have bath submitted for con- sideration if Mr. Gladstone had been returned to power with a sufficiently large Liberal vote to support him against the vote of the Irish Party. We are, therefore, undoubtedly yielding to a class of agitators whose only desire is to injure England, and who have been aided in obtaining their present place and power by a system of terrorism and crime unknown in any other part of Her Majesty's dominions. Their object is not Union, but Eieparation. • I can, therefore. confidently promise that if you slormid honour me with your confidence I shall strive to the utmost of my power to resist any measures which te,d to destroy tha su- premacy of the Imperial Parliament or injure the Union now existing between the two countries. Whilst adopting that course, I shall always be ready to assist in removing any real grievance of which the Irish people may have just Cause to complain. I would govern Ireland by the same laws as those which govern my fellow-electors in this Division, but we must first maintain law *sad order, and secure to life and property that value which every civilized Biate ensures for the commu- nity. I tee carcely add that it will ever be my desire to pro- mote the interests of every industry in this Division, whether agricultural. commercial, or manufacturing, and this as well for employed as employer, so that the depression now unfor- tunately existing may be effectually removed. To this end the establishment of a settled and stable Govern- ment will best contribute. I am, Gentlemen, Your obedient cervant, NOBERT VERDIN. The Brockhurst. Northwich, 21st June, 1886.
